items.title: The Backlash Against Data Centers
items.description: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings , watch full episodes here , or listen to the weekly podcast here . On a special edition of Washington Week With The Atlantic , the Atlantic staff writer Josh Tyrangiel joined for a discussion about the future of AI and what, if anything, the U.S. government plans to do to address the rapid development of the technology. Across the country, massive data centers are being built, and they’re “landing themselves without a whole lot of conversation” in American towns, Tyrangiel said last night. “It’s natural that all the fears about AI—about it taking your jobs, about it rendering human beings obsolete, about the values it changes—all are focused on” these data centers, he argued. “And politicians have been incredibly late to wake up to the anger around AI.” “I don’t think people believe that they are going to partake in the wealth that comes from data centers in their community,” Tyrangiel continued. “Every community is going to make different choices, but what I’m sensing is that, particularly from Trump, the politics are out of line with where people are.” Watch Tyrangial’s full conversation with the editor in chief of The Atlantic , Jeffrey Goldberg, here .

items.title: Rediscover the Ordinary
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. A strange thing happens when you see something every day: Eventually, you stop seeing it. A building you once admired becomes part of your commute. The trees on your block become background. Your favorite coffee mug becomes something you reach for without thinking. This tendency has been compounded by a culture that encourages us to move through life as efficiently as possible: We follow directions instead of wandering, put in headphones instead of listening to the world around us, and fill spare moments by looking at our phone. As Ian Bogost writes in a new article, we’ve become so focused on making life more productive that we risk treating the present as mere preparation for whatever comes next. Wonder can interrupt that habit, Bogost argues—not just the kind inspired by mountains or sunsets, but the kind available in ordinary things. He describes noticing the warmth of a coffee mug, the crunch of gravel underfoot, and the clever engineering of a toaster. Wonder, in this sense, is less about seeking out extraordinary experiences than it is about paying close attention to the ones already around you. On Finding Wonder The Missing Ingredient of Modern Life By Ian Bogost Why we need wonder Read the article. The Ordinary Miracle of Existing By Alan Lightman Being alive at all is the most extraordinary stroke of good luck any of us will ever experience. Read the article. The Cult of Delayed Gratification Is a Lie By Ian Bogost The sensory enchantment of everyday life can upend the bland monotony of our overly optimized, anodyne world. Read the article. Want more wonder in your days? Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary , Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid. Still Curious? The quiet profundity of everyday awe : That feeling—of being in the presence of something vast—is good for us. And, counterintuitively, it can often be found in completely unremarkable circumstances, Dacher Keltner wrote in 2023. The hidden cost of optimizing everything : Ian Bogost talks with Charlie Warzel on his podcast, Galaxy Brain , about how technology is disconnecting us from life’s small pleasures. Other Diversions Gloria Steinem: “Everything we do matters.” How “somatics” became the solution to modern life The dark side of mindfulness PS Courtesy of Nick M. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. Last week, Nick M. shared a picture of Yosemite National Park on a summer morning. We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela

items.title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
items.description: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk. I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him. The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. [ From the February 1991 issue: Out of your car, off your horse ] A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back. When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “ By Heart ,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World , contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since. I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system. It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life. Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things. Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious. Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poem s : “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.” Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way…

items.title: J. D. Vance’s Disingenuous Defense of Tucker Carlson
items.description: When J. D. Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he displayed a surprising side of himself: human, vulnerable, almost touchingly naive. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go. And if you have a disagreement with somebody politically, even over a deeply held issue, you should still be friends with that person, because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.” This was a matter not of politics, Vance was at pains to emphasize, but of friendship . If Vance were to renounce Carlson over a matter as trivial as, say, Carlson’s oddly positive assessment of Adolf Hitler, what hope is there for society? The bonds of affection between Vance and Carlson are the very glue holding together the American experiment. And yet, tempting though it might be to imagine Vance clasping hands with the children of the world and teaching them to sing in perfect harmony, some notes of skepticism are warranted. Perhaps Vance’s affection for Carlson has more to do with holding the loyalty of his friend’s enormous audience. [ Peter Wehner: What J. D. Vance once knew ] For one, Vance is not known for cordially disagreeing with people. He has accumulated an unusual number of bitter enemies by flinging insults at people—including Senate Democrats (“You’re full of shit, and everyone knows it”), reporters (“scumbags”), and “childless cat ladies.” Last month, Vance hurled himself into an obscure debate over burrito prices to make a gratuitous swipe at a conservative Washington Post columnist’s weight. At the very same press conference where he waxed so earnestly about open dialogue, Vance mocked the idea that he would talk to former President Biden at the 9/11 ceremony (“I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden. I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and it’ll be great”) and dismissed the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “a crazy person.” Vance’s dig at El-Sayed, and the context in which he made it, revealed a lot more about his reasons for maintaining the alliance with Carlson than did his encomium to friendship. Vance was trying to illustrate that he and Carlson do not agree on everything. Carlson had recently praised El-Sayed as “America First” and “literally Trumpian,” apparently calculating that the candidate’s anti-Zionism outweighs his many left-wing positions. That view was the one Vance chose to highlight as his point of disagreement, rather than several other controversial remarks Carlson has made. Examples include but are not limited to his endorsement of “Great Replacement” and other conspiracy theories, his expressions of sympathy for Russia and its war against Ukraine, and his sympathetic interviews with figures such as Nick Fuentes, Alex Jones, and the World War II–revisionist historian Darryl Cooper, who called Winston Churchill “the chief villain of the Second World War” and described much of the Holocaust as mistaken deaths resulting from poor planning. All of these statements have left Carlson teetering at the edge of respectability within the Republican Party. He has become one of the most prominent exponents of a strain of right-wing populism that flirts with and in some cases embraces isolationism, anti-Semitism, and general crackpottery. Vance has courted this faction of the right. He and Carlson have a partnership that has lasted nearly a decade and has yielded dozens of interviews. In the course of this partnership, they may well have formed a genuine friendship. But Vance has discarded plenty of friends as he has cycled through various political iden…

items.title: The Rush-Job Presidency
items.description: Construction is notoriously slow-going work. But in Donald Trump’s Washington, cranes and bulldozers appear like DoorDash deliveries: fast, frictionless, and on demand. To build the president’s White House ballroom, roughly 250 workers have been pouring concrete and installing steel framework, keeping the site humming for 20 hours a day, seven days a week. The National Park Service has proposed a similarly intensive schedule for Trump’s planned triumphal arch: Construction will begin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Thursday, in the next two weeks. And officials are trying to shut down the Kennedy Center for two years to carry out renovations that consultants say will take twice as long if the building remains open during the work. These are very different and ambitious projects, but they share the same presumed deadline: January 20, 2029. They also share a risk: The compressed schedules could lead to shoddy work that will require more repairs later. Trump has less than three years to complete his transformation of Washington, D.C., before his projects fall into—and perhaps die in—the hands of a successor. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will,” he told New York magazine. The next president, whomever they are, likely won’t share Trump’s enthusiasm for gold finishes and Italian marble. To get the work done, his administration has found ways to circumvent the procedural obstacles that tend to slow federal projects. Construction—one of the world’s least productive industries—may present its own paradox. Research has shown that long hours, additional shifts, and overlapping work tasks can shorten a project’s timeline—but only to a point. In many cases, the effort to build faster can invite new delays, higher costs, and revisions. Trump’s botched repairs to the Reflecting Pool ahead of the nation’s 250th-birthday celebrations, in July, offer a classic example of the problem. The ballroom project, a hulking party venue that overshadows the White House’s main building and its modest neoclassical design, could be another. The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 this week that its construction could continue, saying that the preservationists trying to halt the project did not have standing to sue. The three liberal dissenting justices—along with, notably, Chief Justice John G. Roberts—argued that the construction was “likely unlawful.” But government filings claim that it’s already 65 percent complete—even as project leaders have continually revised design plans. By the time a new lawsuit from a challenger with stronger standing advances through the courts, how far along will the ballroom be? [ Read: The Court’s ballroom decision is a sign of deeper problems ] “We have hundreds of happy construction workers in D.C. busily doing their job building the finest Ballroom/Military complex anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this week after the Supreme Court decision. With his lawyers saying that the project will be “substantially” finished by November, the clock is ticking fast. Trump’s building spree presents a tricky calculation: The returns he wants are about time rather than cost. But speed in construction can get expensive fast, especially for a project whose anticipated costs have been hard to nail down. When Trump announced the ballroom plans in July 2025, he put the price at roughly $200 million, to be paid for by private donors. By October, he’d knocked down the East Wing of the White House without seeking any approvals. As the work has started, stopped (because of the preservationists’ lawsuit), and started again, the original estimate has tripled to $600 million, and taxpayers are expected to cover half of that amount, according to internal documents from the ballroom’s general contractor, Clark Construction, that were obtained by The Washington Post . items.title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
items.description: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work. Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable. Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. [ John Paul Rollert: A society of cheats ] We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away. The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely. In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively. In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squander the chance to help shape how this technology gets used in the world—ensuring that the private sector will do this for us instead. Colleges must start by being clear about what a degree is actually worth in the AI age. At Dartmouth, the Ivy League university where I am president, we believe it’s our job to teach students how to do what AI can’t: decide which questions to ask, exercise sound judgment, navigate ethical complexity, reckon with uncertainty, and take responsibility for their decisions. Then, we have to give them the chance to practice these skills in concert with AI. Harnessing AI ethically and productively requires understanding what the technology is and where it falls short. This is why Dartmouth, along with other schools such as Johns Hopkins University and Rollins College, has employed a critical AI librarian , an educator who helps students and faculty interrogate these models, recognize their biases, and spot unsupported claims. items.title: Crypto Money Still Matters for the Midterms
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. The crypto industry has always moved in cycles: booms and busts; bull markets and harsh, unforgiving “winters.” We’re in something of a lull right now: Bitcoin, the original cryptocurrency, is worth about two-thirds of what it was last fall. Meanwhile, investors are turning their attention to flashier innovations in artificial intelligence. About half of Americans now use AI chatbots, whereas just about a fifth of the country has ever used or invested in crypto. But the crypto industry isn’t dead—as of today, the combined value of all digital currencies is still more than $2.7 trillion—and neither are its political ambitions. Crypto companies have so far put $206 million toward this year’s midterm elections, more than any other corporate sector, including the AI industry, according to a Public Citizen analysis of OpenSecrets and Federal Election Commission data. Fairshake, the industry’s foremost super PAC, has a giant war chest and a reputation for backing winners from both parties (Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has reportedly warned of the risks of crossing it). Crypto is much further from the spotlight now than it was during its 2024 election-spending spree; back then, the industry was flush with cash, but its reputation was still recovering from the crash of two years prior and from the spectacle of Sam Bankman-Fried’s fraud trial. Even as Americans continue to distrust crypto, they’re now reserving their outrage for other corners of the tech industry, such as data centers and surveillance cameras. Although crypto is no longer as central to the public conversation, it’s still finding ways to flex its power. Fairshake first established itself as a major force during the 2024 election cycle, spending about $133 million in support of its chosen candidates. It started 2026 with a reported $193 million in the bank and has so far spent close to $70 million elevating politicians with an industry-friendly agenda. Fairshake’s record this year has been incredibly strong . Despite a few fairly significant losses , 50 of the 54 candidates it backed ended up winning their race. Not all of them won entirely because of Fairshake’s intervention: Some were incumbents who didn’t have a serious challenger. But an endorsement from Fairshake and its affiliate PACs tends to come with major financial support. The group spent more than $12 million to get a pro-crypto Republican into the general election for Alabama’s open Senate seat—it was “by far the biggest spender” in the primary, per The New York Times . And Protect Progress, Fairshake’s Democrat-focused PAC, spent more than $5 million to make another pro-crypto politician the party’s nominee for the House in Maryland’s Fifth District. Some candidates have incorporated these extreme interventions into their campaign strategy , accusing crypto-backed opponents of being in the industry’s pocket. Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, who won the state’s Democratic primary for the Senate, bashed her opponent for being pro-crypto and for being “funded by crypto and AIPAC and health-insurance companies.” In Florida’s Twenty-Fourth District, Fairshake spent more than $2 million trying to defeat Oliver Gilbert’s bid for the House, but Gilbert won his primary anyway. “Trump and his crypto con-artist billionaires just put a target on my back,” he said in one ad. Bloomberg reports that political candidates have purchased more ads mentioning the word crypto this year than they have in any of the past five years, and that the majority of these candidates are anti-crypto. Voters have never been all that passionate about crypto, and the Americans who do care about the tech are still disinclined to trust it. But the country’s attention has been elsewhere lately. items.title: There’s No Such Thing as an AI ‘Lab’
items.description: When did AI companies become AI labs ? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future. AI companies themselves have embraced the label: When Chris Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic, addressed the pope earlier this year, he repeatedly referred to his company, one of the most powerful AI enterprises in the world, as a lab. Industry press releases, technology commentators, and news publications have all picked up the word too. You’ll see the term on transit advertisements in San Francisco and in the pages of The New York Times (and, yes, The Atlantic ). Here is my proposal: Everyone, please stop. This term has gone too far. Although AI companies do invest heavily in research and development, using a word typically associated with groups of truth-seeking scientists is misleading, odd, and too favorable to these companies’ own ends. As a software engineer working in tech, I’ve seen little evidence that AI companies’ research practices differ significantly from those of the rest of the tech industry. Google and Microsoft, for example, have robust research divisions, but we still call them companies. So why has the laboratory term become so deeply enmeshed with AI? Part of the reason is historical. Over the past century, research laboratories have played a crucial role in computer science. Studies performed at Bell Labs, one of America’s first industrial labs, resulted in the development of the transistor and the cellular network. In the 1970s, scientists at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science pioneered the foundations of modern cryptography. As the Harvard historian Steven Shapin writes in his book The Scientific Life , countless innovations such as these that originated in corporate labs during the 20th century helped change the public’s perception of science. No longer simply knowledge for knowledge’s sake, science became viewed as a key engine of societal and economic progress. In their early years, OpenAI and Anthropic mainly performed research, similar to other industrial labs. Since then, however, they have commercialized rapidly: Each company is now valued near $1 trillion and generates billions in quarterly revenue. Holding on to the lab label seems to have the obvious PR benefit of allowing both companies to lean into their scientific legacy. Because of concerns about child safety, privacy, and job displacement, Americans largely hold a negative perception of the industry—and tech as a whole. That’s translated into popular opposition from politicians, data-center activists, and religious leaders who are concerned about the outsize influence of these companies: Spending on AI as a share of U.S. GDP now rivals defense spending . Meanwhile, scientists remain relatively popular. A 2026 Pew Research Center poll found that more than 75 percent of Americans trust scientists to act in the public interest, but the majority do not trust business leaders to do the same. These positive connotations associated with scientific research help the AI industry signal altruism while downplaying their profit-making ambitions. OpenAI and Anthropic’s leaders write at length about how AI’s risks and perils must be carefully studied for the sake of humanity. Research is portrayed as essential to this mission: OpenAI says it treats “ safety as a science ,” and Anthropic writes that “providing trustworthy research” will improve policy outcomes. The problem is, these companies act much more like private enterprises than bastions of science. Much of the research listed in the Publications section on both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s websites are not peer-reviewed papers accepted by scholarly outlets. I examined 100 recent pieces of research from both companies’ Research pages; the overwhelming majority had no corresponding peer-reviewed paper accepted by a conference or journal.…

items.title: What Tech Titans Don’t Understand About Sci-Fi
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. When I read Thomas More’s Utopia in college, the main thing I retained was that the inhabitants of More’s imaginary island worked just six hours a day and earned what we might now call a universal basic income. But the fact that I came away from this 16th-century classic with only visions of a shorter workday and a generous allowance says more about my undergraduate habits than it does about More’s ideas or intentions. Looking back recently, I remembered that his civilization wasn’t exactly the campus commune of my dreams. Its citizens held slaves, some of whom were shackled for committing adultery. The punishment for premarital sex, meanwhile, was permanent celibacy; the whole place sounded like a punitive surveillance state. I’d somehow missed all of this initially. Still, as Gal Beckerman noted this week in an Atlantic essay about Silicon Valley’s misreadings of science fiction , I wasn’t the first person to make this type of error. Fortunately, my myopia was harmless. Not all misunderstandings are. First, here are five new stories from The Atlantic Books Section: The sexual politics of the “bed trick” What Howard Zinn got wrong “Red Death,” a poem by Dorothea Lasky What to read to wake up your brain Roy Cohn did it first. In her new book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State , the historian Jill Lepore close-reads the science-fiction books that proved formative for Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Peter Thiel. In their early-teen years, these future billionaires devoured the works of Robert Heinlein, Isaac Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke, and other dark fantasists—but they seem to still hold on to the blinkered interpretations from their youth. Their collective misunderstandings fascinated Beckerman. “What they seemed not to get,” he writes of these men, “was that these were cautionary tales, stories that projected deep societal worries into space or onto a future many millennia away.” Instead of seeing the dysfunction behind these invented societies, “these boys just thought the killer robots sounded cool.” Lepore argues that these seeming misreads are partly responsible for their obsessions with technological progress—no matter the human cost. Three centuries after More coined the word utopia (which sounds in Greek like “good place” but actually means “no place”), the philosopher John Stuart Mill effectively popularized its opposite, dystopia , to describe worlds in which the worst things come to pass. In the 20th century, dystopia became a key feature of science fiction. Some of my favorite works in the genre introduce us to societies that seem idyllic, before revealing the rot within these supposedly perfect worlds. They aim, I think, to show that any utopia is probably too good to be true. It’s no place—or worse. More’s Utopia isn’t all that different; it depicts a society that readers might not actually want to live in. More, an English Catholic leader who was executed by King Henry VIII, probably didn’t mean to advocate for an essentially communist society with legalized euthanasia. Critics have long speculated that his depiction was satirical—that the first utopian literary work was, at least in part, dystopian. This wouldn’t surprise me, because years of living and reading have conditioned me to accept that every paradise has a dark side. This is why I was dismayed to hear Sam Altman say, earlier this year, that an AI-driven process to choose the U.S. president could be “awesome.” Seventy years ago, in his short story “Franchise,” Asimov imagined one variation on this scenario: A computer picks one median American to “vote” for president. In the story, democracy becomes nothing more than a statistical quirk. At a moment when artificial intelligence threatens to change society irrevocably, I have to agree with Beckerman: “What happens next,” he writes, “may depend on whether these boys grow up and finally recogniz…

items.title: The Meaning of the Lindsay Clancy Mistrial
items.description: During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something. The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict. Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health. Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party. Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs. These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis. Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion. The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all. As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet. There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court. Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure : the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system. Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it. Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards. What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable. [ Stephanie McCrummen: The women who are obsessed with Lindsay Clancy ] That’s a tidy narrative about what took place in Duxbury that night in 2023, when Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then attempted to end her own life by swallowing prescription drugs, slashing her neck and wrists, and then jumping out of a window. A possible upshot of this view is that it may raise awareness about the inadequacy of treatment options for postpartum mental illnesses—to the degree that raising awareness about any given issue ever meaningfully changes anything. And some elements of it seem inarguably true, such as the idea that Clancy’s psychiatric care was woefully uncoordinated. But this theory also has the odd effect of making Clancy the star of her own murder trial, for whom the viewer at home may be encouraged to root, which risks eliding the gravity of what she did. Simultaneously believing that someone is relatable and vulnerable and that they are nevertheless guilty of and accountable for heinous crimes is…

items.title: OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
items.description: Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines. The company’s “Strategic Futures” team has styled itself, in a sense, as inheriting the task of America’s Founding Fathers: “We labor in service of the ideals of free expression and individual liberty that are enshrined in the humble parchment of the U.S. Constitution,” Dean Ball, the team’s leader, wrote in a new OpenAI blog post. (The post opens with a quote from James Madison in The Federalist Papers .) Ball worries that advanced AI could radically concentrate power in the hands of those who control it, displacing labor in ways that disempower humans. In an extreme scenario, governments will have no need to listen to their citizens if there are robots to wage wars and omniscient software to run the bureaucracy. Ball is interested in studying what new political institutions might be needed to avoid this fate. Many Americans—a majority of whom express distrust toward the AI industry, outrage about data centers, and fears about their job security—already seem to be feeling this loss of agency very deeply. And the AI boom has already generated enormous amounts of wealth in just a handful of tech companies—including OpenAI itself. To say the least, it’s paradoxical for one of the most influential companies in the world’s most powerful industry to decry the AI-enabled concentration of power. So I reached out to Ball to understand more about his unease about the industry he works in, and how he wants to see the United States adapt to AI. Ball, who studies AI policy, is something of a minor celebrity in the industry. Last year, he joined the White House as an AI adviser and helped write the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan , a policy road map for the technology. He eventually departed, seemingly on good terms, from the administration before publicly lambasting it during its dispute with Anthropic earlier this year. Then, in July, he joined OpenAI. “My view is that we basically have transformative AI in the world now,” Ball told me. “You’re living in a world that is being transformed. It is happening.” This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Matteo Wong: You write that concentration of power through AI could upend the basic human freedoms enshrined in the U.S. Constitution. Can you elaborate on how? Dean Ball: Fundamentally, political power is the geographically bounded ability to wield the monopoly on legitimate force and violence. Doing so has heretofore required the cooperation of a great many human beings. You needed militaries, you needed people in those militaries, and you needed people to keep those militaries fed and supplied. And you needed people to pay for all of that through taxation. So people had a seat at the table because, in some sense, everything is being provided by them. Now you have to assume that robotics is going to advance soon in the same way that general digital intelligence has. Maybe it will take longer than I think. But at that point, the ability to project violence no longer requires people. And it is also conceivable that AI might generate sufficient revenue that the government would not need to rely on taxing people. If you look at the politics of AI, I think Americans are smart and have a sense that their seat at the table might be getting smaller. They’re right to be scared. Wong: You’re talking about concentration of power in the government, but generative AI is a technology developed in the private sector. There is potential for a rare and even unprecedented concentration of power in industry. What risks does that pose? Ball: You’re not trying to avoid all concentration of power, but to balance it. If this era gives rise to corporations that have a tremendous amount of power in the world, I think that’s good—so long as those organizations are governed. In other words, so long as the government that oversees them grows in lockst…

items.title: Why So Many Men Are Unraveling
items.description: Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and an actor playing a horse. Host Charlie Warzel talks to Ronson about the disinhibited men who are looking for purpose in all the wrong places. Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The following is a transcript of the episode: Jon Ronson: So I think, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same way anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means. Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas. And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways. And I think that’s what’s happening. You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling. Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , and today we are headed down a rabbit hole that includes ominous castles, public shaming, YouTube, White House cage fighting, all to answer one of life’s burning questions. Why is it that so many men are unraveling these days? Is this part of a changing economy? Part of a bad job market? Is it fallout from the pandemic? Or, is it part of something bigger? A societal failure of some sort, or an outgrowth of what some people have called the masculinity crisis? Now those words, masculinity crisis , can cause some people to roll their eyes. Men, of course, continue to enjoy all kinds of societal privilege, and gender inequities abound. But what is clear, I think, if you spent any time engaging with modern politics and culture, is that over the last few decades there has been a very real, if hard to define, debate over what it means to be a man. Jobs and gender roles—they’ve changed, and culture along with it. Much of it for the better. But that change has also created some uncertainty for the men who have been used to being at the center of every household, every office, every institution, marketing campaign, and political decision. And it’s in that uncertainty that all kinds of voices, pickup artists, politicians, incels on 4chan, Andrew Tate, Jordan Peterson—you name it—they’ve all jumped in to offer these competing visions of masculinity. Now, some of this has taken the form of toxic, misogynistic, manosphere bullshit. Some of it is just positive or harmless—“dudes rock” kind of stuff. And so many of these lessons, they end up being taught or absorbed, for better or for worse, in online communities and communicated by people who may or may not have ulterior motives. So what happens to regular men in this bizarre online stew that we’re all in? My guest today, the writer and podcaster Jon Ronson, explores that in his new book, The Castle . Ronson, to be clear, isn’t really writing about the manosphere or the high-profile grifters or the wild extremes. Instead, Ronson focuses on ordinary people who tend to find themselves in extraordinary situations. For the past three years, Ronson has been reporting on what happens to men when institutions die, when technology lets a million influencers bloom, and culture changes rapidly. What I find so useful about Ronson’s work is that it is curious and is funny, but it’s not overly ideological. The Castle is written partly as a mystery and partly as a work of anthropology. For the last decade, Ronson and I have crossed paths on stories numerous times. Like me, his work is always trying to understand what pushes people to believe strange or awful things, and all the ways that technology warps culture, which in turn warps real human beings. So—are men okay? Has the internet driven us all insane? It turns out this is a very complicated question. And Jon Ronson joins me now to talk a…

items.title: A Movie Can’t Be Just Its Own Thing Anymore
items.description: Onslaught , in theaters this week, should be the perfect early-September treat. The aggressive action thriller is gory, loud, and packed with interesting actors, and it has a straightforward premise: Three murderous super-soldiers, the result of some shadowy extra-governmental experiment, have escaped from a lab and are descending upon a small town in New Mexico. A tough-as-nails retired Army sniper named Celeste (played by Adria Arjona), living somewhat off the grid in a trailer park, must use her grit and know-how to defend herself against the oncoming attack. Yet as simple as that sounds, the film feels needlessly complex. Rather than just delivering on its clean setup, it becomes fixated on teasing future installments—a symptom of the obsession with sequelization that’s affecting even smaller genre films. The director Adam Wingard was, once upon a time, a master of the cheap thrill. This is a compliment; he emerged from the micro-budget mumblecore scene in the 2000s, then made two impressively nasty bits of horror—the slasher You’re Next and the wonderfully tawdry and tense The Guest . But Wingard has spent years trapped in franchise drudgery, offering up an unnecessary follow-up to The Blair Witch Project and a pair of giant-scale, instantly forgettable Godzilla movies . Onslaught initially suggests a more back-to-basics turn for the director, a return to R-rated indies that are unencumbered by cinematic universes. That mission, however, seems to have been a little corrupted by what Wingard’s been working on in the meantime. Onslaught begins on a compelling note. Its aesthetics are top-notch, the opening credits unfolding as an invigorating blitz of conspiratorial imagery that cuts together cable-news clips of several presidents, including Richard Nixon, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush, with drone footage of overseas combat; the entire sequence feels like a fever dream of the early 2000s. Celeste is a veteran of an unspecified overseas combat engagement, and the audience briefly glimpses in flashback the traumatic firefights that preceded her discharge. Living alongside her in the desert trailer park is a crew of other misfits, including the bumbling policeman Kovacks (Eric Wareheim) and a cantankerous older fella named Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson). To Celeste’s annoyance, her ex-husband drops off their cherubic daughter that day to stay the weekend; the tension is, of course, quickly building to a violent incursion. [ Read: Hollywood’s star power is shifting ] Part of my irritation with the film, though, stems from just how jazzed I felt about its first act. The actor Dan Stevens, at this point a longtime collaborator of Wingard’s (including, most recently, the director’s previous Godzilla movie), dons nightmarish makeup to play Dr. Hans Kammler; he’s a German-speaking mad scientist in charge of the military experiment that goes wrong. Rebecca Hall, another Godzilla alum, is Dr. Kammler’s domineering wife, Hanna—a stiletto-clad, cigarette-smoking badass boasting some mysteriously derived authority. The duo’s cartoonish poise is a delight to witness, as is their ridiculous hubris: Whatever lab simulation they’ve designed for their seemingly zombified super-soldiers quickly falls apart, leading the latter to invade the surrounding environs. Some solid gunplay follows, and the final showdown between Celeste and her trailer-park buds and the soldiers has some brutal flourishes—though it irritatingly takes place at night, making the chaos a little harder to see. But the screenplay (written by Simon Barrett) teases revelations throughout, then delivers on practically none of them. Hanna and Dr. Kammler’s work remains nebulous, and Celeste’s backstory is only vaguely filled in. These gaps would be forgivable if Onslaught existed mostly to deliver the frivolity that Wingard once excelled at; instead, it ends on a cliff-hanger that hints at further developments. In interviews, the director has even alluded to the movie belonging…

items.title: Introducing: The Permanent Questions With David Brooks
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube How do you find your purpose? How do you confront your own mortality? How do you repair a broken community? There are a lot of podcasts about the latest developments in politics and finance, health and wellness, entertainment and tech. The Permanent Questions is a new show about the topics that never go away. Each week, the Atlantic staff writer David Brooks speaks with the world’s deepest thinkers about matters of enduring human concern. The Permanent Questions premieres on Sunday, September 13, and new episodes will appear every Sunday after that. Subscribe now on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel or wherever you get your podcasts.
