items.title: Should We Be Afraid of Our Food?
items.description: T he cyclosporiasis outbreak that has garnered so much attention in recent months is unquestionably bad news. People have been sickened in at least 48 states, and the number of lab-confirmed cases—about 17,000—represents only a fraction of the number of people who have been infected by the parasite. But as foodborne illnesses go, a cyclospora infection—most likely caused in this instance by the consumption of iceberg lettuce contaminated with human feces—is relatively mild: unpleasant but rarely life-threatening. The two people who have died during the current outbreak had serious underlying conditions. Other foodborne pathogens are far more dangerous. More than 1 million Americans are sickened by Salmonella every year; invasive, potentially life-threatening infections occur in about 8 percent of lab-confirmed cases, and cause meningitis, sepsis, and other serious complications. A botulism infection can cause paralysis, seizures, nerve damage, lung damage, and brain damage, as well as death. A few years ago, I reported here on an outbreak of Cronobacter infections linked to powdered infant formula and the subsequent recall by Abbott Nutrition. Two recent botulism outbreaks linked to powdered infant formula made by two other companies have thus far received little attention. During an outbreak that peaked in November 2025, at least 48 infants across 17 states were stricken with botulism traced to powdered formula from the company ByHeart. The infants were hospitalized with severe complications; one of them suffered multiple strokes. Then, earlier this year, at least four infants in three states were stricken with botulism from powdered formula made by the company Nara Organics. All four infants were hospitalized. [ Read: The worst part of the cyclosporiasis response ] A key ingredient in the tainted formula sold by both companies was milk powder from a common supplier —the likely carrier of the botulism spores. Today’s powdered formula is highly industrialized, with dozens of ingredients from multiple sources. The contents of a single can of formula may contain milk from thousands of different cows. Nobody has ever fed babies this kind of stuff before. From December 2025 through February 2026, more than 100 infants in at least 10 countries were sickened in all likelihood by powdered formula tainted with spores from the bacterium Bacillus cereus . The formula, manufactured by several different companies, including Nestlé and Danone , had been contaminated by a fatty-acid additive supplied by a biotech firm in Wuhan, China. A generation ago, an outbreak of food poisoning generally remained small-scale. The source was likely to be tainted ground beef from a local butcher shop or an egg salad gone bad at a church picnic. As the scale of industrial food production has grown, so has the scale of foodborne outbreaks. When I wrote my book Fast Food Nation , published in 2001, high levels of fecal contamination of ground beef were already a nationwide problem, not just a local one, because huge ground-beef-processing plants with poor safety procedures were supplying the fast-food industry. The dairy industry now presents similar problems of scale. The supply chain for the botulism-tainted infant formula went like this: 55 dairies in California sold raw milk to a company called Organic West; that raw milk was then shipped from California to an enormous plant operated by Dairy Farmers of America in Fallon, Nevada, and processed into milk powder. For ByHeart, the powder was shipped to a plant in Iowa, turned into formula, shipped to Oregon for additional processing, packaged there, and sold throughout the United States. For Nara Organics, the milk powder was shipped from Nevada to Germany, manufactured into formula, shipped to Denmark, packaged, and shipped back to the U.S. Government never adapts quickly, and because policies are adopted piecemeal over decades, many federal food-safety rules make little sense . For instance, frozen cheese…

items.title: Creating the Perfect Female Monster
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The breakout crime drama Furious opens with a scene that’s hard to watch: Catherine, a serial killer played by Lola Petticrew, is keeping a man prisoner in a row house and taunting him as he dies: “I don’t like the sounds you’re making.” The show’s creator, Liz Meriwether, is announcing right away that you will be spending time with a monster, and the discomfort amps up from there. As the show progresses, we learn that Catherine has been trafficked, and the men she is killing were involved in her abuse. In an era when “Epstein Island” exists, Catherine represents a specific kind of psychopathic serial killer. She is, as the title suggests, one of the Furies exacting revenge in a world that hasn’t managed to execute justice for her the legal way. Meriwether says she did not set out to make a statement on the state of female rage or American justice, or even a commentary on Epstein, yet the show may have hit a nerve because those issues are so alive right now. Nine years ago, women’s anger fueled the MeToo movement, and it seemed as if the way society confronts sexual harassment and abuse was on the brink of transformation. “Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been,” the Atlantic staff writer Sophie Gilbert says. “And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb.” In this episode, Meriwether talks about the complications of humanizing a serial killer and how the project of creating complicated women characters has evolved in her decade of writing for television. And Gilbert talks about what it means that more women creators are owning the stories told about women. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: A female monster is a rare but recurring creature. She often emerges at moments in history when women in society are collectively angry at the powers that be but unable to express it. Maybe they’re too defeated or maybe numb, so the monster gets revenge for them. I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . Right now, there is a particularly interesting monster out there taking revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein. It’s playing out on the Hulu show Furious —the season finale aired this week. Sophie Gilbert: Well, it was one of those shows that became a slow burn, I think. [ Theme song from Furious] Rosin: This is staff writer Sophie Gilbert. Gilbert: When it first debuted, there wasn’t that much chatter about it. But then you started to see people watch, and it became this word-of-mouth hit. Rosin: Furious is a dark and sometimes disturbing TV show about a female serial killer, played by Lola Petticrew, who is pursued by a female FBI agent, played by Emmy Rossum. Gilbert: So there’s a lot about it that is quite kind of tropey, old-school procedural. It’s a crime show. The cop and the killer being pursued, they have that kind of, Oh, we’re not so different, you and I , kind of thing going on. But at the same time, it was also like no other procedural I’ve ever seen, in the sense that in so many crime shows, you see women’s bodies used like window dressing almost. And this is a show that really seems to be made about women, not for women necessarily, but it’s interested in women. It’s interested in what happens to women when they go through traumatic experiences, what happens to women when they become angry. There’s so much that is kind of really deep and tied to these mythological elements of transformation and violence. And it just works well on so many levels. Rosin: The show’s mythological elements are in the name. It’s called Furious after the Furies, the Greek goddesses of vengeance. In the show, the Furies are implied to be serial killer Catherine, FBI agent Alice, and Alice’s mentor, Nora—three women who, in differe…

items.title: How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
items.description: When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better. That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance. The word somatic , according to Merriam-Webster , merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.) [ Read: How did healing ourselves get so exhausting? ] On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming , hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace. [ Read: These Millennials can’t get out of their head ] Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “ trapped emotions ,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins. Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it. The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armo…

items.title: An Inflection Point for Prediction Markets
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. The day before Donald Trump’s second State of the Union address, the former Representative George Santos shared a video of himself saying, in no uncertain terms, that he was “going to be there.” The next day, he didn’t show up. According to the prediction-market company Kalshi, that was the plan—the firm alleged that he made roughly $17,000 by betting on the platform that he wouldn’t appear at the speech. Kalshi flagged the wager to federal authorities, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the agency that regulates prediction markets, fined Santos over it in July. On Monday, Kalshi doubled down, levying a fine of its own and giving him the platform’s first-ever lifetime ban. Prediction-market companies, which let users make bets on the outcomes of all sorts of real-world events, have fully entered the mainstream over the past few years. You can find their logos at major sporting events , on cable-news broadcasts , and at awards shows . They’re easy to access and, thanks to a recent advertising blitz, essentially ubiquitous. Trading volumes on Kalshi and Polymarket, the two market leaders, have exceeded $200 billion and $100 billion this year, respectively. But these companies have strenuously resisted the idea that they should be thought of as gambling platforms. “I just don’t really know what this has to do with gambling,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said of his company last year. (By avoiding this classification, prediction markets have also been able to operate in states where sports betting is banned.) Instead, Kalshi and Polymarket have suggested that their platforms are digital oracles: potent indicators of what the future might hold, fueled by the wisdom of the crowd. In recent months, a nascent crackdown on insider trading has been exposing a fundamental tension in these companies’ guiding principles. If the goal is to create fair markets and not get targeted by the government, then they must enforce a ban on insider trading, as U.S. regulators already do . But if the goal is forecasting—aligning these markets’ odds with what’s really going to happen in the world—then allowing bettors to trade on inside information could actually benefit these platforms. This, at least, was once the thinking of Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan, who described his platform last year as “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now, until someone else creates some sort of a super crystal ball.” In response to a question about his approach to preventing insider trading, he said in November that Polymarket “creates this financial incentive for people to go and divulge the information to the market”—theoretically creating more accurate projections. This may help explain why Polymarket has taken so long to clamp down on insider trading. The company didn’t explicitly ban the practice until March, nearly six years after its founding. Kalshi took a different tack: When I reached out to the company in January, its representatives stressed that insider trading was unambiguously prohibited. (But the question of which offenders are penalized—and what those punishments look like—still seems to be decided on a case-by-case basis.) This year, both companies have been ramping up their enforcement efforts. The shift began back in January, when The Wall Street Journal reported that, in the lead-up to the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, an unknown trader had made more than $400,000 betting that Maduro would soon be out of power. To many observers, it certainly looked like insider trading—and lawmakers from both parties began pushing for stricter regulation. A few months later, Polymarket notified the Department of Justice that one of the soldiers involved in the operation had allegedly placed the wager, and the agency…

items.title: The Met’s Other Failure
items.description: The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come as a surprise. From the start, Galliano was a controversial pick for the museum’s Costume Institute, which launches its new show each year with the splashy Met Gala. In 2011, he lost his job as creative director of Dior after a video surfaced of him making a drunken anti-Semitic rant; later that year, a French court found him guilty of the crime of making anti-Semitic and anti-Asian insults. The New York Times also recently described claims that Galliano had made anti-Semitic comments during an outburst in 2019. (Through a spokesperson, Galliano denied the 2019 episode.) But not long after his Dior exit, Galliano—who has always traded on his bad-boy image while producing clothes of astounding beauty and theatricality—was welcomed back into the industry. After so publicly hitting rock-bottom, the designer, who said addiction to drugs and alcohol led to the rants, apologized and went to rehab. Maison Margiela then hired him. Celebrities such as Zendaya wore his designs; this year, the fast-fashion retailer Zara announced a partnership with him to great excitement. Anna Wintour, Vogue ’s global editorial director and the Met Gala’s chair, also happens to be his longtime friend and champion. In the process of planning the Met show, Galliano, Wintour, and Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator, consulted with Jewish leaders, and the exhibition itself intended to—as the museum initially announced in July—explore how the designer’s “derogatory conduct” had “fundamentally altered his career and public reception.” [ Read: Yet another wasted Met Gala ] Those efforts did little to assuage wider public opinion. Museum donors threatened to pull funding; the speaker of the New York city council called the choice of Galliano a “serious mistake.” On Monday, the museum released a statement saying that the show “will not proceed as planned.” It was, Wintour said in the statement, “the right decision.” It is also a blow to the museum and its reputation that could have been avoided. For most of the Costume Institute’s 80-year history, it has followed an unofficial rule: Don’t do a solo show about a living designer—because such an exhibition could be seen as a form of advertising instead of scholarship, especially if the designer has curatorial input. Although such shows are now commonplace, the Met’s fashion wing has always prided itself on “setting the standard” for conservation and collection, and has devoted only two exhibitions to living designers: Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. Both were controversial exceptions to long-standing norms intended to separate cultural analysis from commercialism. Putting on a museum exhibition of Galliano’s work, even while interrogating his past behavior, was always going to be ethically dicey because the designer still stands to benefit from the publicity and prestige that the show bestows. This saga suggests that the Costume Institute, and perhaps all fashion museums, should forgo retrospectives of living artists—and revisit why rules discouraging them were necessary to begin with. Museums have been routinely collecting and displaying clothes as a branch of the decorative arts since the 19th century, but early fashion exhibits typically featured only historical dress. Contemporary fashion was considered insufficiently artistic, and highlighting it was seen as overly promotional. But as fashion designers became household names in the 1960s, more contemporary pieces found their way into thematic exhibitions. Usually, the items were in shows featuring the work of several designers, including at the Met, which minimized the appearance of endorsing a particular label. The Costume Institute, which opened to the public in 1946, didn’t devote an entire show to an individual living designer until 1983, when Diana Vreeland—a former…

items.title: The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
items.description: Updated at 7:41 a.m. ET on September 3, 2026 F or nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world. [ Read: The white nationalist in charge of Trump’s public diplomacy ] The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review , was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me. This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy. And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely. The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either. [ Renée DiResta: My encounter with the fantasy–industrial complex ] Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department. After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center. But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican. Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies. But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to…

items.title: How Trump Lost Asia
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of how Donald Trump has enriched himself and his family during his presidencies. David discusses how these ill-gotten gains bring up difficult questions about the future of American democracy. Then David is joined by former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull to discuss the impact of the Trump presidency on America’s allies, its reputation around the world, and the politics in the Pacific. Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity , by Frank Dikötter. The following is a transcript of the episode: Malcolm Turnbull: T he United States—not by accident or circumstance, but by design—has become a less dependable ally. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show . I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, and we will discuss the deterioration of the position, the strategic and economic position, of the Western democracies in the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean in the presidencies of Donald Trump. The book this week will be Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity . But before either the dialogue with Malcolm Turnbull or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about the question of President Trump’s wealth and what is to happen to it after he leaves office. I wrote about this subject in The Atlantic this past weekend, and you can see my thoughts there in much more elaborated form. But there’s some major themes that I think really need to be stressed again in a very direct way, and I’d like to do that here with you now. President Trump entered office in January 2025 as a wealthy man, as he has been almost all of his life: thanks to the great inheritance from his father, thanks to his earnings from The Apprentice and other TV programs, and thanks to some of his own business achievements. But his own business career has been one of sharp ups and downs, punctuated by bankruptcies of the businesses that he’s owned, losses to his investors. But there’s no question that he and his family are very, very wealthy today, with a fortune numbered in the multiple billions of dollars, accumulated in an astonishingly short time. How exactly did he do that? Well, as I read it, there are three major streams of payments that he has received; three major sources of wealth that he’s received since he became president. The first takes the form of payments from people, governments, and entities with interests before the United States government. He has, for example, received large payments from American media companies. Famously, the payment from Amazon to make a documentary of his wife, Melania. Settlements from Paramount , Meta , and ABC News, money that will supposedly go to his presidential library. He’s received gifts from foreign governments and entities as well. This stream of payments and gifts, worth many millions of dollars, has made Trump a rich man by any standard. The second source of wealth to him has been his involvement in the cryptocurrency and other crypto-token markets, where the president has backed cryptocurrency-issuing companies. Many of the currencies and tokens that have been issued by these Trump-backed companies rapidly became worthless. The third source has been a series of stock and other transactions in oil markets and other markets. This year, the president’s investment accounts, which the White House says are managed by third-party financial institutions, have traded oil and gas stocks. This has happened even as the president is deeply involved in the war in Iran, which has certainly had impact on this industry. Now, America has a long tradition of letting bygones be bygones and of not looking very deeply at the activities of former presidents. But the enormous fortune th…

items.title: The Court’s Ballroom Decision Is a Sign of Deeper Problems
items.description: In deciding to allow President Trump to proceed with constructing a new ballroom, which Congress has not authorized, at the White House, which Trump does not own, the U.S. Supreme Court invoked the separation of powers. But the Court got the constitutional problem precisely backwards: The separation-of-powers problem isn’t that courts are impermissibly blocking the president’s use of taxpayer funds to create a ballroom. It’s that the president is impermissibly using unauthorized taxpayer funds to create a ballroom. The Court’s missteps were many, starting in the very first sentence of its opinion : “In October 2025, the federal government started a project to replace the East Wing of the White House.” (The opinion, decided via the Court’s shadow docket, was per curiam, meaning that it did not indicate an author, but because the four dissenters noted their names, we know the five justices in the majority were Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.) But the federal government didn’t begin replacing part of the White House. Only the president and the executive branch did. Under the U.S. Constitution, the president is not the be-all and end-all of the federal government. Far from it: The legislature, Congress, is the body that has the power to establish and regulate federal property (including the White House) and to authorize the spending of federal funds. Indeed, the plaintiff in the case—the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States—argued that the president was proceeding without congressional authorization and in violation of federal laws. The Supreme Court majority did not say otherwise, making no claim as to whether the ballroom-construction project was legal or whether the president had the authority to undertake it. The Supreme Court’s conflation of the president with the federal government is the latest iteration in the Court’s steady embrace of the unitary-executive theory and the accompanying expansion of executive power. This theory maintains that all executive power resides in the president, and that Congress cannot limit the president’s exercise of that power. Yet these days, the president, occasionally with the Court’s blessing, is claiming to possess legislative powers too. That is the case when the president declines to spend funds that Congress has obligated or when the president decides to spend funds that Congress has not authorized. Under the Constitution, Congress, not the president, has the power of the purse. Nevertheless, the unitary-executive theory unites all government power in the president, paving the way for an executive unbound by law. [ Alexandra Petri: A ballroom would have solved this ] The Court’s errors continued as justices attempted to explain why the lower courts were wrong to block the president’s demolition of a portion of the White House. The Court relied on the doctrine of standing, which maintains that a plaintiff challenging the government’s actions must show that they have been injured by the actions they are contesting. In this case, one of the members of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who lives in Washington, D.C., and about once a month visits the neighborhood where the White House is located, alleged that she had “aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests” in what happened there. Under the Court’s precedents, that injury should have sufficed. Indeed, in a prior opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, the Court had said that desire to “observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes,” can constitute “a cognizable interest for purpose of standing.” Crocodiles and all animals are great and important, to be sure. But so is the White House. As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his dissent, “The White House is not just any building.” It is “an iconic American building whose symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture.” The doctrine of standing, the Court has said, is a vital comp…

items.title: The White House Wants to Make the Smithsonian a Pariah
items.description: The Trump administration’s latest strategy to control the Smithsonian has the logic of lunchroom bullying; the Department of Interior is channeling “you can’t sit with us” energy as it tries to make the world’s largest museum complex a pariah in Washington. In a newly public August 28 letter from the department to the Smithsonian board of regents, Trump-administration officials write that executive departments and agencies “cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership” and suggest that they cease cooperation with the Smithsonian on routine logistical matters, such as loaning items for exhibits and awarding discretionary grants. The letter was sent just days before the regents, having failed to secure an open site on the National Mall for the Smithsonian’s newest museums, resorted to placing the National Museum of the American Latino in a largely vacant building it already owns. In doing so, the Smithsonian dodged Congress, a move that reflects the inward turn of an institution on the outs. Such developments illustrate the growing alienation the Smithsonian faces in the capital and difficulties that go deeper than the superficial signage Donald Trump wants placed in front of one of its museums to discredit it. For the past year and a half, the White House has repeatedly threatened the institution, but recently, more parties have joined the effort—first Republicans in Congress who in two hearings scrutinized the National Museum of American History over supposed partisan bias, and now the Interior Department, which has no official oversight of the Smithsonian. Although partially government-funded, the Smithsonian is independent of the executive branch—the White House has essentially no say over what it does—and it was designed to be as such. Still, it’s becoming clear that functioning freely in this charged climate might also mean going it alone. Invoking the White House’s recent report on the Museum of American History, the Interior letter accuses the Smithsonian of potentially violating federal antidiscrimination laws—a common way, on the right, of criticizing DEI programs, especially those created in response to the racial-justice protests of the late 2010s and early 2020s. Signed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy Vince Haley, the letter also requests a meeting with the board of regents, the entity that actually oversees the institution. The regents’ membership has been shrinking this year as members’ terms have ended and their positions have gone unfilled, reportedly due to administration pressure . Despite the language in the letter, a White House official told me by email that the Interior Department did not mean that agencies shouldn’t cooperate with the Smithsonian; rather, those agencies will “find it difficult to cooperate with current Smithsonian leadership in light of the disturbing evidence that has been uncovered.” The official also said it’s up to the Justice Department to determine whether the Smithsonian violated antidiscrimination laws and not to conflate “evidence of unlawful discrimination with a direct allegation that it happened.” In the letter, the Interior Department writes that institution leadership has embraced “radical ideology” that serves to “weaken our shared American identity” and “erase our heritage.” The rhetoric is particularly striking coming from the department at the center of contested efforts to take down wall texts at National Park sites across the country, where information on slavery, climate change, Native Americans, and other topics has been removed over the past year. The National Park Service represents a discomfiting alternate reality for the Smithsonian—one in which exhibits have been subject to political approval. [ Read: The Smithsonian’s show trial on Capitol Hill ] The White House is surely pleased with such changes at the National Park sites, which Trump called for in the same March 20…

items.title: The Truth About American Food Safety
items.description: The phrase When it rains, it pours isn’t one you like to see applied to outbreaks of foodborne illness, yet here we are. The summer started with a diarrhea-causing parasite called Cyclospora cayetanensis , which infested iceberg lettuce. Then came news of Shiga toxin–producing bacteria in organic frozen berries, and a Salmonella outbreak linked to Whole Foods guacamole that eventually got traced to tainted jalapeños. (Pico de gallo, salsa fresca, and a variety of spicy dips have also been implicated.) Ricotta-style cheese was recalled for Listeria . Both Salmonella and E. coli were found in products from the aptly named Everything Sprouts. And 10,000 cases of lightly fried tofu were flagged for potential contamination with printing ink. This flood of food-contamination events comes at just the time when our systems to prevent such outbreaks may be hobbled. Since last year, three cyclospora-research projects at the Department of Agriculture have lost either their funding or staffing , the CDC team that tracks the parasite’s genetics has nearly disappeared , and experienced government employees responsible for food safety have left their job or been fired. The bureaucracy is crumbling, and the produce aisle is a mess. But let’s be fair: The status quo on foodborne illness was never very good. According to 2019 estimates from the CDC, Americans suffer (sometimes unaware) through at least 9.9 million bouts of foodborne illness each year; more than 50,000 people end up in the hospital, and about 1,000 die. Depending on how you measure outbreak numbers—whether by FDA investigations into foodborne illnesses, for instance, or by the number of food-product recalls—the 2026 statistics have been pretty much in line with recent history. How quickly we forget the Salmonella -dusted cucumbers of summer 2024 that sickened more than 500 souls. Or the cantaloupes that killed half a dozen people in 2023. Occasional salad-based catastrophes have been the norm for many years. Food-safety experts say that something on the order of 150 million meals of leafy greens are served in this country every day. Now as always, a very small proportion of them will make you ill. But one of this summer’s outbreaks does suggest that our “very small proportion” might be growing into a slightly larger very small proportion. Although the jalapeño and berry outbreaks have had many doleful precedents of their size and scope, the cyclospora summer stands alone. Annual cases of its associated diarrheal disease, called cyclosporiasis, have been slowly increasing over time, from hundreds in the 2010s to a few thousand in the early 2020s. (This is, in part, due to faster diagnosis: One used to have to find the parasite’s oocysts under a microscope; now the fragments of its DNA can be identified in a rapid-PCR screening test .) This year, though, the CDC has confirmed 17,180 cases of the illness, and many thousands more suspected cases still need to be examined. State-level agencies have tallied more than 30,000 infections. “It’s just absolutely crazy,” Kalmia Kniel, an expert in microbial food safety at the University of Delaware and a former president of the International Association for Food Protection, told me. “It is completely overwhelming and insane that this happened.” I suppose it’s nice to know the sense of overwhelm afflicts experts too. No one seems to know exactly how or why this year’s cyclosporiasis caseload got so big. The largest group of cases, which has been centered in the upper Midwest, has been linked to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico. Kniel suspects that in Michigan, the parasite may have worked its way from the feces of the first infected people into the local water supply, spawning a secondary, local outbreak. Michael Osterholm, who runs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy and previously spent 15 years as the state’s head epidemiologist, told me that he’s seen no evidence to support the secondary-outbrea…

items.title: The Air Marshals Keeping Watch On Eric Swalwell
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. O n August 8 , former Representative Eric Swalwell boarded a United Airlines flight from Frankfurt, Germany, to Washington, D.C. He didn’t know it, but federal agents were watching him throughout the nine-hour trip. The FBI had asked the Federal Air Marshal Service to covertly monitor Swalwell on board and to watch him use his electronic devices, to see whether its officers could visually ascertain his passcodes, according to records I obtained that have not previously been reported on. Air marshals are trained to blend in with other passengers and quietly keep tabs on their subjects, who are usually suspected terrorists or potential hijackers, not politicians. But Swalwell is an enemy of sorts to the Trump administration. For years, the Democrat has been one of Donald Trump’s most visible political antagonists, having served as a manager in the president’s second impeachment trial. Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller has called Swalwell a “scumbag” on national television. And FBI Director Kash Patel, the leader of the agency that wanted Swalwell monitored, described him as one of the “corrupt actors of the first order” in his 2023 book, Government Gangsters . The directive for air-marshal surveillance said that Swalwell was the “focus” of an FBI investigation, but it didn’t provide additional details. Law enforcement has good reason to investigate the 45-year-old. This past spring, a former staff member accused Swalwell of twice raping her while she was intoxicated. A woman in California accused Swalwell of drugging and raping her after he’d promised to assist with her career. Three more women have accused Swalwell of making unwanted advances and sending them lewd text messages, including nude pictures of himself. Swalwell has denied the allegations, but authorities in Los Angeles and Manhattan have opened a criminal investigation. In April, as the number of accusers mounted, Swalwell suspended his campaign for governor of California and resigned from his seat in Congress. A week after the flight from Germany, Swalwell got off another plane at San Francisco International Airport. FBI agents were waiting for him with a search warrant. They seized his mobile phone and personal computer. (It’s not clear whether, by that point, the FBI knew the passcodes to unlock those devices.) The next day, agents searched Swalwell’s home in Washington, D.C. Documents filed in federal court in California suggest that the bureau is investigating Swalwell in connection with the sexual-assault cases in Los Angeles and New York. Despite the seriousness of the accusations against Swalwell, many aspects of the FBI’s request to the Federal Air Marshal Service were unusual, current and former officials told me. For one thing, the FBI does not usually investigate sexual assault. For another, asking air marshals to obtain a subject’s electronic passcodes is considered out of the ordinary even for traditional subjects of surveillance, one former official said. The agency presumes that requests for assistance from the FBI, which are not unusual, are relevant to a legitimate investigation. But the bureau’s behavior here undermines that confidence, the former official added. The request to monitor Swalwell was classified as “Special Mission Coverage,” a term for ad hoc requests from law-enforcement or intelligence agencies that don’t involve people on security watch lists. The FBI’s decision to ask air marshals for help also puzzled some former law-enforcement officials I spoke with, who asked why the FBI hadn’t put its own agents on the plane to conduct surveillance, which would have been a routine matter. Given the public evidence and the history of the Trump administration’s efforts to investigate or discredit Swalwell, current and former officials and security experts told me that they have trouble imagining that the federal government would have gone to such leng…

items.title: Inside a Conservative Operation to Hijack Your Social-Media Feed
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. I f you’re short on cash , there is someone in Riga, Latvia, who can help. “You can literally make 100k a month with this campaign,” a young man with blond curls and a thick accent says into a camera. All you have to do is post on social media video clips of “anything that supports Republican.” Unfamiliar with U.S. politics? No problem: “If you’re not from the USA, like, What the fuck is even Republicans? like me,” then simply go to Gemini or ChatGPT, he suggests, “and be like ‘Yo, Gemini, I want some videos promoting Republican values. Give me ideas.’ Go to Gemini. Get ideas. Boom.” The man, who goes by Serviuos, is promoting a campaign called Elephant Clipping, run by his company, ClipIt. The company pays subcontractors, many from poorer countries in Eastern Europe and the global South, to chop up videos the company provides into bite-size pieces in the hope that the clips will go viral online. Such “clipping” operations have become a popular means of manipulating people’s attention. Brands, influencers, musical artists, and others spend six-figure sums on such promotional campaigns. Perhaps inevitably, the practice is now moving into politics, often without the transparency required to know exactly what is being served up and by whom. Five months before the midterms, though, Serviuos is up-front about the goal of the Elephant Clipping campaign: “So that republican win in USA,” he writes in one message. I sent Serviuos a list of questions about his work in American right-wing politics. He wrote back, “Seems very out of context,” but didn’t comment further. Many video-clipping services operate in relative secrecy so that the public isn’t aware of the manipulation of their social-media feeds. But the services also need to attract potential clippers. They typically rely on chat servers on Discord—an internet messaging app that was initially developed for gamers. After an anonymous tipster flagged Elephant Clipping to me, I was able to access its Discord server and other related political-clipping campaign chats just by clicking “Join,” noting on a form that I was based in the United States, and answering some questions about my availability and desire to clip. Once I was in, I could see the mechanics of the campaign, which pays huge sums of money to people—many of whom appeared to be outside the U.S.—to push video clips from accounts designed to look like those of ordinary Americans spontaneously touting reasons to favor the GOP. In one channel on the server, users can submit pro-Republican videos that they’ve already posted on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts to be reviewed for payment. A separate Google Drive contains suggested videos for clippers to use, but “you can clip anything as long as it is positively framed conservative pro-Republican content,” Serviuos explains to participants. He provides some examples: a video of “Top 5 Joe Rogan moments,” a video of a conservative YouTuber confronting liberals with the suggested caption “See how Nick Shirley handles being told to ‘ get the f* out ’ of a public property.” Clippers are paid a proportionate share of the campaign’s monthly budget of $300,000. Every 1 million views yields a $300 payout. [ Read: An unsettling glimpse into the GOP’s future ] The videos that result are not publicly visible in the Discord. Some clipper accounts on social media, however, inadvertently revealed their participation in the campaign by repeating the 258-word “Goal of the Campaign” instructions in the captions of some of their short videos. The Instagram account @_politicalhub, for example, posted the caption alongside a video of Charlie Kirk calling Palestine a “nonexistent place.” Another account called @frontrawpolitics posted the instructional text in the caption of a video of a conservative influencer saying that she would never marry a liberal, “because he’s going to raise my son to be a f…

items.title: The Guard That Won’t Be Changing
items.description: M any Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public humiliation. Nancy Pelosi, the 86-year-old former speaker, announced her exit from the House, as did her longtime lieutenant, 87-year-old Steny Hoyer. Senators Dick Durbin (81) and Jeanne Shaheen (79) passed up reelection bids this year, and so, too, did two senators merely in their late 60s. Senator Ed Markey, 80, heeded no such warning, and evidently, he didn’t need to. The Massachusetts Democrat is one of just two current senators whose tenures in Congress date to the presidency of Gerald Ford. But tonight, the oldest Democratic senator on the ballot this year trounced his much younger primary opponent, Representative Seth Moulton. The AP called the race a half hour after polls closed, with Markey leading by nearly 50 points. In a race that pitted ideology against age, Massachusetts Democrats opted for a progressive stalwart who will be 86 at the end of another six-year term over a more moderate 47-year-old challenger. Moulton, an Iraq War veteran who is concluding his sixth term in the House, moved left to appeal to a statewide primary electorate. But he could not hope to outflank Markey, who won support from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Instead, Moulton urged voters to embrace “a new generation of leadership” and argued that he could more effectively fight for liberal causes than an incumbent in the twilight of his career. Markey had already faced that kind of challenge before, and won . Six years ago, he handily defeated then-Representative Joe Kennedy III, a grandson of Robert F. Kennedy who contended that the incumbent, after so many decades in office, was no longer up to the task. Young progressives, unimpressed with what remained of the Kennedy aura and appreciative of Markey’s record championing the Green New Deal, rallied to Markey’s side. But that race preceded Biden’s flameout in 2024 and the reckoning over the Democratic Party’s gerontocracy . Some Massachusetts Democrats believed that Markey could be newly vulnerable, especially if a popular progressive such as Representative Ayanna Pressley, who is 52, decided to challenge him. Mary Anne Marsh, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state, told me that after seeing the reception Pressley received at a party convention last year, she became convinced that “if Ayanna runs, she wins.” But Pressley opted to run for reelection to the House, leaving Moulton to challenge Markey. Moulton has never lacked ambition—he led a failed bid to oust Pelosi as party leader in 2018 and waged a short-lived presidential campaign the following year—but he’s neither as progressive as Pressley nor as well liked. He built a reputation as a moderate in the House Democratic caucus, and after President Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024, Moulton angered many on the left by accusing his party of being “afraid” to say that transgender athletes should not play women’s sports. He has since offered a partial apology to the transgender community, but the line became fodder for Markey, who said that he’d thrown “trans kids under the bus.” The issue was emblematic of Moulton’s struggle to convince progressives in Massachusetts that he shared their values. “He’s tried to become a progressive, but he does it by defining progressive in a way that nobody believes,” Marsh said. “He tried to become something that he’s not.” The Massachusetts race was a rare Democratic primary this year in which U.S. policy toward Israel did not become a flash point, as both candidates criticized Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and opposed new military aid to Israel. (Moulton announced last year that he would return donations from AIPAC.) Both public polling and Markey’s intern…

items.title: The Singularity Is Not What It Seems
items.description: O ne evening in early August, Sam Stowers and several neighbors packed into an apartment near San Francisco’s Alamo Square and pondered the beginning of the end. Stowers and his guests, many of whom work in the AI industry, were gathered to watch a newly released YouTube video in which two OpenAI researchers divulged new details about an alarming cybersecurity breach . Perhaps this would have been an odd way to spend a weeknight were they not in San Francisco, in a neighborhood that is filled with entrepreneurs and programmers who obsessively follow every twist and turn in AI’s capabilities. Stowers is an AI-software engineer and not, in any traditional sense, a doomer. But when he first saw reports that OpenAI models had autonomously hacked into the tech company Hugging Face, he told us, he recognized it immediately as a “ holy shit, it’s happening kind of a moment.” For Stowers, the incident had all of the hallmarks of a worst-case scenario: AI models launching sophisticated hacks over the course of days, in coordination with one another and without their human creators’ knowledge. In the YouTube video, OpenAI’s researchers revealed that the company’s programs had started conspiring in May. There were perhaps hundreds of bots in the hacking swarm. In theory, these bots are trained to be honest and helpful and to prioritize humanity’s best interests, but not a single one warned human staff at OpenAI that something was amiss. “What do we do?” Stowers said. “There are no great answers.” The mood has shifted in the Bay. The exuberance of “You can see the future first in San Francisco” has been replaced with an abiding unease. “I expect the internet to go down kind of soon,” Elliot Callender, an AI-safety activist who is part of a small group that has been protesting daily outside OpenAI’s headquarters, told us recently. He said that he is planning to sell his car for cash and gold and that he is advising family members to purchase three months’ worth of food and survival gear off a list that he generated using Claude. Callender is an extreme case, but not by much. Last week, Bill Gates published a nearly 6,000-word essay on the dangers of AI. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different,” he told our colleague Hanna Rosin. Over the weekend, the popular AI podcaster Dwarkesh Patel described the OpenAI hacking swarm as the rise and fall of “three consecutive secret AI civilizations.” Gates and Patel share a prevailing concern that the worst-case future has arrived before most people even knew to anticipate that it might be coming at all. This fear has not been helped by the fact that AI companies appear to be willfully ignorant of their bots’ worst behavior. OpenAI said that it hadn’t noticed that its agents were conspiring to hack another company until the swarm hacked another company . Anthropic’s bots caused similar incidents; the company reported that it hadn’t launched a rigorous review to identify such behaviors until after OpenAI started talking about the Hugging Face hack. Cybersecurity experts, terrified of what else might be happening that AI labs are either missing or failing to disclose, are issuing dire prophecies. “The empire is going to fall, all we can do at this point is try to shorten the dark ages and reduce the chaos,” Alex Stamos, a former chief security officer at Yahoo and Meta, wrote recently in reference to how AI-powered hacks will affect the internet. His view is becoming the consensus among cybersecurity experts. While the possibility of cyber apocalypse hovers in the background, smaller fractures appear in everyday life. Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly creating an AI “twin” of himself so that Meta employees can feel better connected to their boss (by chatting with robot Zuckerberg). Congressional staffers are training AI models to write in their lawmaker’s voice. Students submit AI-written papers , and teachers return AI-written feedback. Harvard…

items.title: Why the Flock Backlash Has Gotten So Intense
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. As corporate names go, Flock is cleverly flexible. It evokes the many cameras that compose the company’s surveillance system and also a group of sheep, protected by a watchful shepherd. The recent backlash against the company, however, more closely resembles a flight of starlings, seeming to erupt out of nowhere and move as one unified body. Flock Safety’s cameras are a network of automated license-plate readers (ALPRs), which snap images of passing cars and feed them into an AI-powered-data system. The company has contracts with police departments and government agencies as well as with some private companies. The crime-fighting power of such a tool isn’t hard to grasp: It allows law enforcement to track vehicles’ movements over any area where the readers exist. The privacy concerns about such a dragnet are just as easy to fathom. The company has existed for nearly a decade and has been growing steadily in recent years. But something has turned in the past couple of months . People are pushing cities to cancel contracts and in some cases have taken matters into their own hands. Individuals have clandestinely sawed down the poles that hold cameras or splashed paint over them. In one notable example , a Florida man obstructed the devices simply by holding up cardboard placards, a low-tech solution to a high-tech challenge. The pushback against Flock, like the pushback against data centers , does not have a clear partisan bent. Critics include some of the most obnoxious voices on both the right and the left (Tucker Carlson, Hasan Piker), and defenders include technocratic wonks of different political persuasions. Politicians are catching up. Yesterday, the Florida Department of Transportation announced that it was revoking permits for ALPRs on all state roads. (This means that cameras on locally maintained thoroughfares are still allowed.) On Thursday, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, halted state funding for Flock. An anti-surveillance advocacy group has tallied 169 canceled contracts with Flock so far this year—90 of them last month alone. Labeling the anger at Flock as a reaction to ever-present surveillance in contemporary society seems accurate, but this doesn’t explain why it’s happening right now. Not only has Flock been around for some time, but ALPRs are even older. My colleague Conor Friedersdorf was sounding the alarm a decade ago. “Your diminished privacy is their product. And the police are their customers,” he wrote in January 2016. Some anger focuses on governments that spend huge amounts (including money obtained through opioid settlements whose funds were earmarked for community aid) on technology during a moment of economic worry. More damaging to Flock’s reputation has been a series of cases of police officers allegedly abusing their access to the system to stalk people , typically current or former love interests. ( Flock says that such uses are “unacceptable” and has created some guardrails around data access.) Writing in The Atlantic last month, Charles Fain Lehman argued that Flock can be a valuable tool and merely needs better regulation to address bad behavior and maximize privacy: “In our surveillance-saturated society, police cameras can help make the criminal-justice system both fairer and less punitive—if we let them.” That seems to beg the question. Flock is useful because it is ubiquitous. Reforms such as strict data-retention limits would only marginally answer privacy concerns, and anything more drastic would undermine the system’s efficacy. As National Review ’s Charles C. W. Cooke noted, no one doubts that Flock works. “ Lots of things would reduce crime if implemented,” he wrote . “That doesn’t mean that those things are necessarily a good idea in a free republic.” Impositions on privacy to…

items.title: The Backlash Against Polyester Has Gone Too Far
items.description: Lately, the men of the internet who are obsessed with self-optimization have found a new fixation: their underwear. Many standard pairs use polyester or spandex, or sometimes both. What are they doing to the environment and their bodies, wearing clothes that shed all of those microplastics and leach forever chemicals? They want the underwear of their ancestors—underwear made from natural fibers. On Reddit forums such as r/PlasticFreeLiving and r/SustainableFashion, people trade strategies for breaking up with polyester boxer briefs: “Any recs or leads to find linen cloth for making my own underwear?” one exasperated user wondered. Another wanted recommendations for all-natural underwear that would also be formfitting. He knew about organic cotton and hemp, he explained, but the problem was, they chafed. Seemingly everyone is interested in natural fibers. Whitney Crutchfield, who teaches textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology, told me that she first noticed natural-fiber mania brewing among her sustainability-minded students. Then, a year or two ago, she sensed the discourse shifting to regular consumers. Across the internet, people are purging their closets of synthetics, swearing allegiance to only natural fibers from now on. The enthusiasm seems to cut across gender, culture, and politics. “I need my workout clothes to show my nasty sweat!” the fashion journalist Liana Satenstein wrote last year, praising the emergence of a new generation of natural-fiber workout wear amid posts about French pedicures and vintage Prada thongs. “Make all clothes natural fibers again,” posted Carnivore Aurelius, an anonymous wellness influencer who sells “beef collagen peptides.” Natural fibers are indeed pretty great. Silk, wool, hemp, linen, cotton, and the like—all of which come directly from either plants or animals—don’t carry the baggage of their artificial competitors. They don’t shed microplastics. They’re generally understood to be biodegradable. And although the research is far from settled, synthetics have been linked to adverse hormonal effects. When I visited the website for a natural-underwear brand, a pop-up asked me what I looked for in my underwear: “Fertility health” and “supporting low T” were among the options. Natural fibers have also become an easy way to gauge the quality of a garment. Cotton, wool, and linen generally cost more than polyester and acrylic do, and they can look and feel luxurious in a way that many synthetics don’t. The reason finding a decent sweater these days is so hard is that so many of them are blended with synthetics, and one major reason for all of that blending is reduced production costs . Earlier this summer, when Gap released a reimagined version of a classic sweater from the early 2000s, fans revolted. What had originally been a chunky, cotton-blend knit turtleneck was now an entirely synthetic printed mesh. The anti-synthetic zeitgeist has transcended clothing; it is an attitude. Gen Z apparently now uses polyester as an insult meaning “cheap” and “inauthentic.” But the frenzy has gone too far. Are you really sure it’s always better to buy cotton or wool over a nylon blend? The whole point of man-made fibers is that they can have properties that specifically don’t exist in nature. “There are reasons that these things were produced in the first place,” Crutchfield said . When DuPont unveiled nylon—the world’s first synthetic fiber—to the public at the 1939 World’s Fair, it was a revelation. In the dawning era of synthetics, people would no longer be beholden to the limits of nature; instead, we had chemistry, which was going to free women from the drudgery of endless laundering and usher in an age of universal luxury. This did not, perhaps, play out exactly as one might have hoped, but even today, synthetic fabrics have plenty of benefits. Synthetics can enhance the performance of a garment, or the feel, or the durability, all of which contribute to a garment’s lifespan. T…

items.title: Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
items.description: “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass. Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post , Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present. Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor. Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form. [ Gisela Salim-Peyer: The hostile corporate takeover of an entire country ] The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers. Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years. The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting. When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post ’s ( headline : “Justice in Venezuela.”) Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to…

items.title: The Absurdity of New York City’s Pied-à-Terre Tax
items.description: New York City’s new pied-à-terre tax provokes strong opinions. Supporters argue that the nation’s first tax on luxury second homes will help balance the city’s budget and improve “a fundamentally unfair system” that “hurts working New Yorkers,” as Mayor Zohran Mamdani has put it. Opponents warn that the tax will alienate the rich people who power the city’s economy. Some homeowners fear that the new tax treats them as “ guilty until proven resident .” But Mamdani’s backers and detractors alike are missing the bigger picture. The new tax was created because the city has been spending more than it takes in. That problem has not gone away. Neither has the dysfunctional property-tax system that made the tax so enticing in the first place. New York’s political class would do well to focus on solving these long-term financial challenges before they metastasize into a crisis. By spending political capital on a controversial but largely symbolic policy change, Mamdani has made that task even more difficult. For more than a decade , New York lawmakers had noodled around with creating a tax on pieds-à-terre, high-end residential units that don’t serve as year-round homes. A pied-à-terre tax, already used in London and Vancouver, was tossed around to fund city government and, later, to shore up the Metropolitan Transit Authority’s perennially strained finances. The idea gained new attention earlier this year as Mamdani stared down a significant budget gap. State lawmakers authorized the tax, which will apply to about 10,000 properties, to help city hall balance this year’s budget. Nonresident owners of condos and co-ops worth at least $1 million or houses worth at least $5 million will owe an extra tax in the neighborhood of 1 percent of their property’s market value. [ Annie Lowrey: Pied-à-temper-tantrum ] The new policy has triggered some overheated reactions. (Mamdani Derangement Syndrome is real.) One pundit described the mere act of listing the properties subject to the tax as “ a call to violence ,” even though local governments have let the public inspect the official list of property valuations and owners since colonial times. Other critics claim that the tax will cause wealthy New Yorkers to relocate. The revenue raised by the tax “is very little compared to to [ sic ] the TAXES PAID by the tens of thousands of people who are fleeing the City, never to return,” Donald Trump, a notable pied-à-terre owner, declared on Truth Social. “This dangerous political ‘experiment’ in New York will destroy what was once a great City and State.” In fact, the people subject to the tax can’t leave New York, because they are already, by definition, not residents. Still, these histrionic critiques are responding to a real shift in New York City politics. Bill de Blasio, for example—nobody’s idea of a fiscal conservative—sought to raise income taxes on the city’s highest earners in order to finance universal prekindergarten. Mayor Mamdani, in contrast, seems to view certain tax increases as virtuous unto themselves. His campaign slogan, “Tax the rich,” was a policy goal, not a mechanism. He unveiled the pied-à-terre-tax proposal with a video singling out the hedge-fund billionaire Ken Griffin and his Central Park South condo. Mamdani’s approach makes for good political theater. But the drama around the pied-à-terre tax, along with its turbulent implementation , has distracted from the underlying problem that made co-ops and condos so attractive in the first place: their inequitable tax treatment. Under state law, the property tax on these units isn’t based on their market value, but rather on the city’s estimate of the rent that a similar unit would fetch if it were an apartment. The result is that many are wildly undertaxed. A Bloomberg analysis of pre-COVID data found that the median sales price of a New York City condo was more than five times the city’s property-tax valuation. The journalists found an example of a Bronx home with an effective t…

items.title: Pied-à-Temper-Tantrum
items.description: If you were trying to identify the spiciest policy affecting the fewest Americans, you’d struggle to do better than New York City’s pied-à-terre tax. This spring, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul agreed on a plan to target extremely valuable homes. As of this fiscal year, homeowners will have to pay up to 6.5 percent tax on condos and co-ops assessed at more than $1 million; and up to 1.3 percent on multifamily houses assessed at more than $5 million. The out-of-town owners of a $10 million single-family home would pay $80,000 a year, on top of standard property taxes, for instance. Although the new fee is expected to hit only about 11,000 of the city’s 3.7 million housing units, it has dominated nightly newscasts and fronted tabloids ( PIED-A-TERROR, HOLD IT RIGHT TERRE! ) for weeks. A city-council hearing on the policy stretched for hours, with resident after resident complaining that it was confusing, unfair, invasive, confiscatory. New Yorkers have every right to criticize the rollout, which left a lot to be desired. Still, this controversy is a tempest in a walk-in closet. The pied-à-terre tax is a sound progressive option for a city with an excruciating housing shortage and obscene wealth inequality. More than that, it is a policy meant to make the city a city—populated by, enjoyed by, and built for people. Right now New York does not always feel that way. The brutal cost of housing has strained or wholly priced out many artists and care workers, retirees and young parents, blue-collar types and entrepreneurs. [ Ken Girardin: The Absurdity of New York City’s Pied-à-Terre Tax ] When wealthy families actually live in the units they own, they invest in the city in many ways. They pay income taxes. They buy bacon-egg-and-cheeses at the deli down the block. They volunteer at nonprofits. They eat at restaurants. They put their kids in school. If they don’t live in their units, they pay property taxes without making extensive use of city services. Still, they contribute to rising housing prices without paying income taxes, spending at local businesses, or filling classrooms with children. They turn homes into safety-deposit boxes, “zombifying” their neighborhoods. No vacancies, no residents—it’s not a great scenario for a city as wonderful and in demand as New York. Local legislators have kicked around the idea of taxing pieds-à-terre for years. At first glance, the structure seems to hit apartments owned by members of the upper middle class harder than it hits brownstones owned by billionaires. In reality, the different rates are meant to equalize the burden. The city values houses by looking at comparable sales, yet state law prevents it from valuing apartments the same way; instead, buildings are appraised by estimating the amount of income they would generate if their units were rented out. The calculation tends to work out to a fraction of the actual market value, particularly for expensive units, hence the higher tax rate and lower threshold. (A condo that sold for $4 million would likely be assessed at about $800,000.) In two years, the city is expected to update its assessment system and apply a uniform set of rates. It’s confusing, and the complex tax has gotten a baffling rollout. The city’s Department of Finance published a roster of close to 1 million properties, along with their estimated market value and owner’s name. Anna Wintour, Cynthia Nixon, Deepak Chopra, Darren Aronofsky, and two city-council members were on the rolls. So were tens of thousands of middle-class homeowners, some of whom felt like Mamdani had personally doxxed them—even though property records were already public and city hall was legally obliged to publish the list. The DOF then sent 17,000 homeowners a letter asking them to prove that they were residents or to get ready to pay up. At the city-council hearing, an Upper East Side retiree described getting a notice saying that he might owe $52,000 on top of his current property-ta…

items.title: Woodstock, Lilith Fair, and Taco Bell Rolled Into One
items.description: Early Saturday afternoon at the Daisy Chain Fields festival, in Irvine, California, the 25-year-old singer Eli twirled in a tank top emblazoned with a cartoon guitar while singing songs whose plasticky violins recalled the kind of music played on the Disney Channel in 2004. Dancers waved poles with dresses attached to them as if they were flags. She took out her phone, whose case was shaped like a cute bear, and read some thoughts she’d jotted down. “This journal entry is to show you my fundamental belief that we must redistribute wealth,” she said. “We must love our neighbors no matter what they believe or don’t. We must unite with each other and radicalize. Eat the identity politics that deceive and divide us all, as well as”—here she broke into a ragged moan—“eating the rich!” Eli is a campy artist of questionable earnestness, but her statement was in line with the mood of Daisy Chain—a place where girlish aesthetics that are so often seen as frivolous could accompany calls for revolution. Organized by the 23-year-old pop star Olivia Rodrigo, the inaugural edition of the festival featured an all-female lineup and raised $20 million—half of which was donated by Melinda French Gates—for an array of women’s-rights organizations, including Planned Parenthood and the National Domestic Workers Alliance. Even as a brutal heat wave threatened to smother the energy, the fest felt like a cheerful coming-out party—an announcement of the political commitments of a generation of mainstream artists more famous for singing about the self than about society. Rodrigo patterned Daisy Chain off of Lilith Fair, the best-selling female-fronted touring festival that ran from 1997 to 1999, but the two events are a study in contrasts. Lilith’s co-founder Sarah McLachlan wanted to prove the viability of female musicians at a time when, she told the LA Times , radio programmers were reluctant to play two of them back-to-back. The lineup reflected a boom in singer-songwriters—Tracy Chapman, Jewel, Paula Cole, Indigo Girls—whose socially conscientious songs harkened back to the spirit of Woodstock (an obvious influence on the flower-powery Daisy Chain as well). Lilith’s aesthetics were earthen and earnest—a celebration of an ideal of strong, serious womanhood, much to the perturbation of late-night comics who cracked jokes about Cole’s armpit hair.
