In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment , she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.” [ Read: The real religious ‘renewal’ happening in Gen Z ] Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode , “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.” As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones…

items.title: Roy Cohn Did It First
items.description: The day after Donald Trump won the 2016 election, the conservative political operative Roger Stone was among the lucky few to get through to him on the telephone. The president-elect reminisced about the long-dead friend who had introduced him to Stone: “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment? Boy, do we miss him.” “Roy” was Roy Cohn, who became notorious in the early 1950s as chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy and then built a career as a lawyer and fixer for New York City’s rich and powerful. His roster of clients, many of whom doubled as his friends, included Cardinal Francis Spellman, George Steinbrenner, the media mogul Si Newhouse, and a host of famous mafiosi, including “Fat Tony” Salerno and John Gotti. Trump met Cohn in 1973, when the young developer sought advice about a federal lawsuit alleging racial discrimination by his family’s real-estate company. Cohn proposed countersuing the feds for defamation—even though the company had been marking the applications of prospective Black tenants with a large C , for “colored,” and then telling them no apartments were available. The countersuit, for $100 million, failed as a legal tactic—the company settled with the Justice Department, without admitting wrongdoing, after two years of litigation—but it made headlines, which was the real point. Trump and Cohn had the same attitude toward the law: It was not a system of rules, but a way of getting what you wanted. For a generation of liberal Manhattanites, the mere mention of Cohn’s name produced a visceral loathing. They saw him as a self-serving and unprincipled social climber whose crusade against communism had ruined lives. In documentaries , profiles , and the play Angels in America , he has been portrayed as a villain in the vein of Shakespeare’s Richard III, whose monstrousness can be traced back to his own sense of social exclusion. When Cohn contracted AIDS, he kept his illness and his sexuality secret to the end. He died in 1986 insisting that he had liver cancer, even while enrolled in a clinical trial to receive AZT, an early AIDS medication. In American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey From Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump , Kai Bird—writing with his wife, Susan Goldmark, whom he credits with contributing significant research—aims to bring Cohn into focus as a progenitor of Trump. Bird’s previous work as a biographer has focused on distinguished statesmen and scientists of the mid-20th century, most notably the left-leaning nuclear physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, whom he and Martin J. Sherwin wrote about in American Prometheus , the book adapted by Christopher Nolan for the movie Oppenheimer . Cohn, like Trump, had nothing but contempt for the norms and ethos of that mid-century elite. But Bird argues that this hatred was driven less by a coherent politics than by “dishonesty, narcissism, careless cruelty, and vengefulness.” Both men were avatars of the glitzy New York of the ’70s and ’80s, sharing an obsession with sex, a love of celebrity, and a hatred for expertise. Bird quotes the New York Times reporter Sam Roberts on the lessons Trump learned from Cohn: “1. Never settle, never surrender. 2. Counterattack, counter-sue immediately. 3. No matter what happens, no matter how deeply into the muck you get, claim victory and never admit defeat.” (Bird also implies that Cohn may have had a crush on Trump, blond and blue-eyed men being his ideal type.) In Bird’s telling , the parallels between Cohn and Trump begin with their childhoods. Both grew up in New York’s outer boroughs, in families that were prosperous but resentful of those in the real inner circle. Cohn, born in 1927, lived in the Bronx as a young boy, the only child of a loveless marriage. His maternal grandfather, a wealthy banker, founded the Bank of United States, whose clients were primarily Jewish immigrants. Cohn’s father, active in the Bronx Democratic machine, agreed to marry his mother in return for being made a judge, which her father could pro…

items.title: A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Lily Meyer, a staff writer who has published stories about the wisdom of Holden Caulfield , why making America’s houses bigger may have been a mistake , and the Seinfeld theory of fiction . Lily recommends watching The Sheep Detectives for a heartwarming mystery, listening to any song by the Hold Steady, and reading Brother of the More Famous Jack , by Barbara Trapido, if you want a good cry and a laugh. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor A good recommendation I recently received: My friend Eliza Brooke—a freelance culture writer who often covers movies—told me to watch The Sheep Detectives , which I had assumed was for children, but I trust her. I was absolutely charmed by the film and, at the same time, quite moved by its exploration of how we think and talk about death. Also, it’s a whodunit, and I love whodunits. Hollywood, could we please have fewer sequels and prequels and remakes, and more peaceful detective stories? The upcoming arts event I’m most looking forward to: I can’t wait to see the Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock show opening at the Met this October. I love abstract expressionism, and ever since I read Mary Gabriel’s Ninth Street Women —an exceptional group biography of five abstract expressionist painters, including Krasner—I’ve been fascinated by the arc of her career, which included creating government-sponsored public art during the Depression, making mosaics in the Long Island house she and Pollock shared during their marriage (meanwhile, he got an entire barn as a studio), and the flowering of her own painting practice after his death. Of course I’m excited to see the Pollock paintings at the Met too, but I’m most eager to see the Krasners. An actor I would watch in anything: Greta Gerwig. I saw Frances Ha , the gorgeous, bittersweet ode to female friendship that she starred in and co-wrote, a few weeks after I graduated from college—that is, at a moment when I was heartbroken about no longer living with my closest female friends—and I imprinted on her like a baby duck. The best work of nonfiction I’ve recently read: Vivian Gornick’s The Romance of American Communism . Gornick, a “red-diaper baby” raised in the working-class Jewish Bronx, set out to interview former Communist Party USA members and militants about what their political activity meant to them, years after the party had lost most of its following. The result is a surprisingly beautiful and often wrenching reflection on belief, belonging, self-delusion, and sacrifice. An author I will read anything by: Too many to name, so instead, I’ll give you a translator. I try to read—and believe I have read—everything that Megan McDowell translates. Her taste is impeccable, her style is flawless, and she works with some of the greatest Latin American authors writing today: Mariana Enríquez, Samanta Schweblin, Alejandro Zambra, and many more. A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “It’s Gonna Be Easy,” by the Texas outlaw-country singer Doug Sahm, is a soft, melodic lament for a relationship the singer wishes would be easier to forget. (A recommendation to go with it: Callie Collins’s novel Walk Softly on This Heart of Mine , whose protagonist is loosely inspired by Sahm. Like the song, the book is a gentle heartbreaker.) A loud song is “Waiting Room,” by my D.C. hometown heroes Fugazi. My husband and I asked the DJ to play it at our wedding, and the resulting mini–mosh pit is one of my favorite memories of the night. A musical artist who means a lot to me: The Hold Steady. I’ve been going to their shows since I was 14, and seeing them live is the closest I’ve ever come to a religiou…

items.title: The Golden Girls , but in a Camp Cabin
items.description: A t Camp Social , where grown women return to girlhood, friendship has no preamble. Within 15 minutes of meeting eight of the campers from Cabin 3, I learned this: In their 50s and 60s, they have no use for the menstrual discs in the camp swag bag; one of them found online dating so depressing after her divorce that she’s given up entirely; when they laugh, they pee a little; they feel like they’ve known one another for years, even though most of them met last night. The campers signed up for this weekend-long adult summer camp for exactly this purpose—to make new friends. On August 21, more than 400 women, some as young as 21, some older than 80, arrived at what usually is a children’s sleepaway camp in the Poconos to spend the weekend bunking in twin beds in log cabins, climbing the ropes course, developing middle-school-level inside jokes, making friendship bracelets, and performing choreographed dances at the flagpole to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” Everyone at Camp Social, regardless of age, is referred to as a “girl.” The camp promises to re-create a childhood experience so that grown-ups can bond with one another as easily as they might have as kids. I signed myself up because I wanted to know what kinds of adults would go back to summer camp and how seriously they would take it. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic My new home for the weekend with more than 400 possible friends-to-be The girls of Cabin 3 were all in. When they were younger, they told me, making friends did feel more straightforward. But then they got jobs that kept them late at the office, or their kids grew up, or they stopped drinking, and the friendships they’d made with other parents or neighbors faded. They began wondering: How do you meet new people? Where do you go? None of these women ever really thought they’d end up at an adult summer camp, but they saw ads for it and thought, Maybe I’ll give that a try . Which is how they found themselves at breakfast in the mess hall, cross-talking at Gilmore Girls speed, comparing notes on their adult sons, laughing when one revealed her favorite prank—taking a picture of her cleavage on the disposable cameras passed out at weddings. Over the hollering, Jackie Prendergast, a retiree who smiles so wide she shows both rows of teeth, told me that Cabin 3 had decided that its mascot for the weekend would be the flamingo. When a flamingo loses essential nutrients, as it does when reproducing, the pigment begins to drain from its feathers. With time and nourishment, though, the pink returns. “We’ve lost our color, but we’re going to get it back,” Jackie said. Ten minutes later, we headed to archery. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The vibes were, indeed, good. T he night before , Camp Social’s girls had gathered in the barn for a dance where a band (all male, all handsome) played Prince, Michael Jackson, and Bruno Mars covers. Liv Schreiber, the camp’s 29-year-old founder, took the stage in her Camp Social shirt. “Welcome to camp!” she shouted, then launched into an ecstatic speech about the weekend ahead. If anyone’s job could be described as “friend maker,” it is Schreiber’s. She is the type of person who skips more than she walks, makes it a point to memorize campers’ names, and, as I witnessed when we met up in New York City before camp, can form a real connection with strangers in a coffee shop in 10 minutes flat. She was working in real estate when she launched a viral matchmaking Instagram account and a matchmaking-party business, which morphed into events for adults to meet new friends. She opened Camp Social in 2023 to relive her own sleepaway-camp experience and to give women a place to meet. The waitlist, she told me, now runs north of 60,000 people. Adult summer camps have been cropping up over the past couple of decades—one even dates back to the 1970s—but many of them are co-ed and have the feel of either Club Med in the woods or an all-out bacchanalia. Schreiber’s is one of…

items.title: Which Dan Sullivan Will These Dan Sullivans Vote For?
items.description: W hat in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.” “It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me. “I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me. Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen? To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska. I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”) Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all impostors,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.” In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said. This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages. T he Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says. [ Read: Republicans have only themselves to blame for their Alaskan defeat ] The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaini…

items.title: This El Niño Will Be Unlike Any in the Past Eight Decades
items.description: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box. “Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal. Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas ) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Years of slow, partial recovery followed. This month, Tietjen and her colleagues, part of the Canadian scientist Julia Baum’s lab at the University of Victoria, discovered that nearly half of the island’s remaining corals had already bleached—a prelude, if warming persists, to death. When Tietjen comes back, she may well be swimming over a graveyard. Most of the world experiences El Niño’s ripple effects as the heat building up in the equatorial Pacific radiates into the atmosphere and around the globe. This means great gouts of rain in supercharged storms in some places; in other areas, crop-killing dry spells that can extend for months. Along the Pacific Coast of South America, torrential rains and landslides have forced the temporary closure of a main route to Machu Picchu, in Peru; deadly floods have swept through arid regions of northern Chile. Countries such as India and Ethiopia are enduring some of their driest summers on record. El Niños tend to mean more rainfall across the southern United States and drier stretches across a band in the North. Strong El Niños can mean record-breaking heat, and this one is shaping up to be unlike any catalogued in the past eight decades. A 2-degree-Celsius increase in the Niño 3.4 box typically earns the title of “Super El Niño”; we’re already past that threshold, and experts project that the warming could peak at roughly twice as high. “We are now pretty certain this will be an exceptional event,” Malte Stuecker, the director of the International Pacific Research Center at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told me. Part of the reason Stuecker expects this warmth to keep building is that the buoys along the equator can detect water temperatures well below the surface. Down more than 100 meters, an enormous mass of warm water has built up and will rise to the surface in the months ahead. The amount of heat brewing in the ocean has produced one of those graphs in which the current year departs drastically from past trend lines, wriggling up erratically into unfamiliar territory. Although scientists continue to debate the extent to which climate change makes El Niño cycles more frequent or intense, they agree that these cycles are occurring in an ocean that is warmer than it was. Last Saturday, the daily global average sea-surface temperature reached 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), its highest level on recor…

items.title: How Did Trump’s Trade Fight With Canada Go So Sideways?
items.description: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings , watch full episodes here , or listen to the weekly podcast here . In 1999, the creators of South Park were nominated for an Academy Award for their song “Blame Canada.” “ South Park , of course, is caustic and anarchic satire. But today, somehow, it’s become real,” the editor in chief of The Atlantic , Jeffrey Goldberg, said last night on Washington Week With The Atlantic . What started as a fight over trade has gone dangerously, ridiculously sideways. Why does President Trump loathe Canada but respect North Korea? What might NATO members be thinking about Trump’s treatment of his supposed allies? Joining Goldberg to discuss these questions and more: Stephen Hayes of The Dispatch , Idrees Kahloon of The Atlantic , Ashley Parker of The Atlantic , and Josh Wingrove of Bloomberg News. Watch the full episode here .

items.title: Pick Up Where You Left Off
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. Think about something that you loved doing when you were younger. Maybe you drew, played an instrument, wrote stories, or spent hours learning about something just because it fascinated you. Then school got busier, work took over, or the hobby started to feel less useful than everything else that was competing for your time. In 2023, David Brooks wrote an Atlantic article about people entering a new stage of life after their primary career. Many realized that, on the way up the professional ladder, they had abandoned interests and ambitions that had once mattered to them. In their 60s, they began picking up those lost strands. “The human hunger for meaning and fulfillment is strong,” Brooks wrote. “We shouldn’t have to wait until we’re 65 to learn how to transform our lives.” Returning to an old interest can remind you what it feels like to do something without needing it to lead anywhere. The point is not to re-create your childhood but to make room for interests that don’t fit neatly into the life you’ve already built. This weekend, return to something that you had quietly stopped doing. Pick up the book, racket, paintbrush, or instrument. You may find that you’ve indeed outgrown it—or wonder why you ever put it down. On Returning to What You Love The New Old Age By David Brooks What a new life stage can teach the rest of us about how to find meaning and purpose—before it’s too late ( From 2023 ) Read the article. How to Be Happy Growing Older By Arthur C. Brooks Your future will probably be better than your past. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. The Curious Personality Changes of Older Age By Faith Hill When people lose the ability to control their circumstances, their selves sometimes evolve instead. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. Still Curious? What I wish I’d known when I was younger : Last year, Arthur C. Brooks argued that the three reasons old people are happier can work for any age. Semi-retirees know the key to work-life balance : More and more older adults are working—in large part because they want to, Kate Cray wrote in 2023. Other Diversions Watching Tim Curry have fun was the most fun thing. What a bicentennial baby knows A turning point in AI writing PS Courtesy of Dennis L. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “The bristlecone; awe on a multi-millennial scale,” Dennis L. writes. We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. Reply to this email with a photo and a short description. — Rafaela

items.title: The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
items.description: One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai , which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons. Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop. I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all. [ Read: Why a Chinese animated film has made more money than any Star Wars sequel ] Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping , or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down. In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country— Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai ’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother. The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan , which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xin didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply c…

items.title: A New Way of Seeing Alien Worlds
items.description: Tomorrow morning, if all goes to plan, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, its latest and greatest orbital observatory, will lift off from its launchpad and add a little rocket-booster light to the Florida sunshine. A lot is riding on this mission. If the Roman is successful, it could give humanity a new way to see the planets around other stars and a fresh understanding of the largest-scale objects that we know to exist. But if it fails, NASA’s science program, which is already fending off ruinous budget cuts , will need to seriously rethink its future. The Artemis mission to the moon was a big win for human spaceflight, and now the science side of the house badly needs one. NASA’s engineers have spent more than a decade readying the Roman for this moment. Before the telescope arrived in Florida, it spent more than a year in NASA’s largest clean room at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. To get near it, you had to be mummified alive. When I visited in December, NASA staffers led me to a sterile, fluorescent-lit locker room. They tossed me a white jumpsuit and two sets of booties with tight-fitting straps. They told me to put on a beard net and hair net, and triple-wrapped the gap between my jumpsuit sleeves and gloves with blue tape. The astronomers didn’t want my skin exposed in the clean room. Dry flakes of it could drift off and settle onto the telescope’s ultrasmooth primary mirror. “You’re going to be the dirtiest thing in here,” one of them told me, as we walked through a little chamber where more than 30 nozzles blasted us with air. I jotted down this remark on special mint-green paper that sheds fewer particulates than a regular notebook, and then stepped into a cavernous eight-story white space soundtracked by the hum of six school-bus-size fans. At its center, the Roman stood more than 40 feet high, and it was surrounded by more than a dozen people, all in identical jumpsuits. Half were standing in clusters, talking, while the other half were up on motorized lifts, fussing with the telescope, applying duct tape and making final adjustments. More than a thousand people have worked on this project, and those who are lucky enough to get close to the hardware seem to derive a physical pleasure from the experience. [ Read: Inside Donald Trump’s attack on NASA’s science missions ] The Roman has a pretty shady backstory for a scientific instrument. Its primary mirror was part of a surprise gift bestowed on NASA by the National Reconnaissance Office. The NRO is one of America’s most secretive government agencies, and it apparently had a Hubble-class spare just lying around. A cash-strapped agency can’t afford to be too choosy about provenance: NASA took this mirror that was supposed to point down at the ground , for surveillance, and will instead point it out at the stars. Coronagraph delivery and unboxing (Chris Gunn / NASA) The NRO’s spare mirror has also solved a bit of internal politics for NASA’s science program. The Roman is built to monitor the universe at the very largest scales, to map the cosmic superstructure of galaxy clusters that stretches out from us in every direction, to see how it has expanded over time. These observations might lead scientists to a more refined sense for gravity, and may even help them discover new physics. But the idea for a mission like this was originally conceived of around the early 2000s, shortly after the discovery of dark energy , and a survey of the large-scale universe seemed like the obvious next thing to do. When NASA was finally ready to build the telescope, in the early 2010s, the action in astronomy had shifted closer to home. Scientists were in the midst of discovering thousands of new planets around nearby stars, and they wanted to find more. Although the Roman’s original mission plan did allow for some planet-hunting, the new mirror would allow them to do it in a whole new way. items.title: The Kennedy Center Has a Problem That Courts Can’t Fix
items.description: To put the legal fight over the Kennedy Center in operatic terms, it has become more than a little Wagnerian. After another hearing this week about another attempt to add Donald Trump’s name to its marble facade, the fate of the national cultural center remains grim and unresolved, and no finale is in sight. What could deliver a resolution? That’s still not clear, in part because the defendant in a long-running lawsuit—the Kennedy Center’s board of trustees—keeps making decisions that drag out the ordeal. A judge can restrain the board but has no power to remake it. Congress can remake it, but only through legislative action, which Trump can veto. And meanwhile, his board remains in place—able to make new decisions that invite new challenges that send the parties back to the same judge. In December, Trump’s allies on the Kennedy Center board—billionaires, White House aides, Fox News personalities, and other figures associated with Trump world—voted to add the president’s name to the building, and in March, they signed off on his plan to shut down the center for renovations. But by May, both actions had hit a wall: In a lawsuit filed by a Democratic member of Congress, Joyce Beatty, who serves as one of the board’s ex officio members, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper concluded that the board had exceeded its authority by renaming the Kennedy Center. He also found that its decision to close the center was likely a breach of the trustees’ fiduciary duties, describing that vote as “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” So they revoted this summer to close down, and they okayed a different plan to get Trump’s name back on the center’s exterior—in three places, actually, even though the relevant federal statute states that “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas” of the complex. Whatever the merits of the renovation plan, the Kennedy Center is plainly in crisis. Trump’s takeover drove away artists, donors, and audiences; staff purges have stripped it of institutional memory. There is a reasonable argument that because its brand has become so repellent, the Kennedy Center might as well close temporarily so that tenants such as the National Symphony Orchestra can have a shot at recovery beyond its walls. But the ongoing litigation has exposed other concerns about the institution’s leadership, who include an executive team led by Matt Floca—whose expertise is in facilities, not arts management—and a board, the chair of which is Trump himself. Although boards at nonprofits are charged with oversight, this one has largely rubber-stamped proposals that have come before it. After Cooper ordered the board to take a more detailed look at the renovation proposal, it commissioned a new report from a commercial real-estate firm, JLL. (Five years ago, JLL was tapped to try to sell Trump’s Washington, D.C., hotel, though it backed out after the January 6 riot.) This week, Justice Department lawyers representing the board suggested in a court filing that the entire Kennedy Center complex might have to be “taken down” if the renovation plans are thwarted. Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center has gone largely silent. A tarp still hangs over the facade where Trump’s name was once fastened, a decision that critics have characterized as a petulant display of the president’s vanity. The board has argued in court filings that removing Trump’s name jeopardizes “hundreds of millions of dollars” in donations to a mysterious fundraising vehicle, which it created earlier this year. The board has provided no detailed accounting of how a two-year closure would affect ticket sales, fundraising, or artist relationships—even as reporting from The Washington Post this week revealed that the center’s finances have deteriorated dramatically since Trump’s name was put on the building, issues about which the board was informed.
