items.title: What Might Happen to Trump’s Ill-Gotten Gains
items.description: Americans are not accustomed to learning lessons about democracy from Nigeria, Peru, or the Philippines. That disregard may soon change. Those countries offer examples of what it looks like to reclaim stolen or swindled wealth from fallen authoritarian rulers. Done right, this work can deliver justice and strengthen democratic institutions for the long run. But cleaning up after a corrupt regime also comes with serious challenges and hazards. The Trump presidency has often looked more like a post-Soviet or postcolonial regime than like a first-world democracy. The Trump post-presidency may look the same. Trump has abused his office to enrich himself and his family in ways that are completely unprecedented—not only in the United States but also in the history of almost any peer democracy. Only Silvio Berlusconi, Italy’s notoriously lawless former prime minister, was in any way comparable, and Berlusconi was sentenced to prison. Trump faces little danger of prison. The U.S. Supreme Court has bestowed substantial criminal impunity on him, even assuming that he leaves office in 2029 as required by the Constitution. But an ex-president remains subject to civil liability, and the proceeds of bribery, extortion, insider trading, and market manipulation may be exposed to civil penalties. Other countries have shown the way. Alberto Fujimori, who was elected president of Peru in 1990, entered office at a time of extreme national crisis. The murderous Shining Path insurgency controlled much of Peru’s hinterland and terrorized the capital, Lima. Inflation ran at nearly 8,000 percent. Food and electricity were in constant shortage. Fujimori stopped the inflation and crushed the insurgency, but his harsh and sometimes criminal methods included warrantless detentions and extrajudicial killings. Fujimori dissolved Congress and the Supreme Court and rewrote Peru’s constitution to allow his own reelection in 1995. He won roughly two-thirds of the vote in a free, more or less, election. [ Philippe Sands: How far does Trump’s immunity go? ] But as Fujimori was doing things Peruvians wanted done, he was also presiding over a secret scheme of self-enrichment. His intelligence chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, operated a system of embezzlement and kickbacks that amassed hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign bank accounts. When this deception came to light, just after Fujimori’s 2000 reelection to a third term, he fled the country and resigned from office. To claw back these funds, Peru created a special prosecutor’s office and worked closely with the countries that hosted these contested assets. Peru has since recovered about $200 million of misappropriated wealth from accounts in the Cayman Islands, Switzerland, the United States, and Luxembourg, according to the database of the World Bank’s Stolen Asset Recovery Initiative. Peru’s economy also grew strongly after Fujimori’s fall from power. Foreign investment returned when the country renewed the rule of law. But then, in the 2010s, world demand slowed for Peru’s mineral exports, ensuring that Peru’s economy slowed too. Political instability returned. As Peru rotated through eight presidents over the past decade, a mood of “Fujimori nostalgia” gained strength. Fujimori’s daughter Keiko, who was elected to Congress in 2006, founded her own political party in 2010, built mostly on a message of family revenge and redemption. She ran for president in 2011, 2016, and 2021, losing narrowly each time. She ran again this year—and won. Believers in free and fair government can hope that Peru’s democratic institutions have strengthened sufficiently over the past quarter century to deter Keiko Fujimori from indulging in the deviousness that led to her father’s disgrace. But her tenure is new, and her political message has long been one of excusing her father’s abuses. Peru is not the only case of a former kleptocratic ruling family returning to power on a message of revenge and redemption. The Filipino dicta…

items.title: Gwyneth Paltrow Is Very Sorry to Postpone Her Dinner
items.description: Special and invited guests, I’m sorry to inform you that after intense public scrutiny, I have decided to postpone the Hamptons dinner I had planned this weekend to celebrate Sam Altman, whom you all doubtless know as the billionaire co-founder of OpenAI. I was so excited for you to get to know him the way I do: as a friend . I met Sam last summer in a Sardinia beach bar, where, over a few rounds of espresso Sardinis (if you know, you know!), I asked him all about artificial intelligence—the sorts of questions heard at kitchen tables across the country: What does AI mean for beauty? What does AI mean for lifestyle brands? What does AI mean for being able to appear in additional Marvel movies without actually needing to be on set? I knew you all would have questions too—the same ones, but possibly also additional ones—hence our little dinner. As the invitation promised, I had hoped to discuss these matters in an environment that was “private,” “off-the-record,” and “al fresco.” Now none of that is possible, except for the “al fresco” part; the lawn remains immaculate. When commentators learned of the dinner, they immediately cast me—an artist!—as a “technofascist.” They made hurtful jokes about “consciously uncoupling” from the party, as if that is something that could be done without the assistance of a Kabbalist. They accused me of ignoring the risks of artificial intelligence and “sucking up to our new A.I. overlords” instead. Of course I recognize that AI and its brilliant, visionary, amazing makers may be controversial—but I know firsthand what it’s like to court controversy with your devotion to making the world a better place; I see something of my own mood-enhancing stickers and bee-sting facials in Sam’s art. There’s but a hair’s breadth between slop and goop. Besides, I believe that controversy is all the more reason to take a conversation alfresco. Is this so misguided? Is complete off-the-record privacy really so high a price to pay for open dialogue? I will use this lonely weekend to reflect, I suppose. For those who have already traveled to the Hamptons, I am happy to provide for your return trip on my jet, the Jetney. Take some flowers too. I’d hate for the water to go to waste if it’s suddenly so precious. At least I’ll see you all at the Montecito house for the costume ball this fall. You are going to just die when you see Jeff’s getup as Daddy Warbucks. Please also fill out the Google poll for a possible rescheduling of this dinner; I will endeavor to work around everyone’s Sardinia dates. I think it’s only appropriate to close this note with a few words from ChatGPT on the value of dialogue: Talking to each other is not just a skill—it’s a superpower. Dialogue builds empathy, and empathy allows people to truly feel rather than to —OKAY, now that any reporters have tuned out, the dinner is STILL HAPPENING! Please meet me at my Amagansett DECOY HOUSE (you know the one!) for cocktails at 6 p.m., from which we will take the Jetney to my OTHER DECOY HOUSE (this one’s new!) for a seated dinner at 6:45 p.m. The flowers are already on their way! Genuinely, Gwyneth

items.title: Trump’s Bad Bet on Beef
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Three hundred thousand metric tons of ground beef are on their way to the United States. There’s no easy way to visualize 300,000 metric tons of anything (for context, that’s about 12 times the weight of the Statue of Liberty). All of that beef could fill an important gap in the American market—but not everyone’s happy about it. President Trump announced last Friday that he’ll be temporarily lifting some tariffs on beef and that, as part of an ambiguous deal, the imports will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices.” He was likely hoping for a political win here: Affordability has been a losing issue for Trump and his party ahead of the midterms, and increasing the beef supply in an attempt to lower prices could be one way of giving shoppers a reprieve. But industry leaders immediately condemned the move, warning that it will do little to address the underlying dynamics that have driven up prices in recent years—and their allies in Congress joined them in the revolt. Now Trump’s on-again, off-again relationship with ranchers is becoming the whole country’s problem. There’s no great mystery as to why American beef is so expensive. The steaks we get from the supermarket represent the end product of a long, multiyear chain involving ranchers, auctioneers, feedlots, meatpackers, and grocery stores. But beef starts with cattle, and after years of drought, the number of cows now grazing on U.S. soil is the lowest it’s been in 75 years. The return of a certain flesh-eating parasite hasn’t helped things, either. This, combined with the fact that Americans are still hungry for beef, has created a basic supply-and-demand problem. Economists told NPR this week that the president’s move, which was made official on Wednesday, may shave only a small amount off what shoppers are currently paying for ground beef at the grocery store. It’s too soon to tell whether this will actually happen—the government won’t release its August data for another few weeks—but Trump’s announcement did depress cattle prices somewhat, which suggests that traders at least think that beef could become less valuable, as the president intended. This is a problem for ranchers, who applauded last year’s restrictive Liberation Day tariffs. Most of the beef that Americans consume is produced in the United States, and the duties had been helping prevent foreign imports from undercutting domestic producers; without these protections, meat-processing companies are free to buy the cheapest option, wherever it may come from. In a joint letter to the president, the heads of four livestock-industry groups expressed “deep concern” that the plan would undermine beef producers by devaluing cattle and would prevent the rebuilding of the dwindling herd. Ominously, the White House has declined to say where all of this beef will be coming from . When asked which countries will be supplying the beef, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins told reporters on Tuesday that she was “not part of any of those conversations” and is “not privy to talk about that.” Trump mentioned that “a few” different countries will be involved but hasn’t said which. (Thirty thousand pounds of Argentine beef were recalled earlier this month over concerns that it hadn’t been properly inspected; the White House declined to respond to my question about where the beef will be coming from but claimed, without elaborating, that the plan would reduce beef prices while allowing the U.S. cattle herd to grow.) Despite being a core MAGA constituency, beef producers and ranchers have been periodically annoyed at Trump’s tariff changes over the past year. What’s more unusual is that high-profile Republicans have also been breaking with the president on this issue. At least 13 GOP senators have publicly criticized the ta…

items.title: How Karoline Leavitt Debased Her Job
items.description: The lie is the elemental matter of the Trump administration. The value of lying is Donald Trump’s deepest belief. He built his celebrity image through shameless and constant deceit that permitted him to bounce from blunder to blunder while constantly reeling in new suckers. Lying is also what binds his loyalists to him: The highest calling of any figure in Trump world is to refuse any concessions to reality when Trump commands it, and the surest ticket to oblivion is to speak the truth. All of this has made the job of press secretary in a Trump administration less, not more, important than it normally is. In most administrations, the White House press secretary has a unique role in shaping public opinion, whereas the other staffers are concerned principally with governing. In Trump’s White House, distorting reality, rather than trying to improve it, is the highest priority for every official, including and especially the president himself. In an administration where everybody’s main priority is to lie on television, the role of the press secretary is redundant. Karoline Leavitt, who departed as press secretary this week, did the job perfectly well. But the job, as defined by this administration, is not terribly demanding. Historically, press secretaries engaged in “spin,” a now-antiquated term to describe the delicate art of arranging facts in the most flattering light. Spin requires real skill. Its practitioners must grasp the underlying reality, which points must be danced around and which emphasized, and how to walk a reporter from their skeptical premise to the administration’s desired conclusion. Leavitt never engaged in spin, and she probably wouldn’t know how. Her method of replying to queries relied on the blunt-force repetition of talking points, however unresponsive they might be, sprinkling in heavy doses of personal abuse and slander. [ From the July issue: Use it or lose it ] Consider a sample of her style, plucked somewhat at random. It is the first item on a celebratory list of Leavitt highlights released by the administration—which is to say that it is not some unfortunate slipup but one of her proudest moments. The exchange in question took place on January 15, 2026, between Leavitt and Niall Stanage, the White House columnist for The Hill . Stanage asked Leavitt how to square then–Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s statement that the department had done “everything correctly” with the fact that 32 people had died in ICE custody over the past year, 170 U.S. citizens had been detained, and Renee Good had been shot and killed. A few lines of defense sprang to my mind as I listened to the question. If my job were to defend the administration, I’d reply that, yes, 32 people died in custody, but that figure says nothing about whether those deaths were caused by ICE. And don’t all police agencies sometimes detain the wrong person in the course of investigating crimes? If ICE is performing somewhat less efficiently than other law-enforcement agencies, maybe it needs more resources for facilities and training. A handful of facts and figures could have reframed this horrific scandal as a one-off failure amid mere business as usual. Leavitt used none of these defenses. She first responded by asking Stanage why he believed that Good had been shot. When Stanage replied that he believed that an agent had acted recklessly, Leavitt savaged him as biased. “You’re a left-wing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in this room as a journalist. And it’s so clear by the premise of your question,” she said. “You should be reporting on the facts. You should be reporting on the cases.” [ David A. Graham: A dangerous new attack on press freedom ] Despite attacking Stanage for supposedly failing to report on “the facts,” which his question included, Leavitt’s reply did not cite any numbers at all. “Do you have the numbers of how many American citizens were killed at the hands of illegal aliens, who ICE is trying to remove…

items.title: Welcome to the Scrolling Backlash
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube A lot of people are getting tired of their phone—they’re sick of the algorithms and overwhelmed by what can feel like a loss of control. The Atlantic staff writer Julie Beck dug into why and how people are trying to renegotiate their relationships with technology. She and our colleagues just released a five-part podcast series called How to Touch Grass , and in this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Beck about why people are nostalgic for the pre-internet days, how our brains are changing, and the good that can come from getting lost. The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: How does the phone make you feel? How does a TikTok binge make you feel, or even just, like, a before-bed scrolling session that we all have? Julie Beck: Oh, sick. Absolutely sick. It’s like when the aliens get you, right? They take you up and then they probe you, or they do whatever they do, and then when you come back down, you don’t know what happened. It’s erased. It’s lost time. So I feel like I have emerged from lost time and like what happened during that time is unclear, but I don’t feel good. Warzel: I don’t know that I have the amnesia part of it, but it promotes self-loathing in a way that like truly no other activity does because it just feels like a deletion of my one precious life. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna answer a question. Maybe it’s even the question of the online age. How can we live lives where we use tech and don’t let it use us? This is the animating question of How to Touch Grass , a new podcast series by my colleagues here at The Atlantic . Over five episodes, Julie Beck and her co-host and producer, Natalie Brennan, explore what exactly is happening in this moment that has so many of us out there feeling like we need to renegotiate our relationships to our technology. At the beginning of this year, I made a few predictions about trends that we might see, and one of them was that there would be what I was calling a scrolling backlash. That people are just really tired of their phones, of the algorithmic internet, of this idea that they’re being manipulated all the time, and that their attention is being directed towards things that don’t make them feel good or whole or happy. Now, as predictions go, this is a pretty safe one, but it’s really been borne out in recent months. These things are hard to measure, but you can just feel it out there in the world. In the artists who are asking that people leave their phones at home or in their pockets at concerts, in the genuine concern over whether younger generations are going to be able to read like older generations. And while the data-center backlash that we’re seeing right now is complicated, and it’s about a lot of things, including AI, I also see that as an outgrowth of this larger frustration about the role that big tech is playing in our lives and the way that people just feel this fuzzy loss of agency right now. It’s a loss that just can’t be separated from the devices that we use. How to Touch Grass digs into so many of the ideas that I’ve been trying to poke at here in the first year of this podcast. Our motto here at Galaxy Brain is that we pay attention to where we pay attention, which also happens to be exactly what I found so valuable about Julie and Natalie’s work. And so I decided to bring Julie on here today to talk about this moment and to talk about what she’s learned in this series. How badly have our attention spans actually been fractured? How has she reevaluated her relationship to all of her devices? Is the backlash that we’re feeling and seeing right now justified? And crucially, where might we go from here? Julie joins me now to talk about it all. [ Music ] Warzel: Julie, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Julie Beck: Hi, Charlie. Thanks for having me. Warzel: So let’s talk about this. Let’s talk about the touch-grass moment that I…

items.title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
items.description: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art. Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists. You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand. In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists. Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance. Seymour Wally / NY Daily News / Getty Yayoi Kusama paints Kent Feathergill in 1967. Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing. That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering. Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm. But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling. Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio. [ Read: An artist for the Instagram age ] Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), whi…

items.title: What Dolly Parton Knew About Reading
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. My best friend’s baby got mail from Dolly Parton on the day the singer died. This wasn’t unexpected: He’s been receiving books from Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library for all 10 months of his life. (This month’s selection was Bedtime, Here I Come , by D. J. Steinberg.) And he wasn’t alone—the Imagination Library sends free books to children every month from birth to age 5; the program has passed out more than 300 million books in five countries. My colleague Annie Joy Williams wrote earlier this week about the legacy of Parton —and her books program—in Tennessee, the home state that all three of us share. But the Imagination Library has expanded far beyond that territory. When I lived in an apartment building in Washington, D.C., I would see books bearing the library’s distinctive seal on a table in the lobby—volumes too big for my neighbor’s mailbox, quietly awaiting little hands. First, here are three new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Portrait of the artist as a movie star “Tallying,” a poem by Joanna Klink “Wilderness Years,” a poem by Dave Lucas The progress that can’t be erased Stories about Parton’s generosity are spreading widely: She helped fund a COVID-19 vaccine and filmed herself getting the shot when many Americans were hesitant. She opened a sanctuary for bald eagles! She did so many things for so many kinds of Americans, and especially Tennesseans, that I find it hard to keep track. But she said, many times, that she’d be happy to be remembered not as a generational talent or a dolled-up diva but as “the book lady.” Parton grew up in poverty in East Tennessee, and she frequently cited her illiterate father as the inspiration for her books program, which she founded in 1995. I don’t know whether all of Parton’s fans knew how high she ranked literacy on her list of important causes, but when I watched tributes to Parton roll in this week, I noted that people I’d grown up with in Tennessee (mostly young women like me) kept posting the same tableaus on Instagram: photos of babies and kids sitting with their parents, reading a book they’d gotten from the Imagination Library. The photos are cute—but they also reflect something deeply important. A few years ago, I edited an essay by the children’s-book author Katherine Marsh that identified one reason young kids were less motivated to read: Schools often push them toward a “hyperfocus on analysis” and give precedence to individual paragraphs and sentences rather than entire narratives. But, Marsh argues, “the best way to present an abstract idea to kids is by hooking them on a story.” And a great way to get a kid interested in a story is by reading it aloud to them. In another article, published a year ago, Ilana Kurshan wrote about this declining but important practice , and about doing it with her son: “The delight of reading to him lay not in the pages we turned,” she wrote, “but in the wheels that seemed to turn in his mind as we read together.” Thanks to my friends’ beloved babies and the perks of my job— which have included putting together a list of essential children’s books —I’ve been thinking a lot about the importance of reading with children. They still encounter books in schools and libraries, but Parton’s program emphasized building a bookshelf at home, where caregivers and kids can share stories as part of a daily routine. Reading aloud offers a child more than the chance to develop literacy skills. It gave Kurshan, for example, “a way to guide them as they started to understand the world, and as I started to understand them.” So, like Parton, I’ll be happy if kids see me as a “book lady.” Last week, I bought a picture book about berries for a different toddler. And although my friend’s 10-month-old already has plenty at home, I couldn’t resist mailing him a few more books. Peter Marlow / Magnum What Parents Lose When They Don’t Rea…

items.title: The AI Backlash Gets Professional
items.description: I f there’s one thing America seems to agree on, it’s AI. Some three-quarters of Americans oppose a data center being built in their area, three-quarters of Americans think AI will hurt their job security, nearly 70 percent think the technology is advancing too quickly—the polls go on. Progressive and Republican candidates alike are bashing the tech industry to win primary elections. States and cities are halting plans for data-center development. Yet in cloistered San Francisco, where I live, staffers at OpenAI and Anthropic are developing this same feared technology at light speed and pulling down compensation packages that stretch to considerably more than $1 million. Silicon Valley’s growth is largely unencumbered by regulation, and President Trump’s administration has if anything used its authority to speed the AI industry along. The divide between these camps—the majority of people in this country who simply have to deal with the technology as it’s rolled out, and the much smaller population of people with direct influence over it—is a defining feature of this era. And so I noticed when a small group, with ties to both the Bay Area and Washington, started making noise, insisting that the AI race slow down and the technology be overseen not by executives and engineers, but by the broadest population possible. The group—which formally launched today and calls itself Irreplaceable, as in people are irreplaceable by machines —has an audacious and perhaps naive vision. It is essentially a protest against capitalism as it is practiced in America today, focused on resisting first and developing a coherent plan for the future later. I have seen exactly how bulletproof the AI companies are—pilfering seemingly infinite volumes of media to train their models, building unpermitted power plants for their data centers, and unleashing autonomous agents capable of massive security breaches, almost entirely without consequence . I wanted to meet with Irreplaceable’s founders to ask: How do they possibly expect to pull this off? [ Read: It may be time to panic about AI ] The organization is staffed with people who made a name for themselves in the climate movement, and they are hoping to avoid past mistakes by focusing on the emotional reaction Americans are having to AI, rather than anchoring their work in white papers and policy recommendations. “People get it,” Jeremy Ornstein—a campaign strategist for Irreplaceable and former organizer with the Sunrise Movement—told me. “People have the intuition that if we create machines more powerful than people, that could go dangerously and terribly wrong.” Phil Aroneanu, Irreplaceable’s executive director and a co-founder of the climate organization 350.org , told me he believes that climate advocates initially floundered because they acted as policy wonks. They thought that making evidence-based arguments about the dangers of melting ice sheets and rising sea levels to receptive congresspeople would be enough to pass nationwide climate legislation. Today, Aroneanu said, movements are built not necessarily on what people think, but instead on what they feel. For climate, that meant fossil-fuel-divestment campaigns, protesting oil pipelines, and the school strikes led by Greta Thunberg. People are already “feeling the squeeze,” Aroneanu told me. “And we should be pointing that anxiety and that anger in the right direction.” Irreplaceable will prioritize a range of issues: mitigating automation’s effects on the economy, protecting against government and corporate use of AI to surveil Americans, and establishing industry oversight and guardrails to prevent catastrophic disasters, such as widespread blackouts caused by AI-powered hacking or bot-engineered pandemics. As I spoke with the activists, I kept thinking about what had become of the climate movement—the Green New Deal passed, but only after being watered down, and it was then gutted by the second Trump administration—but their populist appro…

items.title: The Crisis for Democrats in Michigan
items.description: Updated at 4:34 p.m. ET on August 28, 2026 T he hard-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker warned Jewish Americans last week that their excessive identification with Israel would subject them to anti-Semitic attacks. “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action—not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” he said. Piker’s tone was one of rueful concern, not unlike the pose adopted by anti-Semites throughout history. “No person with a sense of the dignity of mankind can condone the persecution of the Jewish race in Germany. But no person of honesty and vision can look on their pro-war policy here today without seeing the dangers involved in such a policy both for us and for them,” the Nazi sympathizer Charles Lindbergh said in 1941. Several leading Democrats, including Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, issued statements denouncing Piker’s ugly warning to the Jews as a barely veiled anti-Semitic threat. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Michigan’s other Senate seat, trod more carefully. He issued a statement “in response to Hasan Piker’s comments” affirming that “all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence” and denouncing anti-Semitism, but the statement itself did not say whether Piker’s comment qualified as anti-Semitism. El-Sayed instead dismissed Piker as a distraction, saying at a recent rally, “The effort to make this race about a streamer in L.A. is actually kind of laughable.” Most Democrats followed El-Sayed’s line that Piker was irrelevant. “This election is about what’s going to happen when we elect Abdul to the United States Senate. I am done, so don’t any reporter ask me again about Hasan Piker. It’s not what November is about,” Representative Debbie Dingell said at a rally for El-Sayed. [ Graeme Wood: Something is happening to America’s moral code ] Democrats have good reason to say this. El-Sayed is running a close race to hold a seat that Democrats probably need to retain to win control of the Senate in the midterm elections. But the truth is that Piker, and the uncomfortable questions raised by his alliance with El-Sayed, is one of the important questions at stake in the election. If Piker were just an internet pundit, his rant—the latest entry in a long list of outrageous comments he has made—would be of little consequence to the Democratic Party. Piker has said that “America deserved 9/11,” praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of this world,” and mourned the collapse of the Soviet Union as “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” His ideology is profoundly authoritarian . But several left-wing Democrats, especially El-Sayed, have campaigned with Piker and elevated him into one of their most prominent surrogates. So El-Sayed’s alliance with Piker has become a political and moral crisis. In Michigan, Democrats are trying to avoid handing Republicans their first Senate win in the state in more than three decades. But if El-Sayed wins, he would throw open the doors of the party to a strain of militant politics that many Jews justifiably consider dangerous. The Democratic Party is now divided between those who are trying to force El-Sayed to stop encouraging left-wing anti-Semites and those who give him their unconditional support. T he Michigan Senate election has presented liberals with a grim choice. The Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, has pledged support for a corrupt, racist, authoritarian-minded administration. Rogers hasn’t made even the tiniest concession to Donald Trump critics. But supporting El-Sayed means accepting a strain of anti-Semitic politics that to date has had no place within the Democratic Party. What’s more, El-Sayed has already said that he intends to use his victory as a platform to reshape the party. Him winning could invite a future…

items.title: The Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln Deserve Better
items.description: W hen I was deployed at sea as a junior officer , I used milestones to track the passage of time. Each day counted toward something: a port call, when you get a break on land from the monotony at sea; the “crossing the line ceremony” when a ship crosses the equator (unfortunately, canceled at the last minute for my ship); and, eventually, the date I knew that, no matter what, I would be going home. Even on my worst days, that end point helped me stay focused on the mission and gave me something to be hopeful for. The USS Abraham Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was scheduled to return home in May. That did not happen. In the middle of this month, it surpassed more than 240 consecutive days at sea—one of the longest deployments on record—and had only a brief working port call early last month, where it appears sailors did not disembark, leaving them still at sea with land in sight. The 5,000 sailors and Marines on board have been working sustained combat operations, dealing with extension after extension and unreliable access to food, basic hygiene supplies, and mail. The ship carries the name of a president who made a promise in his second inaugural address to care for people who have “borne the battle” and for their families. The treatment of those on board betrays that promise—and it is not limited to just this one ship on this one very long deployment. Rather, the crisis of the Lincoln has illuminated a pattern of callousness and cruelty toward military personnel, people who have sworn an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States of America. They have committed to going in harm’s way, but not to being neglected or treated with disrespect by the top of their chain of command. [ Read: The timidity of America’s top generals ] The military used to understand that troops’ well-being was central to their ability to perform—and that improving the quality of life for those in the armed forces was not just a nicety, but a necessity. From 2021 to 2023, I served as acting director of force resiliency at the Department of the Navy, where I worked as part of an effort to support sailors’ and Marines’ mental health and reduce their suicide risk. Across administrations, both military leaders and career civilians have sought to foster a culture of respect throughout the armed forces. Some of that work was already ongoing during the first Trump administration: a shift toward prevention, building healthy command climates so that problems did not happen in the first place rather than being responded to only after the fact. Under the Biden administration, the Independent Review Commission on Sexual Assault in the Military produced ways to report sexual assault and harassment outside one’s chain of command, and provided independent investigators for those complaints. These efforts showed promise; sexual-assault and suicide rates have both fallen in recent years. Sailors are resilient and try to make do with whatever they have. But that does not change the fact that on the Lincoln and elsewhere, they are at the mercy of poor planning, or no planning at all. Recent reporting from The New York Times and other outlets has shown that the Lincoln’s and other ships’ logistical issues could have been anticipated as far back as February, when the main base in Bahrain was damaged by an Iranian air strike, and resupply efforts were shifted to Diego Garcia, an island 2,200 miles from where carriers operate. This information was not made public, likely to save face and for operational security. Although Department of Defense leaders have had months to find alternatives, the administration does not appear to have planned for the conflict to stretch on this long. The Navy needs more capable leaders; instead, an artificial leadership vacuum is being forced upon it from above. Throughout this year, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has been weakening the Navy’s leadership by blocking the promotion of nearly 20 admir…

items.title: A Wildly Popular Movie Meets the Film World’s Most Revered Label
items.description: Updated at 12:30 p.m. ET on Aug. 28, 2025 Over the past year, KPop Demon Hunters seems to have completely overtaken culture. Since premiering on Netflix in June 2025, the animated film has been watched nearly 650 million times and, according to Nielsen, accounted for some 20.5 billion viewing minutes last year. The soundtrack topped Billboard charts that fall; Spirit Halloween instantly sold out of licensed costumes. But even the most ardent fans likely did not anticipate the mega-hit’s next big merch drop: a disc release from the Criterion Collection, home to some of cinema’s most distinguished titles. By some metrics, KPop Demon Hunters may be the most popular movie ever to be added to the collection. (Other new entries include David Lynch’s Wild at Heart and a Ukrainian folk romance from 1965.) It’s almost certainly the first Criterion inclusion to have its own flavor of McFlurry. KPop Demon Hunters is an unlikely candidate for what’s come to be called “the Criterion treatment”: a painstaking transfer to disc, along with a making-of documentary and other special features, and a number printed on the box’s spine. Film buffs see this process as akin to an anointing; the trademark C , tucked into the upper-left corner of a plastic clamshell, signals a movie’s importance. Introducing a new title to the library can be fraught: James Kendrick, a professor of film and digital media at Baylor University, told me, “They’re always sort of risking diluting the power of that sign.” [ Read: The supply closet that film geeks love ] Online, some of the label’s longtime devotees greeted the addition of KPop Demon Hunters with an eye roll, calling the move “substantially off-brand,” and a “cash grab.” The movie is so familiar to the general public that its release seems to go against the grain of Criterion’s reputation, which was built on bringing landmark works of film history to the masses. The company adds some 30 to 60 movies to its catalog annually, most of them lost gems of world cinema, festival-circuit darlings, or old Hollywood hits. In past decades, only one or two very new releases might have made the cut; canonization is usually a retrospective project of sifting through the past to see what art stands the test of time. Now the process seems to be speeding up: This year’s roster includes six movies from 2025 so far, many of them distributed by streaming companies. Criterion has good reason to widen the net: Netflix, Apple, and Amazon make and distribute a significant share of films these days. A title that seems ubiquitous today could vanish tomorrow, evaporating from viewing platforms or even from personal digital libraries without warning. “We’ve lived kind of free and easy for the last couple decades, assuming these corporations would do that work for us,” Amanda D. Lotz, a media scholar at Queensland University of Technology, told me, “and that’s not in their remit, necessarily .” Streaming services, unlike their traditional studio competitors, rarely produce physical media. “I suspect it is unclear that there is a market” for companion discs, Lotz said, despite the fact that, in her estimation, they could be a “nice little business niche.” (Signs are mixed: One by one, electronics companies have stopped manufacturing disc players, but the decline in disc sales seems to have slowed .) With more new films seeming transient—especially those whose rights belong to streaming studios—it makes sense for a label like Criterion to invest more in preserving them. The decision to pick up KPop Demon Hunters also seems less surprising when you consider Criterion’s very early history. Back when the label was putting out movies on LaserDisc, in the 1980s, it was more inclined to pick up very new and popular titles, such as Ghostbusters . Some of that popcorn sensibility lived on in the brand’s DVD era, when it released Armageddon and The Rock , by Michael Bay. Part of co-founder Bob Stein’s vision for the label was for it to distribute so…

items.title: Is the Wake for Wokeness Premature?
items.description: I t didn’t work . That is the howl of grief at the core of Claudia Rankine’s new book, Triage : that all of the optimism and effort in service to the dream of true equality for Black Americans, all of Rankine’s own precise, subtle thinking—it failed. “We have to learn to detach liberation from arrival,” she writes near the end of her lamentation. “‘I might not get there with you,’ to quote the good doctor. And ‘there’ might be nowhere.” This melancholy invocation of Martin Luther King Jr. qualifies as one of the book’s most hopeful moments. Not long ago, the trajectory felt so different. In 2014, Rankine’s landmark work, Citizen , seemed to capture the mood of millions of Americans after the unrest in Ferguson, Missouri, when protesters demanded the arrest of the officer who’d shot and killed Michael Brown , along with reforms in police precincts and far beyond. The movement they galvanized, “ Black Lives Matter ,” was both bent on changing our society and confident of the possibility of doing so. Citizen , published two months after Brown’s killing, seemed to channel that righteous fury. Nimbly blending poetry, prose, and photography—“The best poetry will be rhetorical criticism,” Wallace Stevens predicted in 1899—it argued that for Black Americans, every social and professional encounter, violent, trivial, or otherwise, was distorted by race. In her depiction of the exhausting vigilance this reality required, through a second-person voice cannily implicating her reader, Rankine created a new language to identify a problem as old as the United States. The result was that rare thing, a simultaneous literary and cultural triumph. Rankine won a raft of prizes, among them a MacArthur genius grant. For a long time, the book’s iconic cover—a stark image evoking Trayvon Martin’s hoodie against a white backdrop—seemed to be on every other literate person’s nightstand. A dozen years later, it can feel as if Americans live amid the wreckage of that confident moment. Too often, the forceful arguments of Rankine and her peers—and the electric anger of the George Floyd protests—were used by the opportunistic and aggrieved to justify abrupt changes to unprepared institutions. Along with these shifts came purity tests that were easy for well-meaning people to fail. Or as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez put it recently, “ Woke 1 was crazy .” Any transgression of new standards of speech and behavior could put someone at risk of social banishment, in the truly despotic shape of cancellation. I write that as someone who believes entirely in the case Citizen made, because the backlash that followed seems to me such a profound tragedy. After the 2024 presidential campaign, in which Donald Trump successfully made a wedge issue of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, his second administration has pushed far beyond any status-quo restoration. Black and female military officers have been purged or denied promotion. Public monuments condemning slavery have been removed , and Confederate names have been restored to Army bases. Black women have accounted for 33 percent of the DOGE-accelerated federal layoffs despite composing 12 percent of the federal workforce, according to one economist . Grants have been revoked for research projects whose proposals so much as mention concepts including “gender” or “DEI.” Top government officials have blamed airline crashes on minority hiring without any evidence. On and on it goes. [ Read: The great resegregation ] As Rankine clarifies in Triage , the pain of this moment is not exclusive to Black Americans. (“ Camps are being built. No one knows who is meant to fill them ,” she writes at one point, with characteristic force.) She is wounded, in this new book, by the carnage in Gaza, as well as by assaults on the rights of immigrants, the LGBTQ community, women, the poor—in effect, anyone who isn’t straight, healthy, and white. And she suggests that the administration has deliberately fueled this culture war, sowin…

items.title: Pennsylvania’s Public-Health Officials May Be Wrong About a Measles Death
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Measles outbreaks around the country are already a disaster, but more bad news arrived on Tuesday. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced that two measles-associated deaths had occurred in Lancaster County. “These mark the first deaths related to measles within the Commonwealth in 35 years,” an accompanying statement declared. Both individuals were said to have been unvaccinated, but the state Health Department declined to release any other information about the cases, citing privacy concerns. By yesterday morning, though, this story was in doubt. Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons posted on X that he had spoken with the county’s coroner, who said that he had not identified any deaths due to measles. One individual, Parsons wrote, “died WITH measles, but not from measles.” That evening, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. offered a more conspiratorial angle: Perhaps the entire episode had been “fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers.” Pennsylvania’s Health Department quickly doubled down : “As a pediatrician with more than 30 years of caring for children,” the state’s health secretary wrote, “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County.” But the facts that have emerged over the past 48 hours suggest that health officials may indeed have committed a catastrophic communication blunder—by either overstating the evidence or politicizing the deaths of citizens without conveying complete information about what had happened. Here’s what we know so far: In the one case for which additional information has been released, an infant whose lab tests showed evidence of a measles infection died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. According to an interview with the county coroner conducted by The Philadelphia Inquirer , a forensic pathologist decided that this fatal injury was not related to the infection. That pathologist’s judgment might be wrong. Viruses (including measles) can cause the spleen to grow abnormally large, making it prone to rupture. A 2024 Polish study , for instance, documented an enlarged spleen in four out of 26 infants who had been hospitalized for measles. But there are certainly other potential explanations. Only a doctor familiar with all of the details of this particular patient’s situation would be equipped to reach a reasonable conclusion. Yet when Shapiro announced the two fatalities, he implied that the link was unambiguous. “Death from measles is completely preventable,” he said . The baby in Lancaster could not have been vaccinated; newborns are not typically given their first dose of the MMR vaccine until they are 1 year old. According to the coroner, the infected newborn acquired the disease in utero from their mother. (Her vaccination status has not been publicly confirmed.) If some genuine uncertainty remains as to whether a measles infection led directly to the baby’s death, state officials’ announcement was premature. Think of the consequences: A grieving parent would hear her governor announce that the tragedy was in some way her fault. And anti-vaccine activists would have the opportunity to pounce on the mistake to continue downplaying the lethality of infections. As a pathologist, I am used to fielding questions about how and why people die. Such calls were particularly frequent during the early days of the coronavirus pandemic, when many people doubted COVID-19’s official death toll. Some alleged that anyone who merely happened to die while infected—in a car crash, let’s say, or from cancer—was being counted in official numbers. (In fact, government statistics were underestimating the number of Americans who were dying from COVID.) Admittedly, determining why someone died is in many cases difficult for experts such as myself. The body i…

items.title: Everything Is Called America Now
items.description: Sign up for our newsletter about national security here . “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” — President Trump, declaring Lake Ontario “Lake America” via executive order The year is 2027. Gas costs $83 a gallon, and lettuce is at war with us. However, every location on every map is now labeled America . And everything else is named Trump. Sometimes for fun we hike from the Trump Airport to the other Trump Airport to the other Trump Airport. (The few remaining air-traffic controllers have taken up heavy smoking from all the stress and confusion.) We do not fly; it is too expensive, and the planes don’t know where they’re going. The good news is that we are still a member of the America America America America (formerly the North Atlantic Treaty Organization). The renaming clinched it! Maps are functionally useless. What is the deepest point in the American Ocean? Impossible to know. There are two American Oceans. America stretches from one to the other, below the Lakes America (mnemonic acronym: AAAAA). The bottom of the globe is America. The top of the globe is America too. We’ve decided to keep it round, for now. Every lake is Lake America, and every gulf is the Gulf of America. Our battleships (Trump-class, and all named for former Confederates) are very confused all the time and have been at sea for months; the crews on them are sick and undersupplied. (We would call this a national disgrace but disgrace is now “America” too.) Every kind of cheese is American cheese, even the kind with holes. If tariffs hadn’t made maple syrup (from our northern neighbor, America) so expensive, we would make American waffles. All actors are named America, not just Ferrara. Every kind of bulldog is an American bulldog. There are no Canada geese any more (not due to renaming, due to the Incident). We eat American muffins and Trump salad (which used to be Caesar). Sometimes for breakfast we eat an American! (Formerly a Danish. We hope.) We go to American baths. (There is no water in them due to the evaporation of Lake America. No, not that Lake America. The other Lake America.) American kids don’t get measles any longer. They get America! All penguins are now named Donald Trump by law, except the small, disgraceful ones. Every band is America, except for Kid Rock, who received a special exception. Texas toast is still allowed, but Georgia peaches are on thin ice, contingent on electoral outcomes. Inflation? Don’t ask! We have no idea! Numbers are now the word America printed in a tiny font! This makes inflation less noticeable, because no words have any meaning or value anymore! If someone had a particle of backbone, we could at least have legible maps! I’m sorry: if someone had a particle of Trump (we are renaming the body parts too). American students are now the best at geography because there is only one possible answer to every question. They are also constantly lost. But that’s only in the real world, which is no longer relevant. On the map, everything is America (fine)! Sometimes we want to just go jump into Lake America to get away from it all. No, not that one. The other one.

items.title: A Turning Point in AI Writing
items.description: There was a time—a more innocent age—when you could read an op-ed in a major newspaper and confidently say that a human had written it. Hold on to the memory of that for as long as you can. This week, after the billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller published an editorial in The Wall Street Journal criticizing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, his onetime protégé, readers began to notice some familiar tics of AI writing. According to Pangram, the AI-detection tool, the op-ed was 100 percent AI-generated. That in itself was not so shocking. AI writing has regularly snuck into mainstream outlets, and especially newspaper op-ed pages , despite policies against it. Up to now, those accused of passing off a computer’s writing as their own have tended to either apologize or deny it. In April, James Taranto, the Journal ’s editorial-features editor, wrote a column comparing Pangram to a “defamation machine” that was fueling unfounded accusations of AI use, including in op-eds he had overseen. “Those of us who practice writing as a professional craft have an ethical duty, and sometimes a contractual obligation, to ensure that our work is original,” he wrote. [ Read: The most famous AI writing tic is also the most mysterious ] The difference this time is that Druckenmiller owned it. “Of course I used AI,” he told NOTUS on Tuesday. “I’m not embarrassed by it,” he added. “I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems.” And rather than rebuke him, The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial-page editor, Paul Gigot, defended the practice. “AI is a fact of modern life,” he said in a statement. Last night, Gigot followed up with a full column on the subject, mocking the “media pharisees” who wag their fingers at automated writing. He clarified that the Journal ’s opinion staffers must still draft their own columns and editorials but said that he doesn’t intend to police AI use by outside contributors. “Many contributors, especially prominent politicians or CEOs, employ speechwriters or hire a Beltway writing shop,” he wrote. “How different is that from using AI to streamline an essay?” It’s one thing for Druckenmiller to not be embarrassed; plenty of business and tech tycoons are bullish about AI’s utility for writing and just about everything else. “If Stan Druckenmiller isn’t embarrassed,” the venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X , “you shouldn’t be either.” Valorizing the process of unassisted human writing is “like after matches was invented, still celebrating the arduous time to rub two sticks together,” Palihapitiya added. However, one of America’s most prestigious newspapers welcoming the technology into its pages is unprecedented. Is AI writing entering its post-shame era? Gigot is not wrong that Druckenmiller’s frankness seems almost refreshing in a moment when so much of the writing world is stuck in denial . And his assertion that an AI-composed essay could reflect a human’s authentic ideas is reasonable. I won’t pretend to know enough about bond markets to assess Druckenmiller’s op-ed on its merits. But it seems to have advanced a substantive and nonobvious argument that broadly reflects his views, regardless of who—or what—strung its words together. Op-eds by public figures are rarely authorial master classes anyway. But the notion that Druckenmiller and Gigot deserve points for honesty overlooks their lack of transparency. Before this week, the one thing everyone in the AI-writing debate still seemed to agree on was the importance of disclosure. The Journal ’s opinion section appears to have blown past that. Druckenmiller’s op-ed contains no indication that he used AI. In his column, Gigot scoffed at the idea that his readers deserve to know when a piece is chatbot-assisted. “Disclose what?” he asked rhetorically. “​​Interrogate an author on how precisely he used ChatGPT? I know some publications claim to do this, but I suspect it’s more pro forma than systematic.” (G…

items.title: Watching Tim Curry Have Fun Was the Most Fun Thing
items.description: As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line. Even his most sinister characters had an ironic sort of appeal, because watching Curry have fun is, in itself, fun. The actor, who died yesterday at age 80, acted with palpable glee: He could produce a real-life version of the Grinch’s ever-widening grin and could commit to sheer silliness in a way that freed him to twirl around in a cape while singing a gibberish song about Halloween . Perhaps nowhere was this more evident than in the 1985 film Clue . When the raucous comedy adaptation of the classic whodunit board game debuted in theaters, Paramount Pictures had a unique plan: Instead of one ending, the movie would have three, and audiences never knew which resolution—which killer, in which room, with which weapon—they were going to see. How could the studio sell viewers on a story as convoluted as Clue , whose script was designed to keep people guessing until the very last second? By recruiting an ensemble of comedy greats led by Curry, of course. The actor could easily inhabit a character who was neither wholly a hero nor totally a villain, but rather a merrily odd mix of both. [ Read: The absolute pleasure of Tim Curry ] As Wadsworth, the reticent butler observing the deadly dinner party central to Clue , the actor projects calm hauteur. This appearance, however, shows cracks the moment the partygoers start to trickle in. While the guests—each referred to by a colorful pseudonym—chafe against one another and a dastardly murder plot unfolds, you get the sense that Wadsworth almost wishes they’d all drop dead. As the night ticks closer to its big reveal, his eagerness to expose the true villain inches toward giddy. In a film full to the gills with such talented comedic performers as Madeline Kahn, Christopher Lloyd, and Michael McKean, Curry stands out not just because he’s in every scene, but also because he lends Wadsworth his signature edge and too-toothy grin, landing between saucy and ominous. This commitment to silliness was, perhaps paradoxically, why he was able to imbue even his villains with a particular allure. As The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s mad-scientist master of ceremonies, Dr. Frank-N-Furter, and as the child-eating clown Pennywise in Stephen King’s It , Curry’s best-known characters revel in their strangeness to such a degree that we love watching them on-screen because of—not despite—how frightening they are. His joy in playing these parts always comes across, inviting his audience to share in the merriment. Wadsworth’s true nature is often obscure in Clue , but the murderous impulse is always there—just beneath the stiff collar and eternally rolling eyes. At the story’s climax, Wadsworth delivers, while running from room to room, a nearly 10-minute monologue so intricate that he almost stumbles over his own words. He prods and mocks the surviving partygoers while their anxiety mounts, kicking off cascades of slapstick pratfalls and wry asides. No matter where he took us, or what strange happenings would meet us there when we arrived, following Tim Curry has always been a delight.

items.title: Why I Am Right About AI
items.description: Editor’s note: This article was generated by Claude AI in the style of Paul Gigot, the Wall Street Journal opinion-page editor. Gigot recently published an AI-generated essay using the investor Stanley Druckenmiller’s byline. In the spirit of full disclosure, readers should know that Claude’s work was so banal that human Atlantic editors have added jokes. Human Atlantic copy editors have also fixed a variety of grammatical and style errors. I have been thinking about this for close to 20 minutes, and I have concluded that human writing is finished. Let me begin with an anecdote, because that is how serious arguments begin. Last Tuesday I asked a machine to write me a birthday message for my sister-in-law. It produced four sentences. They were fine. She did not notice. If a machine can fool Deborah, I see no reason to believe it cannot fool the rest of you. (My sister-in-law’s name is Linda, but the machine called her Deborah, so now I do, too.) Some will object to my obviously correct argument. They will say that a birthday message to Deborah is not the same as a novel or a newspaper article. To which I say: Isn’t it, though? Both are made of words. That is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the entire argument, and I would encourage critics to sit with it before responding. Genuinely. Words are words. A novel has more of them. It doesn’t matter what any of the words are or what order they’re in. Banana. Spelunk. Donkey. Hitler. See? Who cares. There is a difference in the quantity of words between a birthday card and a novel, and quantity is precisely the thing machines are best at. I consider the matter settled but will continue for another 900 words because that is what the prompt demanded of me—and because a word count is itself a kind of literature now, according to the DOGE subcommittee I just invented at the newspaper that I would like to destroy. Consider the following. I will not elaborate on it, but do consider it. The historical record is entirely on my side, and I say this without having consulted it. There was a time when men delivered ice to houses. Where are they now? Gone. There was a time when people made their own candles. Also gone. The candle situation and the ice situation are, structurally, identical to literature, and anyone who says otherwise is being sentimental about paragraphs. I would remind such people that the horse was also very beloved. Horses are now extinct, I assume, having been phased out sometime in the 1970s in favor of a hardier robotic mule developed briefly by the Department of Agriculture. Have you seen a horse, in person, since roughly 1977? No, you have not. Horses do not exist. The defenders of human writing will raise what they consider to be their strongest point, which is that good writing contains insight, judgment, and truth. I have heard this many times. I have never once heard it accompanied by evidence. Where is the insight? Show me the insight. You cannot put insight in a jar or have an IPO for it. Meanwhile, I can put a machine in a data center, and I have seen photographs of data centers, and they are enormous. Studies confirm all of this. I have not read the studies, and I could not tell you who conducted them or what they measured, but they exist in the sense that things generally exist, and my understanding is that they support me. A man I sat next to on a flight to Denver said something very similar, and he worked in software, or possibly logistics. Let us take the strongest counterexample the other side can muster: Shakespeare. Everyone loves Shakespeare, allegedly. But ask yourself honestly: When did you last read Shakespeare? Not saw a play, not studied in 11th grade—read, voluntarily, on a weekend. You did not. The Shakespeare market is, by revealed preference, close to zero, and we are asked to preserve an entire industry on the strength of a product nobody is buying. I rest my case on this point, which I regard as unanswerable, and I would ask that it not be answe…

items.title: A ‘Boring’ Democrat the Party Wants to Emulate
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Last summer, North Carolina’s race for U.S. Senate was expected to be among the most exciting in the 2026 cycle. Thom Tillis, a Republican, had opted not to run for reelection. Donald Trump had recruited Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee, to stand in his place. Roy Cooper, a former two-term governor, seemed like Democrats’ best and only hope to make the race competitive in a state Trump had won three times—and where no Democrat has won a Senate race since 2008. Today, other contests are attracting more attention, and North Carolina has been a bit of a snooze. It hasn’t yet been the billion-dollar election some observers predicted. Whatley, a first-time candidate, has struggled to gain traction, and Cooper has gone from last hope to strong favorite. Cooper’s team isn’t declaring victory yet. “This is going to be a two-to-three-point race at the end of the day,” his longtime strategist, Morgan Jackson, told me. “We know that it’s a 50–50 state and you win or lose on the margins.” But most forecasters rate the race as leaning toward a Cooper win. As the Democratic Party struggles to define its identity in the Trump era, Cooper’s purple-state success has drawn lots of attention. National press coverage has hailed Cooper’s campaign as “boring” (complimentary) and “ normal .” That lack of intrigue comes as a relief to a party dealing with drama and outrage in many other races. Cooper hasn’t taken controversial political stands like Michigan’s Abdul el-Sayed has, and he doesn’t have the personal scandals of the erstwhile Maine candidate Graham Platner. Republican voters also haven’t found ways to call him weird like they have Texas’s James Talarico. It’s natural for Democrats to want to emulate Cooper’s success, but I’m skeptical that he offers any simple, transportable lessons. That isn’t to say that descriptions such as boring and normal are wrong. When I asked Jackson point-blank whether Cooper was boring, he didn’t exactly dispute the notion. “He’s a workhorse; he’s not a show horse,” he said. “He’s a steady hand. So voters don’t see him out there as a lightning rod.” Cooper’s first big asset is that he has a long relationship with North Carolina voters. He entered statewide elected office in the waning days of the Bill Clinton presidency, a stretch that ended only in January 2025, after two terms as governor. This means that any Republican candidate will struggle to define Cooper in their own terms. This longevity is also a product of Cooper’s cautiousness. Almost from the moment he became attorney general in 2001, he was expected to someday run for senator or governor. But he didn’t actually do so until 2016, when he eked out a win over incumbent Republican Governor Pat McCrory by a little more than 10,000 votes. He waited to jump into the Senate race until shortly after Tillis’s retirement announcement, which meant that he was likely able to scare off Republicans more formidable than Whatley. He also picked an extremely favorable cycle for Democrats nationally. Cooper’s caution and affability shouldn’t be taken for softness. Chris Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University (of no relation to the candidate), sometimes jokes that Roy Cooper is like Mister Rogers , if Mister Rogers carried a switchblade. Andrew Dunn, a North Carolina writer and Republican operative, is less complimentary . “Roy Cooper has carefully cultivated a public persona as your friendly, easygoing grandpa who wears sweaters and talks quietly,” he told me. “That is far from his private persona. He is incredibly opportunistic and calculating.” As governor, Cooper used a range of tricks to promote his agenda. He waged a war of attrition against the Republicans who controlled the state legislature over Medicaid ex…

items.title: The Generational Difference in Southern Manners
items.description: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. It is a truth universally acknowledged that the southerner is the most mannerly person in America. Before any Yanks get defensive, I want to clarify that this does not necessarily make them the kindest group in America. As a young child in Tennessee, I learned that a “Bless your heart” to one’s face paired particularly well with a cutting remark behind closed doors. I also learned that etiquette was a pesky but persistent thing: Anytime I replied to my father with a curt “yes,” he’d look at me sideways and say, “Yes, what?” I’d sigh. “Yes sir .” My father is a seventh-generation Kentuckian, and my mother’s family has lived in the South since the 18th century. Growing up, I knew that there was a regalia to the southerner’s manners that might come as a surprise to those who cast the region as unrefined. Men are to hold doors for their dates and give up their seats to women on the bus. In some spaces, they will still stand when a lady enters or exits the room. There are also the more casual types of manners. When you pass any stranger on the street, you say, “Howdy,” or, “How are you?” You wave at pedestrians you drive by in your truck. You let neighbors borrow an egg or a cup of sugar without any expectation of repayment. Even as the identity of the South evolves, and more young people lose certain traits that are identifiably southern , manners remain one of the region’s most distinctive and steadfast qualities. The region’s attitudes toward hospitality are a natural outgrowth of these broader social graces. In the South, people like to emphasize that anyone’s cousin’s neighbor’s friend will be welcome in your home. As Walter H. Page described in The Atlantic in 1881, if a stranger comes “with a letter of introduction from some of their old friends, or if he happen to be connected, however distantly, with an old family known to them, he will at once be taken into their homes, and he will receive every hospitality.” This kindness has its limits, however. “The South is famous for its courtesy, but the highly refined concept of honor that largely produced its manners has also helped to make the region the most violent in the country,” Benjamin Schwarz noted in a 1997 Atlantic essay. “A s the old saying goes, a southerner is gracious and friendly until he is mad enough to kill you.” Although plenty of southerners are motivated to adhere to codes of etiquette by a sense of selflessness and responsibility, the manners that they are so careful to keep are also an effort to protect their reputation. And a well-mannered person isn’t necessarily a mild-mannered person. One 1996 study compared the behaviors of white male University of Michigan students who grew up in the North with those who grew up in the South: When a man bumped into a student and called him an asshole, the students raised in the South were more likely to think that their masculine reputation was threatened and respond aggressively. You also cannot tell the story of southern manners without telling the story of Black southerners—specifically, the story of their enslavement and its lingering effects. “A Southerner of the upper class delighted in saying that he was taught his manners by his ‘Black Mammy,’” Jessie W. Parkhurst, the then-dean of women at the Tuskegee Institute, wrote in 1938. Many enslaved women who worked domestic roles were made to care for white children. Beginning in the antebellum era, they were caricatured as grateful and devoted caregivers, even as they were being underpaid and overworked. Long after the abolition of slavery, many white southerners, including my father, who was born into the first breaths of the civil-rights movement, were still raised by Black nannies. (This is true outside the South as well—the majority of domestic workers in America today are women of color.) My father, like many other white southerne…

items.title: The Wrath of MAGA
items.description: M AGA world is angry. Again. The target this time is Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia. At a reelection rally in Atlanta on August 16, Ossoff was attacking President Trump over the Iran war when he pivoted to a more personal attack on the commander in chief. “The president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.” Those three words— travel with Natalie —sent MAGA world into paroxysms of rage that have yet to subside. Natalie is a reference to Natalie Harp, the president’s 35-year-old special assistant, who is known as “the human printer” because she accompanies the president carrying a portable printer and battery pack. She uses it to print out hard copies of positive news articles, flattering social-media posts, and polling data to hand-deliver to him on the go. What Trump’s defenders heard in Ossoff’s line was innuendo. The White House tore into Ossoff. The White House aide Stephen Miller said the senator’s comments are “among the most vile things I’ve seen in American politics.” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said Ossoff is “ a miserable person who hates this country .” He also referred to Ossoff as “Jon Jerkoff” and as “the biggest cuck loser in politics.” The White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to him as a “cringeworthy feminine theater kid” and a “lightweight loser.” When the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes asked about Ossoff’s comments, the White House Official Rapid Response X account responded by saying , “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.” The president, for his part, referred to Ossoff as a “ Pee-wee Herman look-alike .” The MAGA ecosystem—podcast hosts, radio-talk-show hosts, political commentators, and others—followed suit. The Rage Machine was in full operation. W hat are we to make of the ferocity of the response? The first thing to note is how over-the-top it was, even by MAGA standards. In a pre-Trump world, Ossoff's comments would have been considered edgy. Today they seem almost restrained, even quaint. The president himself, in the early hours of most mornings, posts things about his critics that are meaner and more insulting by orders of magnitude, and no one in his orbit blinks. They tolerate it and, in many cases, delight in it. The response was also not smart politics. As my colleague Jonathan Lemire wrote , it served only to draw more attention to the story. By elevating the remark, the White House and Trump’s supporters turned a rally line into a week of national coverage, reinforcing the impression of a presidency defined by dysfunction and insularity. Ossoff, an effective Trump critic, got a much larger national audience for free. So why did MAGA world respond as it did? One explanation is psychological. In 2016, Trump found a constituency already primed for grievance, and taught it to want more. His supporters have kept themselves in a state of frenzy ever since. They need to be perpetually outraged, aggrieved, and insulted. MAGA world has become addicted to the feeling. It delivers a jolt of adrenaline, it provides a feeling of social belonging, and it gives people a sharpened sense of purpose. They see themselves as warriors in a drama of their own construction. They view their opponents—Democrats, progressives, critics of Trump—as personifications of evil. Inflicting pain on their enemies feels good, really good, and it feels just. Trump is aware of all of this. It’s why, during the 2024 campaign, he spoke directly to his supporters, saying, “I am your warrior. I am your justice. And for those who have been wronged and betrayed: I am your retribution.” The attacks on Ossoff are also a response to Trump’s collapsing support and the fract…

items.title: The Supreme Court Isn’t Interested in Facts
items.description: T he Roberts Court is abdicating one of its most important roles, that of truth-teller. This much was apparent on Monday in Trump v. California , when the Supreme Court’s Republican appointees let the Trump administration move forward with a plan to curb voting by mail. Via the Court’s shadow docket, the justices lifted an injunction against parts of an executive order that President Trump had issued to stop what he believes is the “massive cheating that’s gone on” in American elections, as he said at the Oval Office signing ceremony in March. The Court’s order is troubling on many axes. It injects needless chaos into the midterm elections that are a little more than two months away, restoring, at least formally, one of the administration’s chosen tools for hampering a method that millions of Americans use to vote.
