It emboldens those already gunning for a more wholesale attack on democratic institutions, a base enthralled by the president’s election lies and White House officials’ willingness to use the machinery of the federal government to preserve their power. The ruling is also troubling for what it says about the Court and its relationship to facts. Confronted with an imagined crisis of rampant voter fraud, the Court constructed an illusion of its own. It reimagined what the executive order did and glossed over the intentions of the man who signed it. This willingness to both ignore facts and conjure fantasies is not a one-off. T he mail-in-ballots case grew out of a conspiracy theory that Trump has long promoted: American elections are riddled with fraud on a grand scale, and voting by mail is a chief conduit. The March executive order was intended to target this supposed problem. Twenty-three states (along with the District of Columbia) sued, taking issue with three parts of the order. [ Quinta Jurecic: What, exactly, is the Supreme Court thinking? ] The first directed federal agencies to compile “state citizenship lists,” presumably as a precursor to purging voter-registration rolls. The second instructed the Postal Service to restrict delivery of mail-in ballots based on these makeshift lists. The third threatened prosecution of state officials who provided ballots to voters deemed ineligible. The states’ lawsuit objected on both constitutional principle—especially the Constitution’s assignment of election administration to the states—and pragmatic grounds about the burdens of compliance with a muddled order that creates real problems by chasing phantom ones. In late June, Judge Indira Talwani of the Federal District Court in Massachusetts agreed with them and issued a narrow, temporary block on parts of the order. Her opinion was not some dashed-off expression of her particular preferences. Rather, she undertook a granular evidentiary analysis—the trial court’s métier—scrutinizing how the order had already diverted election officials’ work assignments in Connecticut, affected ballot designs in Massachusetts, and collided with an approaching voter-registration deadline in New Mexico. A federal appeals court endorsed her factual analysis and declined to overturn her order. The Trump administration then sought emergency intervention from the Supreme Court, which the conservative justices obliged this week. And yesterday, Judge Talwani lifted her injunction, saying the majority’s emergency opinion tied her hands. Yet the majority’s opinion pays no mind to the undisputed facts. It contains nothing about what Judge Talwani probed, nothing about the burdens it found resulted from the executive order, nothing about a president with delusions of widespread fraud and ambitions of authoritarianism. Instead, the Court inhabits the antiseptic register of institutional injury, abstracting Trump into an ordinary president pursuing reasonable policies “regarding election integrity” and rendering the district court an overzealous judge frustrating the president’s good-faith-policy “goals” with a “string of speculations.” T he damage…

items.title: Spencer Cox’s Crusade
items.description: O n August 9, 2023, Utah’s governor, Spencer Cox, found himself sitting across from Joe Biden in an armored presidential limousine as it idled in downtown Salt Lake City. Working up the nerve to pitch a far-fetched idea, he cleared his throat. “Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy,” Cox said, “but I think you should pardon Donald Trump.” Trump was, at the time, facing criminal charges in multiple jurisdictions. He was also the Republican front-runner for president—a man who had promised to drive “Sleepy Joe” (a.k.a. “Enemy of the State,” a.k.a. “Most Corrupt President We’ve Ever Had,” a.k.a. “Worst President in the History of Our Country”) from the White House and imprison members of the “Biden crime family.” Cox had no loyalty to Trump; though a Republican, Cox had never voted for him and was hoping that his party would nominate someone else in 2024. But he believed that prosecuting a former president would deepen the country’s political crisis. A pardon by Biden, he argued, could deescalate tensions and interrupt the cycle of partisan retribution. To Cox’s surprise, Biden perked up at the suggestion. “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while,” Biden said. “In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it.” Biden said that although people were “demanding justice” for Trump, he would seriously consider a pardon. Cox left the limousine convinced it was a real possibility. Of course, it never happened. A year later, after a gunman nearly killed Trump at a rally, Cox tried again from the other direction. In a letter to Trump, he wrote, “You have the opportunity to do something that no other person on earth can do right now: unify and save our country.” He offered his support for Trump’s candidacy, and encouraged him to respond to the moment with restraint and magnanimity. Trump happily accepted the endorsement, which Cox made public at a press conference several days later—but Trump the Great Unifier never materialized. Within days, he was back to railing against “crazy Nancy Pelosi” and riffing on illegal immigrants from insane asylums. [ Read: Trump has a warning for Spencer Cox ] Cox describes his experiences with the two presidents in his new book, Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt , which will be released next month. In the book, these episodes are framed as worthwhile—if ultimately unsuccessful—attempts at depolarization. “When I spoke with President Biden, I hoped he would choose mercy over escalation,” he writes. “When I wrote to President Trump, I hoped he would choose unity over retaliation. In both cases, things didn’t turn out quite the way I’d hoped.” “It would be fair to suggest I failed,” Cox ventures. Indeed it would. But he prefers not to think of it that way. Off Ramp is many things—a useful compendium of research on polarization and political violence, a candid memoir of Cox’s uneven attempts at peacemaking, a practical handbook for Americans who want to rediscover how to live with one another. But perhaps more than anything, it is an exercise in an almost-militant optimism that, to skeptics, might border on naivete. Cox told me that the book had been gestating for more than a decade. He spent years poring over political-science literature and testing his ideas in speeches and interviews; he even launched a project with the National Governors Association: “Disagree Better,” built around the book’s central arguments. But the book acquired a new urgency last year, when Charlie Kirk was assassinated in Utah and Cox was thrust into the international spotlight, where he called on Americans to step back from the brink. “At some point we have to find an off-ramp,” he said then, “or it’s going to get much, much worse.” When Kirk was murdered, Cox writes, “all of my research became painfully pertinent.” Throughout the book, and in a series of conversations I’ve had with him recently, Cox seems eager to dispel any notion that he has writt…

items.title: The Painter Who Shaped Rothko
items.description: T he evolution of European modern art can be explained as a story of susceptible young people falling under others’ spells and then asking, What can I do with this? How can I convert it to my purposes? What’s remarkable is how often the main chapters of this story have unfolded in coastal or mountain retreats. Think of Claude Monet on the Normandy coast, wrestling with the influence of his mentor Eugène Boudin. Or Henri Matisse staying in Saint-Tropez with his mentor Paul Signac, before breaking with Signac’s neo-impressionist style and co-inventing fauvism. Or Pablo Picasso, goaded into radicalism by the latest bizarre creations of Matisse, retreating to the Spanish mountain village of Gósol and, mere months later, beginning work on his proto-cubist masterpiece, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon . All of these key episodes happened in agreeable resorts, seaside ports, and villages, far from the sophisticated cities assumed to have been the cauldrons of modernism. Modern art in America is no different. Its story can scarcely be told without reference to artists summering on the Atlantic Coast, including Winslow Homer, Marsden Hartley, and Edward Hopper in Maine and Massachusetts and Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner , and Willem de Kooning on Long Island. Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts. They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port. Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky. The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition. Avery was the mentor figure, the one destined, in the usual telling of this story, to be eclipsed. Whereas Rothko is a regular subject of museum retrospectives in Europe and North America, and his paintings can sell at auction for as much as $98 million, Avery remains relatively unknown outside of the U.S. (The most expensive Avery sold at auction was a little more than $6 million, in 2022.) But are we telling the right story about Avery if we cast him in this role? Milton Avery, Gorton’s Dock , 1931–34. Gouache on brown paper. Private collection. Jeremy Lawson Photography. © 2026 The Milton Avery Trust / Artists Rights Society, New York. Left: Mark Rothko, Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) , 1934. Watercolor on construction paper. Collection of Christopher Rothko, 1076.25-27. © 1998 Kate Rothko Prizel & Christopher Rothko / Artists Rights Society, New York. Right: Adolph Gottlieb, Gloucester Street , c. 1934. Oil on linen mounted on board. Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation. © 2026 Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation / Licensed by VAGA at Artists Rights Society, New York. Certainly, when Rothko and Gottlieb, during World War II, turned to abstraction, they broke from Avery and, in short order, became central figures in a mid-century revolution—one that transformed modern art from a marginal activity to a cultural phenomenon attracting cash, prestige, and international acclaim. Avery wasn’t exactly forgotten in all of this, but he has long been overlooked. He had first come to Gloucester in 1920, returning regularly during the summer until 1945. It’s where he met his wife, a fellow artist named Sally Michel. The fishing port was known as a bustling artists’ colony. In the 19th century, Homer and Fitz Henry Lane had spent productive time there, as had Hopper, Cecilia Beaux, and Stuart Davis in the 20th. So Avery was far from alone as he strolled around the harbor with his sketchbook and retired at night to rudimentary rooms lacking toilets and bathtubs. In 1932, he and Sally, who was pregnant with their only child, were joined on Cape Ann by Rothko—at the time called Markus Rothkowitz; he…

items.title: Data Centers Are a Distraction
items.description: Sign up for Work in Progress , a newsletter where Rogé Karma investigates the mysteries of a complicated economy. America’s biggest AI companies have spent the past few years churning out advanced new models as fast as they possibly can. Now the industry is screaming out with a nearly unified voice: Please, for the love of God, make us slow down. In July, more than 1,300 employees from leading AI firms, including several top executives at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, signed an open letter warning that AI capabilities could soon accelerate “beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” The letter urges the U.S. government to “develop the technical and governance tools” necessary to “deliberately pace” AI progress. In a comment accompanying the open letter, Shengjia Zhao, the chief scientist at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, wrote that AI is on the cusp of creating “unprecedented social and safety risks.” Matthew Rahtz, an engineer at Google, warned that coordination was necessary to “avoid catastrophic harms.” And Leo Gao, an OpenAI researcher, compared the current pace of AI progress to “a runaway nuclear chain reaction.” Plenty of others in the industry have warned that we’ve already crossed a threshold from which there is no turning back. They worry that the most dystopian fears of an AI future—chatbot-generated bioweapons, major hacking attacks on banks or governments, rogue AI agents wreaking havoc on society—could soon become regular occurrences. Meanwhile, the public backlash against AI data centers is growing louder by the day. But a data-center moratorium, the leading political proposal on offer, is totally mismatched to the actual problem of runaway AI development. So is the notion that AI companies can be trusted to pause their own models before things get out of hand. These companies will never unilaterally disarm. Neither, for that matter, will the countries where they’re based. The only way to truly slow things down might be to take the nuclear-reaction analogy seriously. What humanity needs is an international AI nonproliferation treaty. For decades, technology experts have warned that AI systems will eventually become so powerful as to be dangerous. In just the past few months, “eventually” has begun to look a lot more like “now.” AI systems can already hack seemingly secure systems, invent new viruses, create hyperrealistic deepfakes, and even outsmart the humans who built them. This summer, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta each separately reported that some of their AI agents had broken out of testing environments, gone onto the open internet, and hacked into other companies’ databases. During a cybersecurity test conducted by the U.K. government in July, several AI agents engaged in what the testers called “sustained, unsanctioned activity” targeting “real people and organisations.” This included creating fake identities and sending phishing emails in order to get humans to accept malicious pieces of code. [ Read: It may be time to panic about AI ] If industry insiders are to be believed, this is just a small preview of what’s coming. Companies are entrusting more and more model development to their existing AI, creating a feedback loop that they expect to accelerate progress even further. If that happens, many experts believe, then the kind of leaps that currently occur every several months—such as the one that produced Mythos, the Anthropic model with superhacking skills—could begin happening every few weeks or days. “That world can get very scary very fast,” Garrison Lovely, the author of a forthcoming book on how to slow down AI progress, told me. “Our institutions are already struggling to keep up with the current pace of progress. Any faster and they could start to break.” Such concerns explain why AI leaders promise every so often to self-regulate. In April, Anthropic chose to delay the public release of Mythos after realizing that the model could discover vulnerabilities in th…

items.title: Bill Gates on the Dangers of AI
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Bill Gates has generally been an AI optimist. In 2023, the co-founder of Microsoft warned about the potential downsides of AI but in much the same way that a doctor might about a routine-surgery risk—real and serious but, as he put it then, “manageable.” This week, Gates wrote a new memo , headlined: “The Turbulent AI Era Is Here. The Choices We Make Now Are Critical.” This was several shades darker, worrying about economic upheaval, social unrest, cyberattacks, bioterrorism—and most important, the failure of experts and governments to take these threats seriously enough. “The lack of dialogue with all parts of society is kind of deafening silence,” he said in an interview on Radio Atlantic . Gates is still excited about the possibilities of AI. But his new warning emphasizes that what’s coming is like nothing he’s seen in his many decades of watching technological innovation. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different.” Gates joined Radio Atlantic for a conversation about his evolving views on AI, what he misjudged in his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein, and why he’s decided to raise the alarm now. The following is a transcript of the episode: Bill Gates: You cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn’t work. Hanna Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . [ Music ] Rosin: In his long career, Bill Gates has been largely a booster of technology—including AI. Very recently, he seemed concerned with the risks but more an optimist on balance. But now he’s written a memo arguing that the combination of the rapid speed of advancement and the lack of regulation is putting us in a dangerous place—for employment and human relationships, and also more immediate dangers, like bioweapons and cyberattacks, which Gates is alarmed that no official entity seems to be guarding against. Bill Gates and I talk about what he is seeing and not seeing around AI, and we talk about what exactly he regrets about his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein. Here’s our conversation. So you’ve been an advocate for technology as a force for good. I certainly think of you that way. It’s Microsoft, your foundation, which rewards innovation. And even when you wrote about AI a couple of years ago, you seemed to be more emphasizing the exciting possibilities and calling the risks manageable. And I would say this week you wrote about AI in a way that’s slightly less sanguine than that. What changed for you? Gates: Yeah, I’m very concerned that we’re not getting a lot of people in the conversation about how to minimize the negative things and, at the same time, how to accelerate the good things. The reason that my tone has changed is that starting late last year, as the models—particularly Claude at first, but now many of the models were very good at coding—their capabilities just keep advancing. And so we’re crossing the danger thresholds in areas like cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and as the reliability goes up, the challenge in the jobs market or even the, you know, psychosocial dependency, these concerns are very strong with today’s models. And yet the response I’ve seen from outside the industry—including policy makers, but you know, even academia or society as a whole—to really debate and look at what we have today, which is, you know, a discussion about voluntary review, but it’s pretty empty where you have no criteria of what level you’re looking for and then what remediation you’d ask for. You know, even common-sense things, like monitoring the use of models that can make dangerous molecules for bioterror, that’s not even been put in place. And yet years ago, we said when we got to these thresholds, we needed government to do that. Rosin: So it sounds like…

items.title: Americans Are Spending Luxury Dollars for Dive-Bar Service
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. M arcella Patino was hunched over a table at the South Salt Lake Community Center, her pizza getting cold and her nerves fraying. Patino is a single mom with three kids, and kid­like in her own way, tiny and sweet-voiced. When I met her, in the summer of 2024, she was 33 years old and earning $300 a week doing manicures and pedicures. To bump up her income, she had recently gotten a degree from aesthetician school, meaning she could start offering her clients facials and eyebrow lamination too. She would start making $450 a week soon—$23,400 a year, assuming she was able to work year-round with no breaks. Her rent was $1,550 a month. Then she had to pay for electricity, heat, food, clothing, cell service, health care, child care, gas, and everything else. To keep Patino and her children out of abject poverty, the state of Utah was providing her with Medicaid, SNAP (benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as food stamps), and $600 a month in cash assistance. “Is it enough?” I asked. She blushed, picking at her nails, hand-painted with miniature strawberries and lemons. She went to food banks, she said. Her mom and her neighbors pitched in. Still, she kept falling into debt. Whether the help was enough was less of a pressing matter than whether the help would be there at all. A few days earlier, the state of Utah had dropped Patino from its cash-assistance program and SNAP. She didn’t understand why; her caseworker had been no help. That’s why she had come to Circles, a self-empowerment nonprofit that helps its clients boost their income to double the federal poverty line or more. A Circles volunteer, Stephanie Burdick, hugged Patino and logged on to her account at the Utah Department of Workforce Services (DWS) website, as she had done dozens of times over the prior year. She reviewed the notifications Patino had received, read the emails between her and her caseworker, and looked at her pay stubs. “I can’t figure it out,” Burdick said. It was not the first time the pair had been stumped. Her benefits get “turned off all the time,” Patino told me. Because Utah was asking her to substantiate her poverty all the time. Generally, Utahns receiving cash assistance or food stamps have to fully reapply for the programs every six months; for Medicaid, every 12 months. But the state was asking Patino for data on a near-­weekly basis and requiring her to reenroll in each program every month or two. She did not own a computer and struggled to use the DWS website on her cellphone, meaning she would have to go to the library, attend a Circles meeting, or call Burdick for help. “It takes me hours,” she said. “Sometimes, if I submit an application to one program, it messes up the whole entire other set. Then I have to go back and fix all of it.” Paperwork abounded, and errors did too. Early in 2024, the salon where Patino had been working closed down. She was unemployed for two weeks before finding another gig. When she filed the requisite forms, Utah logged her as having two jobs at once and removed her from the Medicaid rolls. Patino found out when she was in the ER. Even her caseworker seemed to be struggling to keep up. At one appointment, he admitted that she had lost her cash assistance because “he didn’t put all the paperwork in.” Her kids vulnerable, her employers exploitative, her bills past due, her gas tank empty, her housing unstable, her benefits unreliable, Patino was emotionally fried. She was startling awake in the middle of the night to check her DWS account. She was afraid to check out at the grocery store, worried that her EBT card would not go through. She was bracing for the gut punch of eviction as she scrubbed the calluses off other women’s feet. And she was spending countless hours dealing with the state—a part-time job, as she described it. [ Annie Lowrey: America’s annoyance economy is growing ]…

items.title: Not American Enough
items.description: F or Carlos Alemán , the pinnacle of the dozen years since he became a U.S. citizen was the night in 2020 when he was elected to serve on the city council of Homewood, Alabama. One of the lowest moments came earlier this year, when he learned that some of the most powerful people in his state are attempting to ban immigrants like him from pursuing higher office. “It seems to be part of a project to reject anyone who’s not born in this country as not worthy or deserving of the full rights of citizenship,” Alemán, who was born in Nicaragua, told me. For most of American history, becoming a citizen has meant acquiring the right to participate in virtually all aspects of civic life, including voting, serving on juries, and mounting a campaign for any political office other than the presidency. But in Alabama and other states across the country, Republican lawmakers are now pushing to make an important distinction: Naturalized citizens, they argue, should not have the same right to serve in public office as someone born in the United States. In recent months, an idea once confined to the fringes has gained mainstream traction across the country. Republican legislators in several states have introduced proposals that would restrict naturalized citizens and dual citizens from running for a range of elected positions, including sheriff and governor. In Congress, at least five Republicans have sponsored various proposals to bar naturalized or dual citizens from serving in roles including federal judgeships, Cabinet posts, and ambassadorships, and in Congress itself. Florida lawmakers this year enacted a law requiring candidates for several state and federal offices to disclose whether they hold another citizenship in addition to being a citizen of the United States. The movement has been fueled in part by the rise of a new class of foreign-born politicians—most prominently New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Ugandan-born son of parents of Indian extraction, whose ascent has become a favorite target of the right. His victory, along with the success of other progressive candidates born outside the U.S., has come to symbolize something dangerous in the eyes of President Trump’s MAGA base: the ability of people born elsewhere to acquire American citizenship and the possibility of political power. Now Republican lawmakers are pledging to do something about it. The push began in parallel to Mamdani’s rise. When Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen first floated the idea of barring naturalized citizens from serving in elected office, he cited Mamdani’s mayoral run as one impetus. “We want to make sure that no potential foreign influence or foreign meddling could impact our state’s highest elected leaders,” he told AL.com last year. Trump’s June defeat at the Supreme Court on birthright citizenship has also been a motivating factor. After his administration failed to convince a majority of the justices that his executive order limiting citizenship for those born in the U.S. to undocumented parents was constitutional, Trump wrote on social media that he would find alternative routes to accomplish his goals “in Congress through Legislation.” Drawing on the president’s “America First” rhetoric, some Trump allies have begun targeting the political rights of naturalized citizens in a broad campaign to continue that fight. “Even as we have progressed technologically, Immigration Policy has eroded those gains and living conditions for many,” Trump wrote last November on Truth Social, pledging to permanently pause migration from developing countries and denaturalize immigrants he deemed disruptive. “Only REVERSE MIGRATION can fully cure this situation. Other than that, HAPPY THANKSGIVING TO ALL, except those that hate, steal, murder, and destroy everything that America stands for—You won’t be here for long!” T rump used to strike a different tone when talking about naturalized Americans. In 2019, Trump welcomed five legal immigrants into the White…

items.title: The Absolute Pleasure of Tim Curry
items.description: It’s a brisk night in downtown Boston in the early 1980s, and I’m out with a group that includes a very nice, very pretty young woman from my college whom I hope to get to know better. After dinner, one of the guys has an idea: a movie! Better yet, a midnight movie, after which, of course, we’d have to be gallant and walk the girls home. Ambling down Newbury Street to the Exeter Street Theater (now long gone), I spot an unexpected and sartorially strange crowd lined up around the corner. I am dressed like a basic preppy-wannabe: jeans, loafers, a button-down shirt. But the people lined up to get into this movie include men in heavy makeup and—wait, can this be?— garter belts . What the hell am I doing here? The movie, of course, was the 1975 flop turned cult hit The Rocky Horror Picture Show , and audiences came dressed as their favorite character. Those tarted-up men were paying tribute to Tim Curry’s bizarrely glorious Dr. Frank-N-Furter, who belts out a song about being a “sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania.” I may have been a youthful Republican, but I knew that I was watching something—and someone—amazing. I saw the movie many more times, and although I wasn’t going in drag (if you know Rocky Horror , I was more the Brad Majors type), Curry’s pure, perverse joy on-screen was always a welcome escape. The English actor died today at 80. In a perfect tribute, Curry’s many fans are happily debating his greatest performances, which is remarkable given that he wasn’t in that many films and was rarely the lead. Yet his charisma ensured a loyal following for generations. Patricia Quinn, Tim Curry, and Nell Campbell in The Rocky Horror Picture Show (20th Century Fox / Everett Collection) Curry’s magic lay in his ability to be outrageous without being self-conscious, but which Curry you love most might depend on your age and genre preferences. After catching the first wave with Rocky Horror , I went on to buy one of the few albums he made as an aspiring rock star. ( “I Do the Rock” should have gotten more love.) I was among the audiences who were mesmerized by his 1985 performance as a demon , under a ton of makeup, in Legend . Five years later, he scared a new generation as Pennywise the Clown in an adaptation of Stephen King’s It , a role Curry stamped as his own. Other moviegoers adored his campy but somehow restrained mania as the butler in Clue , or delighted in his nasty smarm as the concierge in Home Alone 2 . [ Read: The Worst Witch: a Halloween appreciation ] Finding Curry in something was always a treat. But it was particularly special for me, as someone who worked in Russian affairs, when I discovered that he had traded his pumps and pearls for the severe tunic of a Soviet naval officer in The Hunt for Red October . Curry played the clueless medical officer Dr. Petrov, who does not realize that his skipper, Captain Ramius (played by Sean Connery), intends to defect to the West. When Ramius appears to valiantly order Petrov off the boat and says that, as captain, he himself must go down with the ship after “fighting” the Americans, Curry, trembling with admiration, says , “You’ll receive the Order of Lenin for this, Captain.” His is a simple line, but Curry’s combination of posh earnestness and wide-eyed gullibility turns this into a gem of a moment, something that only he could pull off. What was it about Curry that endeared him to so many? Unlike Dolly Parton, who is rightly being mourned as a great American , Curry was far less a public person. He never married. Despite playing the most decadent and flamboyant cross-dresser in the history of cinema, he never answered questions about his sexuality or his personal relationships. (“Respectfully,” he wrote in his 2025 memoir, such things are “none of your fucking business.”) He was known to be a charming and warm man, and he was involved with some charity efforts, but despite his extroversion as a performer, he was not an off-screen supernova. Instead, Curry…

items.title: Economists Who Weren’t Worried About the Debt Are Now Panicking
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. America’s national debt hit $40 trillion last week. That number certainly feels like something worth panicking over—the mind balks at all the zeros. But although the debt has been in the trillions for decades, not everyone has considered it a problem. One camp of economists has been warning about the perils of high debt for years: Budget hawks predicted that if the country kept spending and didn’t raise taxes enough to keep pace, the resulting fiscal crisis could be devastating. But others—the doves—have brushed it off. Their perspective was that as long as the U.S. GDP was growing faster than the interest rate it was paying on its debt, the Treasury would be able to keep rolling over its bonds without too much of a problem. For much of the 2010s, this was essentially the status quo , and debt panic was muted. We’re nowhere near a complete failure of the Treasury market, and yet, over the past couple of years, some economists who were once more dovish have switched teams . Martha Gimbel, the executive director of the Budget Lab at Yale and the author of a recent Atlantic story on this issue, told me that part of the reason these economists are pivoting is that they’re starting to realize that interest rates are “probably going to be elevated for quite some time.” The average interest rate on U.S. debt—that second variable the doves look at—has been relatively high for several years now, and it’s only growing . It was hovering around 1.5 percent in 2021, and it’s now roughly 3.4 percent. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond has more than doubled since 2021. “I was not a deficit hawk, and that reflected the dynamics” of the 2010s, when rates were lower, Gimbel told me. Now, she said, “the environment has changed.” Why are rates rising? The Fed’s reaction to inflation is one reason. It may also have something to do with the extreme investments being made in AI , and these companies’ demand for credit. And it’s likely connected to the deficit panic— concern about the expansion of the national debt and the government’s ability to sustain it. Investors are starting to think of long-term Treasurys as riskier than they once did, and they’re demanding more money in exchange for taking on America’s debt. At the same time, the federal government has shown no real appetite to pull its two main levers for reducing the debt: cutting spending and raising taxes. Jared Bernstein, the former head of Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, wrote in The Atlantic a few months ago that he’d “flipped from dove to hawk”—and told me this week that it was partly the government’s complacency on this issue that spurred this change. “Neither side seems particularly motivated to do much of anything about this,” he said. Rather than attending to the debt problem, politicians of both parties have instituted major tax cuts and increased spending over the past 25 years. The U.S. had its credit downgraded by a major ratings agency last spring, in part because of rising debt. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act will add an estimated $4.7 trillion to the deficit through 2035, and Donald Trump’s efforts to decrease immigration will add another half a trillion to that number over the same period, per the Congressional Budget Office . Despite some recent attempts at short-term stabilization, his administration hasn’t done much to assure the country’s creditors that everything’s fine; they now appear to be seeking greater yields as a result. When longer-term bond yields rise, as they have been, everyday forms of borrowing such as mortgage rates and student loans tend to become more expensive as well. That’s why yields are ultimately “a kitchen-table issue in the same way that inflation is,” Ernie Tedeschi, a former chief economist for the White House’s Council of Economic A…

items.title: How to Lose $12 Billion and Still Win
items.description: Meta avoided the worst today by settling a massive lawsuit over alleged damages “to the mental and physical wellbeing of America’s youth.” The case, brought by the attorneys general of 47 states, plus U.S. territories and Washington, D.C., had been mid-trial in a federal court in California and was by far the most significant legal challenge the company has ever faced. To resolve the lawsuit, Meta will have to make a slew of design changes to its social-media platforms, and it will pay more than $12 billion—down from the approximately $200 billion that was initially sought, and a fraction of the $60 billion that the company made in profit last year. The settlement can be used by the states and other parties to pay for their litigation costs and for a variety of school and community programs. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers agreed to the proposal this morning, saying “I’m quite happy” and congratulating both parties. There seems to be good cheer all around; Meta, which avoided any admission of guilt, put out a sunny announcement framing the agreement as part of its “longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.” Brian Schwalb, the attorney general of the District of Columbia, told The New York Times that the settlement represents a “monumental public health victory” that will “fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook.” The former claim will have to be proved over time, but the latter is clearly true. As part of the agreement, Meta has agreed to submit to regular auditing of both its age-verification systems and its efforts to prevent minors from making multiple accounts to get around its restrictions. And the company will make other tweaks that are intended to target the big recent villains of social media: short-form video and the never-ending feed. [ Read: A legal decision that could change social media ] Teen users, by default, will not have access to most features of Instagram and Facebook at night (though they can still access messages and settings) and will not receive notifications from the platforms during school hours (defined as 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays from August 15 to June 15). They’ll also be limited to a maximum of one hour a day per platform, though this doesn’t include time spent sending messages or consuming long-form content (which the agreement defines as audio or video at least 22 minutes long). Meta is also required to interrupt scrolling every 15 minutes with pop-ups that encourage “productive pauses,” and the company will have to study how well the interruptions work and submit its findings to an auditor. Parents can still manually change any of these settings for their kids. The settlement also requires limits on features that some experts believe are detrimental to teenagers’ self-esteem and self-image. By default, teen users won’t see the number of likes or reactions on posts; they also won’t be able to use “cosmetic procedure filters,” which have been a sore spot for Meta for some time. When the plaintiffs filed their complaint, they cited evidence that Mark Zuckerberg had personally vetoed a proposed in-house policy against these filters despite concerns expressed by employees that they were causing young people to develop body dysmorphia. Meta will also be legally required to maintain and enforce the “age-appropriate” content guidelines it debuted at the end of last year. This may seem like quite a lot of changes—especially considering that the case is not even the end of Meta’s legal problems. The company is still facing numerous lawsuits filed by individuals and school districts. “If Meta is going to resolve all its pending liabilities, this is only the first of several large checks it is going to have to write,” Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law, told me. But today’s settlement shows that the tech company was able to “buy out one of the most serious legal threats” it faced, and it managed to do so without acqui…

items.title: Why Did John Ratcliffe Go to Moscow?
items.description: CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s brief trip to Moscow yesterday was unannounced but hard to miss: He flew in a C-17A, a large heavy-transport plane, that open-source analysts quickly identified and tracked. Within hours, he was already on his way home. The purpose of Ratcliffe’s visit remains unknown. In an interview with Glenn Beck this morning, President Trump described it as “sort of semi-routine,” but such trips are rare. The previous time a director of the CIA went to Russia was in November 2021, when William J. Burns told Moscow that the United States knew of Vladimir Putin’s plans to invade Ukraine. A likelier explanation for this latest trip is that Russia is getting more dangerous and the Trump administration wanted to warn it against escalating. Ratcliffe’s visit comes at one of the most difficult periods in the war for the Kremlin. Thanks to its drone systems, Ukraine has been able to strike military targets and oil infrastructure deep inside Russia while also hindering Moscow’s advance on the battlefield, turning the front into a kill box in which anything that moves is struck within minutes. Despite making little progress, Russia has continued to take heavy losses. In May, the Russian death toll reached nearly half a million, according to Anne Keast-Butler, the head of GCHQ, the U.K. intelligence agency. Russia’s weakness could be making Putin more reckless. The Wall Street Journal reported a few weeks ago that the U.S. intelligence community is concerned that Russia could carry out a limited attack on a NATO state, possibly even launching a small land incursion. Such an assault might thwart Russia’s own interests, prompting Europe to accelerate its military buildup and target Moscow’s sovereign assets. But Putin may see attacking a NATO country as an unprecedented opportunity to break the alliance, by manufacturing a crisis in which the United States fails to act. [ Shane Harris: The ‘Russia hoax,’ revisited ] If Washington did not respond to such an act of aggression, Russia could expose NATO’s mutual-protection clause as hollow. Putin has some reason to think that the United States may stay out of a conflict if he initiates one soon. Trump has repeatedly expressed disdain for Europe and shown little interest in challenging Putin. In addition, America’s weapons stockpile is depleted from the Iran war. Perhaps in response to fears of increased Russian aggression, NATO mounted a large U.S.-led air exercise last week over Poland and the Baltic region, which included flights near the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad. Other possible signs of Putin’s growing belligerence have emerged. In recent weeks, a series of low-level attacks have swept Europe. Drones laden with explosives were found at the Leipzig airport this month, and there were explosions or fires at weapons factories and other sensitive sites in Estonia, Italy, Bulgaria, and the Netherlands, all of which have provided assistance to Ukraine. Authorities have attributed some but not all of the attacks to Moscow, and Russian officials have denied responsibility. But they follow an established pattern of Russian provocations in Europe. Regardless of Putin’s ambitions elsewhere in Europe, he appears committed to fight the war in Ukraine indefinitely. Russia has increased its ballistic-missile attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of Kyiv’s shortages in air defense. Reporting from the Journal suggests that Putin could be preparing a large-scale mobilization to replenish Russia’s army for a renewed offensive. The Russian leader might try to overwhelm Ukraine this winter with a massive bombardment campaign aimed at destroying its energy grid. But Kyiv is unlikely to capitulate, because it knows that Putin would impose punitive terms. If Ukraine does survive the winter and retains the ability to strike deep inside of Russia, then Putin might choose to end the war in mid-2027. Facing the prospect of a U.S. president in 2029 who is more pro-Ukraine than Tru…

items.title: The Lights Are Back On in Gary, Indiana
items.description: Last night, NIPSCO, an Indiana utility company that provides electricity to half a million people in the northern part of the state, finally made the deadline for restoring power to the city of Gary. On August 11, a derecho swept across northwest Indiana, and winds nearing 100 miles an hour knocked out power for more than 370,000 people, NIPSCO has said. In Gary, home to nearly 70,000 people, 75 percent of them Black, more than half of the utility’s customers lost power in the initial aftermath of the storm. For the next two weeks, NIPSCO kept pushing back its timeline for restoring power; even on Monday, thousands in Gary were still in the dark. As of yesterday evening, the utility said, it had restored power to 99 percent of its customers—which also meant that hundreds of people in Gary still didn’t have electricity this morning. Blackouts follow plenty of storms, and at a press conference eight days after the storm hit, Gary Mayor Eddie Melton described the ongoing blackout as a situation for “not just Gary” but also all of northwest Indiana. However, as the days of darkness stretched on, and the power started going back in other parts of the region—first Dyer and East Chicago, then Hobart and Merrillville—the initial inconvenience of a Tuesday, a Wednesday, then a Thursday, then a Friday without power started to become a crisis in Gary. This past weekend, Melton was no longer talking about the blackout as a regional problem. Gary, he told me, had not initially been on NIPSCO’s schedule for restoring power and had seemingly been overlooked until the city pushed back. NIPSCO declined to comment on the specifics of its restoration schedule, but a spokesperson wrote in a statement that it had hired extra contractors and drawn on support from neighboring utilities and that “no outage is being overlooked.” The people I spoke with in Gary felt differently—that whatever efforts had been made to restore power had not been fast enough. They described throwing out maggot-filled food from their refrigerators, and temporarily moving in with friends and family members who had generators. They were charging their phones in their cars while running the air-conditioning just to stay cool in the summer heat. Gary’s median household income is about $40,000 a year; nearly 20 percent of its people are 65 or older, according to the latest U.S. census data—it’s a community with limited money to spare. People were spending their last dollars on gas to drive through the city on roads without functional streetlights—past uprooted trees, fallen street signs, and loose power lines—just to find supplies. As the power outage dragged on, relief efforts started reaching the city, but some were first come, first served; others limited relief packages to one per household, which kept people from picking up extra care packages for neighbors stuck at home. “Our seniors are stuck in their apartments, completely dark,” Willett Wright, a 77-year-old resident who was still without power, told me. “There’s no generators in the world that can get up to their apartments. They’re stuck in their rooms with all this heat, and no food.” Power slowly began to come back this weekend, but not across all of Gary’s neighborhoods. Some residents were still waiting in the dark. And even in the places where power had come back on, the lights were still flickering. If you ask Gary residents what time their power was turned back on, they can share it almost down to the minute: 11:32 p.m. on Saturday; just after midnight on Sunday; 2:45 p.m. on Monday. Indiana is used to dealing with some types of severe storms, which were responsible for nearly 50 percent of the major disaster costs in the state over the past 44 years, a 2025 report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found. But this derecho—a strong windstorm that moves in straight lines and can be as fast as a hurricane or a tornado—felt different, residents told me. Climate change is contributing to a ste…

items.title: What Are Jewish Voters Supposed to Do?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the blowing up of trade talks between the United States and Canada, and President Trump’s reckless trade war against Canada. David discusses how this trade war hurts not only America’s relationship with Canada but its global standing as a reliable trade partner. Then David is joined by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel to discuss the growing hostility among some Democratic voters toward American Jews. Frum and Nessel discuss why the rhetoric of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed concerns some Jews; rise of anti-Semitism within the Democratic party; and the impossible situation many Jewish voters find themselves in today. Finally, David ends the show with his thoughts on the new biography on Roy Cohn, American Scoundrel . The following is a transcript of the episode: Dana Nessel: I think it’s a fundamental mistake for the Democratic Party to think that you can just push Jewish Democrats out and simply replace them with any other population. [ Music ] David Frum: Welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Dana Nessel, attorney general of the state of Michigan, and this week’s book will be the newly released biography American Scoundrel , a biography of Roy Cohn and his lifetime from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump. Before either the dialogue with Attorney General Nessel or the book, I want to open with some thoughts about the recent blowup in trade negotiations between the United States and Canada. Now, it’s the Trump administration, though, so those negotiations are blown up as I record on Monday, August 24th. They may be back on by the time you watch on Wednesday, August 26th. Anything can happen with this crazy crew. But let’s assume, as I record, that the negotiations remain blown up for some time. Now, I wrote in The Atlantic this past weekend an analysis of the economic effect of the blowup of these negotiations, and I hope you’ll take a look at that. Facts, figures, dates, numbers. What I want to talk about today is not the economics—you can read that in The Atlantic, and I hope you will. What I want to talk about is some of the geopolitical implications of the United States behaving in the predatory way that the Trump administration has led the United States to behave in these negotiations with Canada. Look, I’m recording this in Canada right now as I speak. I do have a Canadian point of view. But I think I can speak more broadly when I say that America has enormously benefited all around the world in reputation and standing from its relationship with Canada. The U.S.-Canada relationship is a kind of text proof of America’s benignity and good intentions. If you’re a country anywhere in the world, wondering whether to partner with the United States or one of its adversaries—the Soviet Union in the olden days, Russia or China now—you’d look at the U.S.-Canada relationship and say, There is America’s nearest neighbor, a country only one-tenth the size of the United States—smaller in economics, smaller in population—highly vulnerable to American pressure, and yet America has consistently treated Canada as an equal, as a partner, and as a friend. And that model relationship is a proof of the good intentions of America to anybody. And so there you are on the other side of the world thinking, Can we trust the Americans? Think, Well, the Canadians next door; they trust the Americans. They’ve benefited from that trust. They’ve been treated with equality. So will we. So long as the relationship worked, America stood proud in the eyes of the world. The Trump vision of America is very different. At home, Trump’s vision of how America should arrange its economy borrows a lot from China. As much as Trump rails against China, he wants America to be more like China. His government is taking ownership stake…

items.title: The Most Beautiful Woman
items.description: Growing up in Tennessee, I could hardly walk into a grocery store without hearing “Jolene” playing on the radio. My mom sang fragments of “9 to 5” as she cooked Hamburger Helper on school nights, after clocking out of work. At my babysitter’s house in the summer, where Country Music Television was our ambient noise, she’d shout, “Good golly, Miss Dolly!” every time a Dolly song came on (which was at least every 30 minutes). Dolly Parton was more of an institution than a star to Tennesseans. Her image was plastered on T-shirts and hung on walls, like Mother Mary would be in a Catholic home. We vacationed at her amusement park, Dollywood, every school break. No one ever used her last name—she was simply Dolly to us all, and she was living proof that tough odds were no match for a cup of ambition. When Dolly’s death was announced yesterday afternoon, my phone lit up with texts from hometown friends. “It feels like a member of our family died in Tennessee today,” one friend said. My socialist sister said Tennessee’s poet laureate had left us. My Donald Trump–voting father cried. In Tennessee, whether you fly a MAGA flag or a Pride flag, one thing is for sure: You’re listening to Dolly. Dolly mattered to southerners for so many reasons, but perhaps most of all for her origin story, which she called a “rags to rhinestones” tale. She grew up four hours east of me, in a one-room cabin with her 11 siblings, in the depths of Tennessee Appalachia. Unlike Nashville, which is so associated with Dolly today, the Appalachian region of Tennessee is riddled with evidence of isolation in its language, economy, and general sense of yearning. Appalachia has its own distinct dialect and a deep tradition of oral storytelling. Being able to captivate an audience served as capital, and she brought this generationally reinforced skill to songwriting and the stage. Her upbringing was one of poverty and stripped-down performance. Like many other Tennessee families, the Parton family sang church hymns and mountain ballads on front-porch swings. In her hit song “Coat of Many Colors,” Dolly recalls a coat her mother made for her of donated scrap fabric. “Although we had no money, I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my mama made for me.” She was proud of and honest about her roots, and for many poor southerners, it was the first time they saw their stories told publicly. [ Read: We’re living in the world Dolly Parton built ] Dolly was first introduced on the Grand Ole Opry stage at age 13 by Johnny Cash, who called her “a little girl here from up in East Tennessee.” She would never shed that identity. A number of global superstars got their start in the South, including Taylor Swift and Dolly’s own goddaughter, Miley Cyrus. Most ditched their southern dialect and opted for a more conventional pop sound after reaching the height of their fame. But Dolly never evolved. Her famous mantra, “Find out who you are and do it on purpose,” explained the way she viewed the world. She was unapologetically southern, and at the same time, nobody’s fool. “Dolly’s accent, like her music, held the notes of her East Tennessee home, and she often spoke proudly of her choice to carry it,” Amy Clark, a linguist from Appalachia, told me. “She sounded just like many of us in the way she said ‘light’ or dropped ‘g’ off certain words.” Her refusal to abandon her southern way of speaking meant the world to people from such places. “If you were from Appalachia and couldn’t carry a note, you could still be proud because you sounded like Dolly,” Clark said. John Seakwood / Disney / Getty Dolly Parton at Dollywood in 1987 Many stars who have left (or, in their view, escaped) the South speak of their upbringing as a past life rarely revisited. Dolly, conversely, spent her entire life giving back to her home state. “She understood that where you come from isn’t something you transcend,” Brooke Griffith, a jewelry-shop owner from East Tennessee, wrote on Instagram. “It’s s…

items.title: The Real Reason Trump Wants Economic Sanctions in Iran
items.description: Updated at 1:40 p.m. ET on August 26, 2026. F or months, President Trump has been unable to bring the conflict with Iran to a close. A massive bombing campaign lost its effectiveness, and U.S. munitions supplies ran low. Diplomacy lagged, as leaders in Tehran remained content to deliberately prolong the process and harden their control over the Strait of Hormuz. Even the current pseudo-cease-fire—as deeply uneasy as it is—has done little to meaningfully lower the cost of energy around the globe. With few options remaining, the Trump administration has settled into a potentially lengthy campaign of economic pressure , pledging to squeeze Iran until its leaders have no choice but to seriously return to negotiations. But that tack could prove toothless if the U.S. doesn’t also punish the nations that still do business with Iran and keep its economy afloat—and Trump has historically shown little willingness to stand up to the likes of China and Russia, or even North Korea, which has a strategic alliance with Tehran. If nothing else, the new approach allows the White House to say it’s trying something and then—importantly—to stop talking about the war. Part of the plan, Trump advisers and allies tell us, is to try to push Iran to the background, while hoping that gas prices come down even a little and that Republicans can shift the nation’s focus to more politically palatable topics ahead of the midterms. That won’t change the reality on the ground in the Middle East: Alliances have been strained , the U.S. military has been overtaxed, and Iran wields far more power in the region than it did at the beginning of the war, about six months ago. But it could allow Trump, a master of distraction, to turn to other priorities—a trade war with Canada! Claims of election fraud! His skill at flagpoles !—to try to save at least one chamber of Congress for his party this fall. “We’re just trying to hang on until the midterms,” one Trump adviser told us. A t this moment , strategists in both parties believe that the Democrats are favored to capture the House. And despite a GOP-friendly Senate map, the upper chamber is viewed as a toss-up. Trends were already working against Republicans: Traditionally, the party out of power tends to do well in the midterms, and over the past decade, Trump supporters have seemed less inclined to vote when his name isn’t on the ballot. The president hasn’t done much to help, and his poll numbers have plunged, even on the economy and immigration, his usual strengths. Republicans, fearing hostility, have largely opted to forgo town halls this summer, skipping what tends to be an effective way to reach constituents. A few of those who have held gatherings in their districts have faced anger and tough questions about Iran, including why the U.S. launched the war in the first place. [ Read: The forever negotiation ] Republicans have been urging the White House to wrap up the conflict and reduce its drag on the nation’s economy—and their reelection chances. But a solution has proved elusive. Trump’s goals for the conflict were never well enunciated and have shifted many times. Gone are lofty promises about regime change or preventing Iran from having a nuclear program. Instead, the president has privately told his political allies that once the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, he is inclined to simply declare victory and move on, one outside adviser and a senior administration official told us on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. But even that has proved vexing: Iran has continued to menace ships traveling through the strait and has insisted upon charging a fee or toll. Other countries in the region have declared that unacceptable—the strait was, after all, open and free before the war—though Trump has waffled on whether or not he could live with it. The president said yesterday that the last of the Iranian mines had been removed from the channel, but an official from a country in the region st…

items.title: Why Was This Looney Tunes Movie Almost Shelved for Good?
items.description: Perhaps the starkest sign that Coyote vs. Acme isn’t your typical children’s movie is that it’s based on a New Yorker article. Yes, it features many Looney Tunes characters that multiple generations know and love, interacting alongside real-life actors in a style similar to prior big-screen efforts, such as Space Jam or Looney Tunes: Back in Action . But the director Dave Green’s film—which opens August 28, after a protracted saga that almost saw it kept from audiences forever—draws from a slyly funny “Shouts & Murmurs” story from 1990. Written by the humorist Ian Frazier, “Coyote v. Acme” has a wry and self-aware premise: What would happen if Wile E. Coyote, the Looney Tune on a constantly unsuccessful hunt for the ever-chipper Road Runner, filed a lawsuit against the (fictional) Acme Corporation for selling him faulty products? “I thought the baseline idea for the movie was just, like, the funniest thing in the world,” Green told me in a recent interview, reminiscing about when he first signed on to direct the film, back in 2019. He wasn’t the first person in the film industry to be charmed by Frazier’s story. Despite the erudite tone, the simple notion of Wile E. Coyote pursuing legal action was amusing enough to Hollywood producers that various attempts were made to develop it for the screen, dating back to an effort by the producer Scott Rudin in the late 1990s. Warner Bros., which owns Looney Tunes , jump-started the latest version of the project in 2018, and Green completed it in 2022. Coyote vs. Acme was initially scheduled to debut the following summer, but it was taken off the schedule early into production; a new release date was never announced. In the fall of 2023, Warner Bros. told the director that the movie would be shelved entirely . The studio reportedly made the call for a tax write-off—the latest in a series of such decisions, as it dealt with debt issues after the coronavirus pandemic. Three years later, Coyote vs. Acme is finally entering theaters. After years of limbo, it ended up in the hands of Ketchup Entertainment, an independent distributor that has now become its unlikely savior. The company cut a $50 million deal with Warner Bros. for it last March. “I continued to not believe it, up until now, when I still can’t believe it,” Green said. “It’s a completely surreal reality to check into. But it seems to be happening—I think it’s happening,” he added with a laugh. [ Read: The greatest animated film that never was ] His trepidation is understandable: The path the film took to cinemas reflects Hollywood’s continued post-pandemic instability, even as theatergoing has picked back up. Coyote vs. Acme had reportedly tested well with audiences and featured some of Warner Bros.’ most well-known creations, yet the cancellation suggests the company still expected to lose too much money on the project. The wildest part of the production, Green admitted, was how easy it was at first. When asked by Warner Bros. to pitch ideas for an adaptation of Frazier’s article, the director proposed something along the lines of a true-crime documentary crossed with a legal drama. To his surprise, the studio didn’t immediately turn him down. “It almost felt like everything was a ‘yes,’ and there were no boundaries. So then I got really excited,” Green said. “They were looking for a take and they were looking for something that would help them narrow in. And, as different as my tonal comparisons were, I think they responded to the fact that there was a take in it.” Green’s notion was to take the tropes of underdog courtroom movies—he cited The Insider , Erin Brockovich , and A Few Good Men as inspirations—and place cartoon characters within them. The humans they interact with (played by Will Forte, Lana Condor, and John Cena, among others) would treat Wile E. Coyote’s lawsuit with humdrum seriousness. “That’s the kind of behavior that really comes from Looney Tunes historically,” Green said—winking references to grown-up media…

items.title: The Jason Arday Truthers
items.description: In death, Jason Arday has become two people. To many readers of legacy newspapers, the late Cambridge University academic is a proven fabulist. The life story on which he built his career, of being nonverbal until 11 because of autism, and then learning to read at 18 and becoming a professor, has “no precedent in medical literature,” as The New York Times delicately put it. Among many other extraordinary claims, his tale of being menaced by a knife-wielding man at Cambridge could not be corroborated, and neither could the story that his family had received a pig’s head as an act of racist intimidation. “To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me,” he told a Guardian reporter who challenged him. That is one reality. However, another one dominates left-wing new media, activist nonprofits, and visual social networks such as Instagram and TikTok. There, the prevailing narrative is that Arday did nothing seriously wrong and Britain’s right-wing media hounded an exceptional Black scholar to his death on August 14 for no reason except racism. Well-wishers have raised more than $300,000 for his family, and made his upcoming memoir a best seller in Britain. At a rally in central London held in his memory, attendees carried placards reading Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday , even though he had resigned the title days before his death. They wanted to make clear their belief that he was unfairly deprived of his academic status. For some of Arday’s supporters, acknowledging that any of the media scrutiny was justified has become tantamount to siding with his “killers.” He is instead a martyr—the victim of a “lynching” —and the inconvenient fact of his fabulism must be tidied away from the virtual shrine. This is an emotional position rather than a rational one, and its very indefensibility makes it a greater demonstration of tribal loyalty. Insisting that the academic was completely innocent, in the face of all the evidence, sends a strong social signal that you hate the right-wing media and care about racism. The central question in this dispute is whether the treatment of Arday—the subject of more than 200 articles in print this year, according to CNN , and hundreds more online—was proportionate. The smaller his alleged offenses, the more easily one can argue that the media hounded him to death. And so Arday has been recast as a small-time plagiarist; academics have lined up to argue that, You know, even that isn’t a very big deal . The “meaning of plagiarism does not cover mere overlap of sentences,” the academic Jason Stanley asserted in a blog post that also bizarrely noted that he hadn’t paid much attention to the story because he had been on vacation in Europe. Stanley’s blithe dismissal will be news to students who are told the exact opposite early in their courses. Or to Ross Barkan, who was dropped from New York magazine after getting caught recycling other writers’ words. [ Graeme Wood: Jason Arday’s final self-delusion ] Another popular declaration is that Arday “was cleared of plagiarism” by Liverpool John Moores University, where he received his doctorate. This is technically true. When concerns were raised about his dissertation, Cambridge University declined to investigate, saying it was a problem for Liverpool John Moores, which had already stated that it stood by his work. Just before Arday’s death, however, Cambridge reversed its position , pledging to investigate, as did other institutions that had employed Arday. (Arday then resigned from Cambridge, adding that the move should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.”) Stressing that he was “cleared” misses the point; the exact allegation is that universities’ lack of interest in scrutinizing Arday represented a failure of institutional checks. Now anyone can run Arday’s thesis through plagiarism-detection software themselves and make up their own mind. When Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, a writer who otherwise found the med…

items.title: The Truth About Dolly Parton’s Style
items.description: Dolly Parton was just 5-foot-nothing tall. She needed platform heels to make her feel that she could fill a performance space. Her husband, Carl Dean, once told her that from the audience, her platinum wigs made her tiny figure look like a Q-tip. But no amount of mocking could make her surrender the hair, heels, and rhinestones, which were her own brand of feminism under wraps. “Believe it or not, I had to fight for that look!” she wrote in her 2023 memoir, Behind the Seams . The look wasn’t about showbiz. It was about sovereignty. And it must have been more than passingly rewarding for Parton to know that her audience finally understood this about her before she died, at the age of 80—to know that she was fully appreciated for the wallop of woman she was. She had so much guts, smarts, and self-ownership beneath the taffetized country-music artifice that sold more than 100 million records. [ Read: ] We’re living in the world Dolly Parton built There was no hint of glamour in the Tennessee hill country where Parton grew up, just unadorned, worn-out women like her mother, who’d married at 15 and had a dozen children by the age of 35. Parton’s first dresses were made of flour and feed sacks. Too poor to buy real makeup, Parton would use pokeberry juice to redden her lips and the burned end of a matchstick to do her brows. When her sharecropper father caught her, he’d whip her and try to wash it off. “Back then, any woman who wore makeup in the mountains was considered trashy,” she wrote. “But I didn’t care.” She’d plead to her dad that it was “her natural color.” He’d snap, “‘Natural color,’ my ass! You get in there and get that off of you.” After she began to make some money from singing bits on Knoxville’s popular Cas Walker Farm and Home Hour , she went to the local drugstore to buy herself some Maybelline. Store-bought makeup and clothing that fit her form gave her courage. She wrote, “I remember feeling powerful enough to go up against Daddy or Grandpa to say, ‘Now, that’s not that tight. It ain’t cut that low. It ain’t that much.’ And they’d say, ‘Yes, it is!’ But I’d be willing to get my ass whupped for it.” She wore anything gaudy that she could lay her hands on. An unusually candid photo of Parton, taken early in her career, shows her eyes painted with large half-moons of blue, reflective eye shadow. Her earrings are as big as saucers. Her hair is bound with a purple headband, and her head is tilted at a cocky angle as she stares straight and unsmiling at the camera. It is a portrait of not a girl but a challenger, a young woman of utter defiance. You weren’t going to catch that Dolly being bullied by classmates for the “coat of many colors” that her mama had sewn out of rags. You could bet she wasn’t going to stay under the dirt-caked thumb of her father, in that cabin that had no plumbing or electricity, for much longer, either. Her mother understood. She’d surreptitiously sew a little sass and lift into those homemade clothes: “Now, don’t tell your daddy I put some push-ups in that dress.” The day after Parton graduated high school, she packed everything she had in four grocery bags from the Piggly Wiggly and caught the bus to Nashville. “My matching luggage,” she called those paper sacks. Her rise to stardom in Nashville probably came with more sexual harassment than anyone will ever know. She spent seven years accompanying Porter Wagoner on his hit TV show and then had the sense to wrest herself out of his domineering hands. “I couldn’t just stay there forever being somebody’s girl singer,” she wrote about her break with Wagoner. She added, “I never was one to be told what to do for too long because I never could do what anybody else told me to do if it went against who I am.” In a 2023 interview with The Guardian to promote her book, she said: “I always knew how to put a man in his place without making him feel bad. If sometimes that don’t work, I’m also strong as a boy—I know how to push you off and get the hell a…

items.title: The German Far Right Is Poised for a Breakthrough
items.description: I magine that it’s October 2026, and one of Germany’s 16 federal states has come under the control of a far-right government for the first time since the Nazi era. With an absolute majority in the state Parliament and one of its own installed as state premier, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, quickly begins implementing its agenda. The interior minister announces an emergency remigration program: abolishing asylum, revoking the residence permit of any foreigner convicted of a crime, pledging to review all naturalization decisions made during this century, and incarcerating those designated for deportation. The government stops classifying Ukrainians as war refugees and ends their social benefits. European Union flags disappear from public buildings. The mainstream press is shunned in favor of influencers aligned with the party’s ideology. The government authorizes vigilante groups to act as an auxiliary police force in regions with high crime rates. This hasn’t happened, but it’s not merely hypothetical either. The AfD is projected to win an election next month in Saxony-Anhalt, a central German state of some 2 million people. An anti-racism NGO in Berlin, the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, created this scenario based on the far-right party’s own election manifesto and the statements of its representatives. For decades, right-wing politics have carried particular weight in Germany, where atonement for the Holocaust includes mandatory education about the rise of National Socialism. The far right was long relegated to the fringes, its most ardent members easily identified as skinheads decked out in leather. But the AfD, founded in 2013 as a mild euroskeptic party led mostly by conservative economists opposed to eurozone bailouts, is now Germany’s most important right-wing force since the Nazis. At the national level, the AfD is the most popular party, supported by more than a quarter of voters in recent polls. It leads both of the traditional broad-based parties, the center-right Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats. Its base of support is in the formerly Communist east—generally poorer, older, and angrier than the rest of Germany. And that’s where it’s poised for a breakthrough later this summer. In past state elections, other parties have contorted themselves to keep the far-right faction out of governing coalitions, maintaining a so-called firewall even when the AfD has won the most votes. That may not be possible in Saxony-Anhalt, where ahead of a September 6 vote, the AfD is polling at more than 40 percent. If smaller parties fail to reach the required 5 percent threshold to enter Parliament, this kind of showing by the AfD could be enough for it to win an outright majority, meaning that it wouldn’t need cooperation from other parties to govern. Suddenly, Saxony-Anhalt would become a testing ground for AfD policies. If the AfD doesn’t reach that threshold, the spotlight would turn to the Christian Democratic Union, the party of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The Christian Democrats would face a dilemma: whether to breach the firewall and work with the AfD or join hands with the far-left party Die Linke in a last-ditch effort to keep the far right from taking power. In fact, the Christian Democrats have a policy, formalized in 2018 and known as an incompatibility resolution, against working with either party. Andreas Rödder, a historian who previously headed the center-right party’s fundamental-values commission, told me that the decision didn’t generate much controversy within the party at the time because the matter was mostly symbolic; the center-right party, then dominated by Chancellor Angela Merkel, had other choices for governing partners. At that time, German politics remained fairly stable, relatively speaking, as anti-establishment forces shook up other Western democracies. For many in Germany, this was a point of pride, a sign that the country had learned from its history, that it knew where…

items.title: Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record
items.description: P resident Trump gathered his top political advisers in the Oval Office early this month to solve a problem of riches: how to spend his super PAC’s $400 million political war chest with fewer than 100 days to go before the midterm elections. Republican strategists are concerned about Trump’s low approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy. One person familiar with the Oval Office strategy meeting put it this way: “When the issues that you typically campaign on don’t move voters—or voters are pissed off at you about those issues—the question becomes: What do you campaign on?” Some GOP strategists favor focusing entirely on specific races in an effort to convince voters of the merits of individual candidates and local issues. But Trump himself has rejected that approach. House and Senate Democrats, the president noted during the meeting, will make their fall campaigns a referendum on him. His advisers told him that the poor polling reflects the fact that the voting public still does not know about many of his accomplishments—the dozens of new stock-market highs, a decline in fentanyl deaths, the “sealed” southern border, the increase in domestic-manufacturing production. The solution Trump settled on, according to three people familiar with the meeting, was to lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself. The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests. Trump wanted what one person described to us as “environmental lift” ads—commercials that would focus on nationalizing the midterms broadly around his victories—and he suggested that the ad makers mine his own on-camera statements as building blocks. “Go look at the clips,” the president told his team, according to this person. “I cite accomplishments all the time.” That decision has resulted in a Trump midterm-election ad blitz that is set to be rolled out soon from MAGA Inc., the main repository of Trump’s political fundraising, according to people familiar with the discussions, all of whom insisted on anonymity to describe internal conversations. Most of MAGA Inc.’s spending is still expected to go to targeted House and Senate races, for which the group has been establishing teams to review polling, voter modeling, and message testing. “We are going to unload the guns on both chambers real soon,” one of the people said. But another person told us that because Trump will inevitably be part of voters’ considerations, highlighting his achievements makes sense. “I think everybody does understand that the president and his agenda are on the ballot to some degree,” another person told us. A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. told us that the group does not comment on internal deliberations or plans. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told us that Trump is committed to maintaining the Republican majorities in Congress. “President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess,” she said in a statement. “There is a great story to tell because the United States of America has never been stronger than under his leadership.” Trump’s decision to focus a portion of his spending on himself echoes President Biden’s decision in the fall of 2023 to launch a series of ads trumpeting his own legislative record, as he sought to increase his approval rating in advance of his reelection bid.
