But Trump is not on the ballot this fall, which presents new risks. A new strategy of touting Trump’s achievements could well backfire by aiding Democratic efforts to make each race about national issues at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at record lows. Yet given the midterm headwinds, Republicans may have little choice but to present their most effective communicator to voters. T he political climate —an economic election in which voters don’t feel that their life has gotten better, despite some positive indicators—is in many ways similar to what Democrats faced in 2010 and…

items.title: We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
items.description: Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character. Parton’s self-construction project began in her childhood. She was born the fourth of 12 kids in a tiny cabin in Pittman Center, Tennessee. Her parents were so poor that they paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. As a girl, she sang songs on her porch into a fake mic fashioned from a tin can and a tobacco stick, envisioning herself at the Grand Ole Opry. Her talent drew attention from local radio and TV personalities, and by age 13, she was singing on the real Opry stage. The craftiness and self-consciousness that came from growing up impoverished shaped her outlook for life. As she’d sing in her 1971 song “Coat of Many Colors”—her signature (and favorite) hit—her mother used to sew rags into garments that the young Parton would flaunt at school. Mockery from other kids taught her the lesson in self-determination that she’d turn into one of her defining lyrics: “One is only poor only if they choose to be.” As a young woman, she modeled her fashion off a “town tramp”—as she later put it —whom she’d grown up around. Her preacher grandfather whipped her for dressing that way, but to her, women with heels and push-up bras weren’t trashy; they were glamorous and confident. A fascination with stereotypes—with fulfilling them and subverting them—gave her an edge when she moved to Nashville. In 1966, her first solo hit, “Dumb Blonde” (written by Curly Putman), saw her singing that despite her looks, she “ain’t nobody’s fool.” On the TV variety series The Porter Wagoner Show , she played the aw-shucks second fiddle to the titular star even as she wrote songs that outcompeted Wagoner’s music. Her 1970 hit “Joshua” spun a tale in which the narrator approaches a mean-looking backwoods hermit, someone whom the rest of the town fears, only to realize that he has a heart of gold. It was an example of how her penchant for social criticism and her interest in flipping expectations made her songwriting stand out. [ Read: The transcendence of Dolly Parton ] Dolly Parton at her theme park, Dollywood, in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee (Ron Davis / Getty) She left Wagoner behind in 1974 to court an audience that transcended country music. Her songs sparkled with fun production touches, clever lyrical twists, and melodies that seemed at once as winding as a lazy river and as smartly constructed as good Levi’s. For 1980’s “9 to 5,” the sound of her fingernail clicks did as much work as the lyrics—and the movie the song accompanied—in celebrating the hustle of women at work. “Jolene,” her enduring ballad of jealousy, built itself around a chorus so plaintive that it seemed surely scraped from a harrowing chapter of Parton’s own life—but she was quick, in interviews, to say that the song’s story was more or less fiction. As she settled into icon status, she seemed to revel in the franchisability of her image: Dolly Parton was an idea that everyone could benefit from. She founded a theme park in her home state, selling a blend of rustic realness and fun kitsch. She only ever seemed tickled that Whitney Houston’s cover of “I Will Always Love You” eclipsed Parton’s original in eminence. She made childhood literacy the central focus of her philanthropic efforts—another subversion of the “dumb blonde” image (and one that channeled her upbringing by a father who couldn’t read). In recent years, Parton’s persona has come to take on political significance. She was, as my colleague David Graham has written, the rare public figure who seemed beloved by both red and blue America . She maintained that…

items.title: ICE Has Quietly Changed Its Deadly-Force Rule
items.description: I CE quietly enacted new rules this month that will keep officers involved in deadly-force incidents—such as firing a gun and using a choke hold—off the streets until the completion of an investigation. Previously, these officers were able to return to their regular job in as few as three days. Now they must remain on desk duty until they are cleared by investigators, according to two senior ICE officials with knowledge of the change, who spoke with me on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to discuss agency matters with reporters. Under the old rules, ICE supervisors could lengthen an officer’s period of leave, but such an extension was often viewed internally as signaling a lack of confidence in the officer and their version of events. At ICE and other law-enforcement agencies, officers are typically eager to return to full patrol duties as quickly as possible, and not remain in limbo as an investigation plays out. The change, which has not been publicly announced, means that officers who fire their guns, choke someone, or use some other form of deadly force—even if no one is killed—will potentially be limited to performing administrative duties for much longer periods. Acting ICE Director David Venturella and other senior ICE leaders ordered the change late last month, the two senior officials said. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to my questions about why the policy change was made or how many such incidents have occurred since President Trump returned to office. ICE officers have shot at least 16 people since last January, four of them fatally, according to public records. Last month, there were two fatal shootings during traffic stops: On July 7, ICE officers in Texas killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old contractor from Mexico, and six days later, an officer in Maine fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant. DHS said the officers fired in self-defense, but the incidents are under federal investigation. Veteran ICE officials have worried for months about the competence of the thousands of new recruits who were added during a hiring binge last fall, many of whom were rushed onto the streets after taking a fast-track training course. The ICE officer in Maine, David Brouillette, was a new hire, and his relatives told reporters he had a history of mental-health issues and violent behavior that should have disqualified him from getting a badge and gun. [ Read: The secretary of homeland ] Violent confrontations during traffic stops particularly concern ICE leaders; the agency has not typically had so many officers pulling over vehicles and attempting to arrest people who are in cars. After the shootings last month, ICE and DHS pledged to expedite the deployment of body-worn cameras for ICE officers. Although most of the cameras have been delivered, the officials told me that they don’t know when all of ICE’s roughly 15,000 deportation officers will be wearing them. After the killing in Maine, Venturella and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin halted the use of nonemergency traffic stops—but Trump reversed the directive when immigration hard-liners said it made the White House look weak. The president has said that ICE officers “make mistakes sometimes” and can be “too rough,” but they’re doing a “GREAT job.” A rrests by ICE totaled nearly 50,000 in July, the highest level in a single month since Trump returned to office, the officials told me. The agency is no longer using a city-by-city approach to surge arrests, as it did last year under then–Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem , and this has led to fewer clashes with protesters. But officers remain under pressure to maximize arrests and deportations, and new videos continue to emerge showing officers tackling immigrants and pointing guns at people who are filming them or are allegedly disobeying their orders. ICE leaders say they’re looking for ways to reduce the use…

items.title: The Transcendence of Dolly Parton
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Dolly Parton transcended. It almost didn’t matter what: class, gender, region, musical genre, partisanship. She transcended boundaries in all of them. During an era when politicians act like pop stars, pop stars are expected to engage in politics, and politics divide fiercely, Parton was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection. Her death today, at 80, leaves an absence that no contemporary cultural figure could dream of filling. Parton’s origin story was, in the most literal sense, a rags-to-riches tale. She was born in a one-room cabin in the Appalachian Mountains of East Tennessee, one of 12 children of an illiterate sharecropper father. She memorialized her impoverished childhood in “Coat of Many Colors,” which tells of how her mother sewed a jacket from rags. When she wears it to school, “with patches on my britches / and holes in both my shoes,” her classmates mock and laugh at her. Rather than a hard-luck story, this is a triumph. Parton gets the last laugh: “But they didn’t understand it and I tried to make them see / That one is only poor only if they choose to be.” The song showcases one of the keys to Parton’s success: the ability to bare her soul while keeping a sense of humor and a smile. Her rise to fame began when she was hired by the rhinestone-adorned country singer Porter Wagoner as a “girl singer” in his act. Parton quickly demonstrated that she had more than an attractive face and voice, writing a string of successful songs, such as “Jolene” and “My Tennessee Mountain Home.” One indication of her songwriting talent was that her most famous song was a bigger hit for another singer. Parton had initially hoped that Elvis Presley would record “I Will Always Love You,” but she refused his manager’s demand to give Presley songwriting credit, and she cut the song herself. It topped the country charts twice, but after Whitney Houston rerecorded the song for The Bodyguard ’s soundtrack in 1992, it was a No. 1 pop hit for weeks. The country singers and collaborators Porter Wagoner and Dolly Parton pose for a portrait with their backup band, the Wagonmasters, circa 1968. Wagoner is wearing a Nudie Suit designed by Nudie Cohn of Nudie’s Rodeo Tailors. (Michael Ochs Archives / Getty) Today, little separation exists between country music and the mainstream, but the genre garnered much less respect when Parton’s career began. She helped tear down old prejudices in an era when many music listeners might have professed to like “anything other than country.” Her success helped pave a path for later crossover stars such as Shania Twain and Taylor Swift. She pursued her own genre experimentation, too, collaborating with a range of artists. When she was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, she protested that she wasn’t a rock musician and tried to withdraw from consideration. When the hall refused, she announced with appealing humility that she would earn the honor by making a rock album—her 49th and final—with guests including Joan Jett, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney. Parton always maintained her connection to rural southern music. Few country stars could claim a more authentic origin. She kept her down-home accent and platinum-bouffant hairstyle, and she spoke openly about her abiding Christian faith. These traits may have allowed her to take stands that might otherwise have been controversial. (She also avoided electoral politics, and declined Presidential Medals of Freedom from both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.) Like her predecessor Loretta Lynn, she cultivated a no-nonsense strain of feminism in her lyrics. In 1980, she starred alongside the outspoken liberals Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the movie 9 to 5 , a workplace comedy in which three women conspire to get eve…

items.title: Dolly Parton: Photos From an Extraordinary Life and Career
items.description: Paul Natkin / Getty Dolly Parton performs at the Mill Run Theater in Niles, Illinois, on August 29, 1977. Michael Ochs Archives / Getty Dolly Parton and her collaborator Porter Wagoner perform onstage, circa 1967. items.title: More American Families Are Refusing Vaccines
items.description: As millions of children around the country start another school year, they’ll be confronting new classes, new teachers, and, inevitably, a new slate of germs. And this fall, they’ll be more vulnerable to infectious disease than children have been in decades. Earlier this month, President Trump signed yet another executive order insisting that the United States shrink its schedule of recommended vaccines—federal guidance that currently guards Americans against 17 diseases with safe, effective shots. He also demanded that the U.S. split the MMR vaccine into three separate courses for measles, mumps, and rubella, without citing solid scientific evidence or acknowledging the infeasibility of such a system. (Scholars have already questioned whether the order has legal power.) Days later, the CDC released new data showing that, under Trump, the nationwide vaccine-exemption rate among kindergartners has reached a record high. The new exemption rate of 4.2 percent is a relatively modest bump, up from the previous school year’s 3.6. The national numbers, though, paper over widening gaps among states. Roughly 98 to 99 percent of West Virginia kindergartners, for instance, are still getting routine shots. Meanwhile, in Idaho, the percentage of kindergartners who are up-to-date on vaccines that guard against diseases such as polio, chickenpox, and measles has tumbled to about 75 percent—well below the estimated thresholds for reliably staving off such outbreaks. These numbers reflect what Thomas Patterson, the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Idaho chapter, has been seeing and hearing in the hospitals and clinics where he works: more families expressing skepticism, more families refusing or delaying shots, and more families opting out of his care after he reveals that he supports all of the vaccines that the AAP recommends. (The professional society has sued Trump’s Department of Health and Human Services over its attempts to pare down vaccine recommendations.) Idaho also bans employers, schools, and day cares from requiring medical interventions, including vaccines. Its vaccine-exemption rate is now 17.5 percent , the highest in the nation. National polls show that the majority of Americans still think vaccines work well to prevent disease, and that at least two-thirds support requiring vaccines in schools. Those sentiments remain especially common in Democratic strongholds. Jennifer Shu, a pediatrician in Atlanta, told me that in the past year and a half, she and her colleagues have been flooded with calls from families who are worried that the vaccines they want for their children could soon be taken away. In response to a request for comment, Kush Desai, a White House spokesperson, told me in an email, “None of the Trump administration’s actions undermine access to or insurance coverage of any vaccine—they instead create an environment that fosters parents making informed decisions together with physicians and public health officials who are supposed to guide and support, not force, crucial vaccinations to ultimately ensure that American children do not suffer from serious vaccine preventable infections.” (HHS did not respond to a request for comment.) At the same time, surveys show that national confidence in vaccine safety has eroded, especially among Republicans, who are also far less likely to support school requirements for shots. Since the start of the coronavirus pandemic, the partisan split around vaccine attitudes has been widening. The second Trump administration has exacerbated those tensions, pediatricians around the country told me—and top health officials’ inaccurate portrayals of vaccine side effects seem to have emboldened more people to push back against standard medical advice. Elizabeth Hawse, a pediatrician in Lexington, Kentucky, told me that many of her patients have begun asking whether she’s aware of any new research to indicate that vaccines need to be newly restricted. Those questions tend to…

items.title: The Latest Empty Threat Against Iran
items.description: N o sooner had Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the latest tool for achieving what he said would be the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran than he revealed the reason he was reluctant to use it. Secondary sanctions—penalties on countries, individuals, or entities that do business with Iran—are ready to go, Bessent announced to reporters in the Treasury’s ornate Cash Room yesterday. But he went out of his way not to name the chief offenders that help Tehran: China and Russia. So, Bessent was asked, why threaten rather than just do it, particularly after President Trump last week warned of economic warfare “on an unprecedented scale” if Iran doesn’t surrender to U.S. demands? “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded, explaining that the administration is offering a bureaucratic grace period before the hammer falls. Secondary sanctions, he insisted, “are a very powerful tool.” Which is true. But the administration has repeatedly offered vivid explanations of what its powerful weapons can do, be they military or financial, and then declined to use them. Remember when Trump threatened to erase Iran as a civilization ? The warnings may be intended to intimidate, but the lack of follow-through instead exposes just how narrow the administration’s options in Iran have become. The possibilities for ending the war have been steadily closed off. The list of useful military targets is diminishing, and munitions stockpiles are perilously depleted , while the tools that were supposed to do what missiles could not—sanctions, blockades, financial pressure—have failed to produce the Iranian capitulation Washington promised. Iran has absorbed enormous damage, both military and economic, without surrendering its capacity to fight. And the countries that matter most to the financial-pressure campaign, including China and Russia, have shown little inclination to help Washington finish the job. S oon after Trump took office last year, he announced that he was “restoring maximum pressure” on Iran, directing his administration to tighten sanctions and drive down Iranian oil exports. Eighteen months later, Bessent is promising what he describes as the “toughest sanctions in history.” Maximum pressure, it appears, has a sequel, much as Trump’s contention last June that Iran’s nuclear facilities had been obliterated was followed in February by a war to destroy Iran’s nuclear capabilities. Trump, in a Truth Social post last week, hinted at what that sequel to maximum pressure would look like. “ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote, before listing oil smuggling, financial swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, and front companies that “all” need to stop “NOW.” It was the kind of warning designed to make the entire global financial system sit up straight. Then Bessent arrived at the Cash Room making equally stark threats, before pointing to a major reason why he shouldn’t follow through, assuming countries don’t voluntarily comply. That leaves the administration in an uncomfortable position. The war has lasted far longer than Trump suggested it would, and its economic consequences are now a central issue in the midterm elections. Sanctions have inflicted economic pain on Iran for years without producing the result Washington wants. Yet China continues to buy Iranian oil, while Russia and other oil-producing countries stand to benefit from the drain of prolonged U.S. military action in Iran and from disruptions to energy exported from the Persian Gulf. “No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” Bessent said when asked about China specifically. But Beijing and Moscow might not comply with Bessent’s demands. The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in…

items.title: Portrait of the Artist as a Movie Star
items.description: A few months ago, I traveled to a new city in a foreign country to talk about a book I’d written. At lunch one day, my host told me about a publishing acquaintance of hers who’d hosted the writer Rachel Cusk some years back, only to find herself seemingly replicated later, in cartoonish and (she felt) unflattering form, within one of the books in Cusk’s Outline trilogy. The woman was apparently devastated; although Cusk had withheld some details, the portrait, according to its presumptive subject, was specific and precise enough that anyone who knew her and read the book would immediately recognize the person being portrayed. “Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is indefensible,” Janet Malcolm wrote in her classic 1990 book, The Journalist and the Murderer , about a nonfiction writer who used ethically questionable means to get close to a subject. Does the same theory hold true for autofiction? The license that art allows is generous, which Cusk has learned to make use of. On the occasions when she’s written openly autobiographical works, she’s been pilloried, or even sued: Her 2001 book about motherhood, A Life’s Work , was lambasted in the British press for its frank portrait of maternal self-abnegation, and her 2009 book The Last Supper sparked a libel lawsuit from a man who took issue with her depiction of him. (The publisher settled the suit and printed a revised version of the book.) But it was Cusk’s 2012 memoir about her divorce, Aftermath , and the excoriation she received for its exposure of supposed private family matters, that seemed to bring her to a breaking point. “Without wishing to sound melodramatic, it was creative death after Aftermath ,” she told The Guardian two years after publication. “That was the end. I was heading into total silence—an interesting place to find yourself when you are quite developed as an artist.” [ Read: The uncoupling ] Instead of retreating, she turned that silence into its own ingenious form. Outline , published in 2014, is about a writer named Faye who’s traveling to Greece to teach creative writing, and its conceit is that Faye is an almost entirely passive vehicle for other people’s stories, which different characters spill out to her with unguarded enthusiasm. The book and two following installments, Transit and Kudos , were categorized as novels, which offered more protection than Cusk had previously been allowed. Still, Cusk made clear that what she was really interested in as a writer was truth—the resonance of pure reality. “I’m certain autobiography is increasingly the only form in all the arts,” she said in that same Guardian interview, which is an unusual thing to declare on a promotional tour for a work of ostensible fiction. Life of M , Cusk’s newest book, takes autofiction’s familiar dance of authorial ambiguity and shakes it into something odd and unsettling. “A little while ago I told the actor M that I was thinking of writing her autobiography,” it begins. M, as has been widely reported, is believed to be either based on or inspired by the actor Natalie Portman, who has praised Cusk’s writing and featured it in her book club. Both women live in Paris, where Life of M seems to be set. M is described as having first become famous as a child, and two of her roles—playing a ballerina and a performer who survives a school shooting—seem easily recognizable as Portman’s roles in Black Swan and Vox Lux . M, like Portman, is an avid reader, a mother, and a star of such renown that the world bends itself to accommodate her. When the narrator proposes writing about M to her, the actor initially likes the idea, asking wryly, “Would you just make it up?” For most of the book, like M, we’re left to wonder what the answer to that question is. Cusk has long blown up form and genre in her attempts to capture the authenticity of female experience. Her pursuit is relentless and uncompromising; it’s also bou…

items.title: The Qataris Gave Trump an Airplane. He Crippled Their Country in Return.
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. D onald Trump really wanted the plane. The Qataris had flown the $400 million Boeing 747 to West Palm Beach just after he returned to the White House so he could run his hands over the soft leather chairs and inspect the sycamore- and wacapou-wood veneers. A sales brochure had described the en-suite master bathroom, with its mother-of-pearl inlays, as “almost a piece of art.” The plane was a flying palace fit for a Persian Gulf monarch, or an American president who would like to live like one. But its operating costs—about $25,000 per flight hour—were steep even for the Qatari royal family. The government had been trying to sell it for five years. The Qataris knew Trump would want the plane. They understood the man, and his taste. It sat in the same aesthetic register as the comparatively puny “Trump Force One,” the gold-heavy Boeing 757 that he had flown as a private citizen. They also knew that Trump didn’t like the aging, baby-blue 747s that had been carrying presidents since 1990. He’d ordered two new planes from Boeing in 2018, but they were years behind schedule. Trump wanted the 11-bathroom Qatari plane, repainted in a red-white-and-blue color scheme. And he wanted it in time for a flyover on America’s 250th birthday. This was an absurd demand. Air Force One is meant to serve as an airborne military command post. The Qatari jet would have to be stripped to the studs and retrofitted with encrypted-communications equipment, as well as special material to shield it against the radiological blast of a nuclear weapon, and a variety of countermeasures to foil missiles and rockets. It had taken a Parisian design firm four years to complete the plane’s interiors. It could take American engineers at least that long to convert the jet into a flying fortress. But these were details to be worked out later. Or not. The Qataris drew up the paperwork for a government-to-government sale. But they should have seen Trump’s next move coming. People close to Trump—it’s still not clear who—suggested to the Qataris that instead of selling the plane, they could donate it to the United States. A gift. A freebie from “friends” who had already put hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s son-in-law’s private-equity firm and bought a debt-laden Manhattan hotel belonging to Steve Witkoff, his Middle East special envoy, for $623 million. That’s to say nothing of the $8 billion they’d spent to build the Americans an air base—the biggest U.S. military base in the Middle East—or their plans to spend $10 billion more to enhance and maintain it. What was another $400 million, for a plane that the president so dearly loved? Even some Qatari leaders were surprised by the president’s gall. But they did what they’ve always done when an American official has asked them for something dubious—politically, ethically, or even legally. They said yes. It’s not easy to buy good press, though the Qataris have tried. But it also takes real effort to generate the kind of bad press the plane brought to a country whose name many Americans probably can’t pronounce correctly (it’s kah -tar). The bipartisan outrage in Washington was incandescent. The plane was a flying emolument, an obvious constitutional violation. “Only a FOOL would not accept this gift on behalf of our Country,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. But what Trump couldn’t, or wouldn’t, see is that only a fool would view the plane as anything other than a massive bribe, especially given that Trump said publicly that he planned to have it transferred to his presidential library once he leaves office. [ Paul Rosenzweig: American corruption ] Even by the immoderate standards of the Persian Gulf, it’s quite a move to give a world leader a free airplane. But the Qataris had already given one to the president of Turkey, and they saw that bad press dissipates. And as the Qataris know, probably better than anyone, the price wit…

items.title: Party in the (Downwardly Mobile) U.S.A.
items.description: With every passing year, Miley Cyrus’s 2009 single “Party in the U.S.A.” comes to feel more like an artifact of an empire before its fall. When the Disney Channel star sang about hopping off the plane at LAX with a dream and a cardigan—on the way to turn her country-girl ambitions of fame into Hollywood reality—she projected an image of a nation that still believed in its own myths, trusted its power centers, and grooved together to the same songs. The guitars fizzed like a fresh can of Coke, and Cyrus advertised to the world’s strivers that making it in America is a breeze. Released less than a year after the 2008 financial crash, “Party in the U.S.A.” was part of a crop of songs that have, in recent years, been labeled “recession pop.” It’s an affectionate term for happy, uncomplicated anthems—think Katy Perry’s “Teenage Dream” or the Black Eyed Peas’ “I Gotta Feeling”—that once distracted from headlines about bailouts and foreclosures. The optimism of those songs now seems rarer in American life, but over the past few years, TikTok pundits and media commentators have theorized that a new wave of recession pop might come “back” to suit the economic weirdness of the mid-2020s. [ Read: Is this the worst-ever era of American pop culture? ] I’ve never really bought that argument, for a few reasons. Perky pop largely faded from the charts in the mid-2010s not because of the national mood but because of changes in how people listen: Streaming eroded the top-down distribution channels, such as radio and network TV, that loved to broadcast sugary, universally appealing sing-alongs. More audience-segmented styles—country, hip-hop, confessional bedroom songwriters—now rule the charts. So-called pure pop has become a subculture , almost akin to indie rock. And what’s been happening lately in that subculture is more interesting than a mere revival of carefree times. This summer has served up a slate of great party songs that are full of twisted nostalgia and tarnished glamour. Pop is dancing in the ruins of the American dream—or at least in the ruins of the traditional record business. “Party in the U.S.A.” came to mind while I was listening to “ Ain’t in LA ,” a tasty new single by the rising star Adéla. She is a 22-year-old Slovakian musician who learned English by watching Hannah Montana , and the song is an obvious Cyrus homage. It revisits the trap-pop sound of Cyrus’s 2013 hit “We Can’t Stop” and features that song’s deep-voiced rapper, Theron Thomas. The breezy, yelled chorus seems designed to, as Cyrus put it in ’09, make the butterflies fly away. But the track has a naggingly wistful undercurrent—and its lyrics flip “Party in the U.S.A.” on its head. The verses describe the yearnings of a young girl with Madonna and Destiny’s Child posters pinned to her wall. She wants to be a star—but watching American media taught her that “her dreams don’t live at home.” Then the chorus booms a corrective: “It’s all a lie / The baddest bitches ain’t in LA.” In the music video, Adéla balls out in stereotypical ways—twerking, joyriding, writhing on top of a pile of gold trophies—in her hometown of Bratislava, alongside kid dancers in Slovakian folk garb. She has a message for “girls in them unknown cities”: It’s hot to stay put. Adéla would know. As a teenager, she traveled to Hollywood in hope of a big break on the 2023 reality show The Debut: Dream Academy . A co-production of Geffen Records and the Korean firm Hybe, the series recruited young women from around the world to audition to be part of a girl group subjected to the rigorous management style of K-pop. A trained ballerina with a fierce pout, Adéla performed strongly—but after she was criticized for not perfectly gelling with the other performers, she became one of the first girls cut from the running. Dream Academy represented the response of the U.S.’s faltering star-making machine to international competition. Over the past decade or so, K-pop has become the premiere global source…

items.title: Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
items.description: Last Tuesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei hosted a wake for his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Among the thousands who thronged Tehran’s biggest mosque were the country’s most prominent political figures and several of the elder Khamenei’s sons. One person was notably absent: Mojtaba, the event’s official host. Almost six months since his anointment, Iran’s supreme leader has been entirely obscured from the public eye. Not a single contemporaneous picture, video, or audio recording of him has been released. Many of the country’s top political leaders admit that they haven’t seen him—among them Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister and a member of the National Security Council. IranWire , a London-based opposition outlet, reports that not a single cabinet member has met with Mojtaba since he became supreme leader. Not even Mojtaba’s close friends and relatives have seen him. Fewer than five people have met with Mojtaba since his ascent to power, Mohammad Hossein Khoshvaght, a former official and a relative of Mojataba’s told me, “due to security precautions.” The rationale is not implausible. Mojtaba would be a likely target for an Israeli or U.S. air strike, such as the one that killed his father. Direct communication from him could supply Iran’s enemies with clues to his whereabouts. He is also said to have sustained injuries in the February strike on his family that have made public speeches and appearances difficult. [ Graeme Wood: ‘The most dangerous man in the world’ ] But the totality of Mojtaba’s invisibility and a recent decline in statements from his office have set Tehran abuzz with new rumors of his death. Some sources inside and close to the government speculated to me that Mojtaba recently died from the injuries that he had sustained in February. And irrespective of his actual status, the uncertainty might have major implications for Iran. “I believe Mojtaba has either passed away or is brain-dead,” a staffer at a government institution in Tehran told me, citing the tailing off of even indirect communication from the leader to the outside world. At least two other government officials told me the same. One said that he believed Mojtaba died or became brain-dead earlier this month. Two sources in the Iranian government recently told IranWire that word had spread among those at the “highest level of the regime” that Mojtaba was doing very poorly and could die at any moment. About two weeks ago, a public appeal went out on a domestic messaging service, asking Iranians to pray for Mojtaba’s health and sacrifice sheep to bless him, as is customary in Islam. Mojtaba’s life was “under threat,” and some “clerics” had warned that he might be killed, the appeal said. Since he was appointed, Mojtaba has ruled by decrees disseminated by his office. Iran’s supreme leader is a religious authority in addition to being the head of state, and on July 27, Mojtaba’s office published a list of his answers to practical questions posed by the devout. One correspondent had requested guidance on eating with bleeding gums, because blood is haram — forbidden—in Islam. Any food contaminated with blood, including from one’s own gums, must be thrown out, Mojtaba ruled. If his office is to be believed, then the leader was well enough to ponder Islamic law and issue relevant rulings as recently as a month ago. The office’s most recent statement came on August 9 and reported that Mojtaba had met with President Masoud Pezeshkian. It didn’t say when the meeting had taken place but noted that it was on the occasion of the president’s third year in office, which puts it on or after July 28. Pezeshkian confirmed to the Iranian media that he spent seven hours with Mojtaba discussing the war and the country’s beleaguered economy. (According to Khoshvaght, Pezeshkian was taken to that meeting “without knowing where it was,” which suggests that he was transported blindfolded, mafia-style.) Also on August 9, Mojtaba issued a…

items.title: The Jews Who Voted for Hitler
items.description: On the evening of February 5, 1930, the art and theater critic Paul Fechter took the podium before the League of Nationalist German Jews, in Berlin, to discuss purported Jewish control of the press and the arts in the country. “When Dr. Max Naumann invited me to give a lecture in your circle, I rather impulsively said yes,” Fechter began. “When he then told me the topic he wanted me to address, my immediate reaction was: Good grief ! One could not have found a better topic for making oneself thoroughly unpopular and for antagonizing everyone in the room.” For too long, Fechter said, people had been too “shy, fearful, cautious” to speak openly about the Jews. Fechter, an editor at the conservative newspaper Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung , was pulling no punches. The popular Jewish humorist Kurt Tucholsky, Fechter said, had insulted the German people with his recent book, Deutschland, Deutschland über alles , an acid satire about the army, the police, the civil service, the national anthem, even Sekt , a popular sparkling wine. “A large portion of the literary and art worlds are in Jewish hands,” Fechter continued. “The theaters, the major publishing houses, the major art dealers are all at least partially under Jewish control.” Jewish art dealers, Fechter said, filled their galleries with works by “Manet and Monet and Renoir and Gauguin and Picasso and Cezanne”—French Impressionists and Modernists, in other words, rather than traditional German painters. The Antigermanismus among Jews, Fechter declared, was “far more robust” than the Antisemitismus among right-wing German nationalists. Naumann, the founder of the league, published the Fechter tirade in his monthly publication , The Nationalist German Jew , circulated to his group’s 7,000 members, mostly middle-class professionals in more than 20 chapters around the country. Naumann himself was a Berlin-based Jewish attorney who was decidedly antidemocratic, belligerently nationalistic, and unapologetically critical of other Jews. He blamed Ostjuden —the “Eastern Jews” fleeing pogroms in Russia, Romania, Austria, Hungary, Poland, and elsewhere—for flooding the country with unwanted immigrants. He felt pity but no solidarity. “It is the same pity we feel when there is talk of the Turks massacring Armenians or of lynch mobs targeting black people in America,” Naumann wrote—an abstract pity without emotional connection. In his league’s founding treatise, On Nationalist German Jews , published in 1920, Naumann had compared Zionists, those seeking a Jewish homeland in Palestine, to Nazis, whose political movement had just been founded. “Both groups, the fanatics of Zion and the knights of the swastika, are basically the same in that they have turned a question of ancestry into a question of nationality,” Naumann argued. Naumann defended his German and Jewish identities in equal measure, a stance reflected in the term nationaldeutscher Jude —a blood-and-soil German Jew. [ Timothy W. Ryback: How Hitler dismantled a democracy in 53 days ] Naumann drifted right with the rest of German politics in the early 1930s, first abiding and then supporting the extremist, right-wing, rabidly anti-Semitic positions of Adolf Hitler. It is impossible to imagine a more tragically misplaced political calculation than Naumann’s embrace of national socialism. Though the Hitler Juden —or Nazi Jews, as Naumann’s adherents came to be known—represented less than 2 percent of Germany’s half-million Jews, they provide a cautionary tale of members of a minority within a minority who cast their lot with a political leader who openly despised them. Naumann was born in 1875 into a middle-class family—bankers, landowners, cloth merchants—in an era of unprecedented opportunity for German Jews. They had recently gained the right to vote. They could run for office. They enjoyed equal protection under the law. Professions formerly restricted were now open—law, medicine, academia. Naumann studied jurisprudence at the Fried…

items.title: Darline Graham Is Not Her Brother
items.description: It’s something that happens so often in politics that there’s a name for it: widow’s succession. Dozens of times over the past century, women have filled a seat previously occupied by their late husband, and some have gone on to serve a long career. What has never happened in Congress before is what Darline Graham is doing: a sister’s succession. Less than 48 hours after Senator Lindsey Graham died suddenly from heart issues last month, South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s younger sister to complete the remaining six months of his term. Soon after that, Darline Graham announced that she would also run for a full six-year term, a bid that came at President Trump’s request. In the solidly red state, her biggest hurdle is likely to come in a primary runoff today. She is running in part on the legacy of her brother—but also in ways that bear no resemblance to the way he approached the job. Where he was chatty and seemed to love campaigning, she is reserved and describes the campaign as “brutal.” Where he was the ultimate Washington insider who served in Congress for more than 31 years, she is running as a populist outsider who previously worked with the disabled and visually impaired. And where he was one of his party’s most prominent and outspoken foreign-policy hawks until the day he died, she has conceded to having no experience and not much interest in such matters. “I’m not that informed on national security,” she said during a debate last week, a blunder that has become a focal point in the final days of an abbreviated campaign. The president came to her defense, praising her for being honest. He has invested significant time and political capital in attempting to give her a late boost in a closer-than-expected primary race. Her late brother comes up during almost every public event she holds—“I knew I could not sit on the sidelines. That’s not how Lindsey and I were raised,” she’s said—and campaign mailers tout that she is “Prepared to Carry on Lindsey’s Legacy.” She tells voters that “no one can ever fill his shoes” but that she will earn his seat. “I don’t just expect it to be handed to me,” she said earlier this month after casting her ballot in the special primary election. [ Read: An unsettling glimpse into the GOP’s future ] Her Republican primary opponent is Ralph Norman, a congressman since 2017 who earlier this summer lost his bid for governor. He has also referenced Lindsey Graham’s pull on the race. “Nobody’s entitled by birthright to this office,” Norman said before the debate last week. “You’ve got to earn it.” He tried to put the situation into college-football terms during an interview with the Associated Press, telling voters to imagine presenting the head coach at Clemson University with a top quarterback prospect who has just this qualification: They’re kin to Tom Brady. “Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here,” Norman said. Although Graham has a famous last name and the president’s endorsement, Norman and his supporters believe that he can win today. Their message: Darline Graham is not Lindsey Graham. A PAC supporting Norman recently began running an ad that asks, “What if Darline Graham had any other last name?” It’s the last name that has gotten her here—the reason she was appointed interim senator. But in the final stretch of the race, it is complicating her campaign, which has become the latest test of the power of Trump’s endorsement. Although the president has often played kingmaker in Republican primaries over the past decade, that influence has significantly weakened: 10 of his picks have failed to advance this year, many of them in the past few weeks. The congressional candidates Cory Mills and Catalina Lauf both lost in Florida last week. Two of his picks in races for governor—Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming and Mike Lindell in Minnesota—lost by double digits. If Graham loses, it will signal a limit to Trump’s ability to direct the MAGA base in one of the most MAGA states.…

items.title: Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers. Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research. The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers. They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.” Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump. The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.” This was no one-off. Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.” This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell. During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians. Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials. Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism. On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism ), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities. Data centers’ political arc has been different. Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits. But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism— politicians changed their view as well . Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison , who are major boosters of and players in the industry. Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them. Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor . Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is. He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside. But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are. Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him. Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less . Though his stump speeches dragged on…

items.title: Logging In Was Never Supposed to Be This Complicated
items.description: One afternoon earlier this month, I pulled up to the rec center and realized that I had a problem. It was not the three boisterous tweens in the back seat who were clamoring to be set loose in the basketball gym. It was my parking app. I had somehow gotten logged out of Passport Parking, which has become the only way to pay for a spot in much of my town, and it was demanding a four-digit PIN to let me back in. My first guess drew a warning message in red letters: “Invalid PIN. PIN cannot contain 4 sequential numbers, 2 repeated digits, or the last 4 digits of your phone number.” I searched my trusty password manager, which was supposed to spare me these predicaments, but it came up empty. By that point, the kids had run ahead and piled themselves against the gym door, waiting for me to let them in. Lately, the process of accessing apps and websites has grown dizzying. “I’m in password hell,” a colleague confided to me recently. “Every login attempt is playing the lottery.” The problem is not just the sheer number of digital accounts, all of which require their own password, ideally unique and unguessable (which usually also means un-memorizable). It’s the pileup of solutions to that problem: all of the different layers of software offering to remember your passwords, the six-digit codes sent to your phone, the authenticator apps, the passkeys. Browsers and operating systems compete with third-party password managers to generate, store, and autofill your credentials. Most of my logins live in 1Password, but others are stored in Apple’s Passwords app (usually by accident), and still others were created via “single sign-on” features such as those offered by Google and Facebook. I vaguely recall certain apps—Facebook is one—prompting me many years ago to copy down a set of “login recovery codes” that would become extremely important should I ever get locked out of my account. Whatever device I stored them on was probably wiped and sold long ago. Logins have always been a hassle. In the 1990s, forgetting your password sometimes meant mailing a po stcard to your service provider and waiting a week or two for it to mail you a new password. In the early 2010s, hackers learned to steal massive troves of logins and then reuse them on other services to steal people’s identities. Things spiraled from there; services started requiring unique, complex passwords with arbitrary requirements. These days, the user experience of logging in is “probably worse than ever,” Troy Hunt, a cybersecurity expert who runs the website Have I Been Pwned, told me. “There’s just no consistency.” Password managers promised a way out, but they often don’t work as seamlessly as you might hope. I click to autofill my password somewhere, and a 1Password authorization appears, only for an iCloud Keychain authorization to pop up directly over it, preventing me from clicking on the 1Password one. When I manually enter a login I thought I remembered, my browser prompts me to remember it; only after I hit “Save” (pro tip: Do not do this) does the website inform me that the password was not recognized. Even when you log in successfully, there’s the tedious dance of waiting for a six-digit authorization code to appear on your phone or in your email, which defeats the concept of a single password for everything. And if you’re somewhere without cell service or you’re sharing a login with someone who isn’t around, you might just be out of luck. All of these steps serve a purpose. At least in theory, each added layer helps prevent hacks and breaches. Erring on the side of safety is worth an amount of inconvenience. At the same time, extra steps can introduce security problems of their own. Last year, Hunt fell for a clever phishing scheme when he clicked a link to log in to his newsletter service. His password manager failed to autofill his information, which should have alerted him that something was wrong, he said. But like the rest of us, he was so used to things not work…

items.title: Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.” A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic. Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds. There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses. Questioning colleges is normal. There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost , and is that more than families can pay ? Who gets in , and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium . [ Read: A deal that would end universities’ independence ] On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education , to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself. I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today. The following is a transcript of the episode: Jack Stripling: We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it , they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person. Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and around the country millions of students are getting ready to head back to school, if they’re not already in class. So today, we need to think about education in uncertain times. Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school. In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed. My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t. In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges. But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve. Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions. Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project. The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures. How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year? Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague. And he joins me now to discuss. Let’s get to questions. Jack, welcome to the show. Stripling: Adam Harris, so good to catch up with you. Harris: Absolutely, man. I want to start with this letter that went out to college leaders recently from Education Secretary Linda McMahon that was effectively the administration’s call to action, right? To prod…

items.title: The Atlantic announces Jessica Goldstein as SVP of events
items.description: The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead and produce the magazine’s robust live programs nationwide. She begins with The Atlantic in early September. Jessica has spent her career telling stories through reporting and creating live experiences that resonate far beyond the stage. She spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live cultural programming, including creating the Tiny Desk Contest, NPR’s annual search for new musical talent, and the How I Built This Summit. She most recently led the Skoll Foundation’s global convenings strategy and directed the Skoll World Forum. At The Atlantic , she will work with Evan to lead one of the most influential and long-running events practices in media. The Atlantic convenes dozens of annual in-person and virtual events that reach thousands of people every year, anchored by its flagship event, The Atlantic Festival , which returns to New York City September 17–19, after being held for nearly two decades in Washington, D.C. The Atlantic is also under way with a new 50-state tour, The Atlantic Across America , that has already held events in 10 states, addressing some of the most complex issues of our time. Below is Evan Smith’s announcement to staff: I’m excited to let you know that we’ve hired the amazing Jessica Goldstein as our new senior vice president of events. As the second-in-command on our growing team, she’ll oversee the operations, planning, and execution of our robust public programs, working closely with our sales, marketing, design, and CSG colleagues to grow The Atlanti c’s audience and revenue; shine a great, big light on our brand; and—most crucially—bring our journalists and our journalism to stages from coast to coast through The Atlantic Festival, The Atlantic Across America, The Atlantic Summits, and so much more. Jessica comes to us most recently from the Skoll Foundation, where she was managing director of convenings, leading the organization’s global events strategy and directing the Skoll World Forum, a weeklong gathering of heads of state, social entrepreneurs, and civil-society partners. But it’s her reputation at NPR that really precedes her—and makes her the ideal hire in this moment. As senior director and executive producer of Events & Experiential, she spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live programming, including the Tiny Desk Contest and the How I Built This Summit. Previously she was a senior supervising producer for NPR Music, a senior producer on the science desk, and a producer of audio documentaries known as NPR Radio Expeditions. A native of New York, Jessica is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin at Madison. Jessica believes in the power of storytelling, of sharing ideas and sparking inspiration, which is precisely how we think about our work in the events space. There is no loftier task before us than getting people from divergent backgrounds—great minds who don’t think alike—in a room to listen and talk and continue the conversation after we’re gone. She will bring to bear her decades of experience, her imagination, her creativity, her calm, and her charisma as we expand the ambitious work of the Live team. Press Contacts : Anna Bross and Paul Jackson | press@theatlantic.com
